files, weighted toward the files the user is working on, cut to a token budget. `map --view repo
--max-tokens N` gives the same answer from Verinoda's own graph, without a model and without the network.

### 83.2 Decisions

- A new view of `architecture_map` (`repo_map`), registered in `VIEWS` next to dead, hotspots and
  sides. It is asked for by name and is not one of the default views.
- The graph is the cycles view's file-to-file dependencies (`_file_deps`: calls, imports, uses and
  inherits between files, with type-only and deferred imports, prose files and Python imports that load
  the standard library left out). The weight of an edge is the square root of its references, so one
  file that calls another fifty times does not outweigh everything else.
- PageRank runs by power iteration in the module (damping 0.85, at most 100 rounds, stops once it
  converges). It does not use `networkx.pagerank`, which needs scipy. 90% of the random jump lands on
  the files in play (split among them) and 10% on all files alike, a fixed share so that the focus
  weighs as much on a thousand files as on ten. Without files in play it is plain PageRank. A file
  without dependencies spreads its rank the way the jump does.
- The files in play are the `--target` files, or the git working-tree changes when none are given (the
  same default as the impact view, `--base` included). A `path::Name` target counts as its file; an
  absolute path inside the repository is made relative, and `.`/`..` are resolved. A target that is no
  file of the graph goes to `focus_unresolved` and is not used; as in the impact view, the CLI then exits
  2, and MCP adds a `next_step`. As in Aider, the files in play are left out of the map because the agent
  is already reading them.
- Each file's rank is shared among its outer symbols by the references other files make to each one,
  plus one so that no symbol gets zero. An outer symbol is a class, a method, or a module function: a
  symbol that no function or method holds. A helper nested in a function is left out.
- A signature is the symbol's definition line with its indentation kept, found past any decorators as the
  first line naming the symbol as a whole word, cut at 160 characters, and cited at `file:line` (entries are
  `at` and `text`; the text names the symbol). A symbol whose line is not found (the file changed since the
  scan) is not shown and is counted in `signatures_not_found`, outside `symbols_total`. Data files (json, toml, ini, cfg, yaml, properties, xml),
  whose keys the extractor emits as symbols, are left out.
- Budget: a line is estimated at (characters + 4) // 4 tokens, the newline counted. Symbols are taken in
  score order until the next one would pass `--max-tokens`, so everything shown outranks everything left
  out. The count covers exactly the lines the text output prints for the files, and a test holds it to
  that. The default budget is 1024 tokens (Aider's default). The CLI rejects `--max-tokens` below 1
  (exit 2).
- Status: each file row is `strong_inference`, because the ranking is a heuristic. The signature text is
  the source line at its `at`.
- Text output (`map_text._repo`) prints the map itself. The token budget bounds it, so `--max-lines` does
  not apply unless it is given.
- MCP: `repo` is added to the `map_view` view Literal and to `VIEWS`. `targets` gives the files in play
  (by default the working-tree changes; `focus_source` says which). No new MCP argument was added: the
  MCP call starts at the default budget and lowers it until the map's JSON fits three quarters of the
  response cap (`budget_note` says so), so `cap_response` does not cut files from it and the counts
  describe what is sent. To keep the core menu under 4,500
  characters, the gateway text of node_inspect and relation_trace was shortened ("a symbol's", "between
  symbols") by as much as "|repo" added.

### 83.3 Measured

- examples/orders_app with `--target orders/api.py`: 17 of 17 signatures in 7 of 8 files, about 239 of
  1024 tokens. Order: config.py, repository.py, service.py, pricing.py, then the tests.
- The same with `--max-tokens 40`: 2 signatures (config.py `load_settings`, repository.py
  `OrderRepository`), 27 tokens. The next symbol did not fit.
- Naming api.py as in play raises service.py's rank above its unweighted rank.
- Core MCP menu JSON: 4,499 characters before, 4,498 after.
- Not measured: time and output on a large repository. This build must not scan the whole repository
  more than once, so none was scanned.
- Review round: on the main repository's existing index (879 ranked files, loaded, not rescanned), the
  first weighting (each file in play ten times any other file) left the map almost unchanged by the focus.
  With the fixed 90% share, focusing examples/orders_app/orders/api.py puts its config.py, repository.py,
  service.py and pricing.py first; focusing verinoda/cli.py puts paths.py, store.py, snapshot.py and
  index.py first. The default map's JSON there is about 9,300 characters, so MCP lowers the budget a
  little. A mistyped `--target` now exits 2, `--max-tokens 0` or below is rejected, a stale line that
  merely contains the name (`budget` for `get`) is no longer quoted as the signature, and entries lost
  `symbol`. Each has a test.

### 83.4 Not done

- The ranking is `strong_inference`: it suggests what to read first, not what matters. Graph edges are
  extractions, not verification, and dynamic dispatch, reflection and DI containers are not resolved.
- Only the first line of a signature is shown. A multi-line parameter list is cut at that line.
- Dependents of the files in play rank only through what they use themselves. The impact view lists
  dependents.
- Unlike Aider, identifiers mentioned in the conversation carry no weight. Only files do.
- The token count is an estimate (four characters a token), not a tokenizer's count.
- The budget takes a prefix of the ranking. It does not skip one large line to fit smaller ones after it,
  so it can end a few tokens under the budget.

### 83.5 Tests

- tests/test_repo_map.py (new):
  - ranking order, and each signature equal to its source line;
  - the files in play weighting the rank and left out of the map, and unresolved targets;
  - the budget keeping a prefix, with the token count equal to the rendered lines;
  - text output, the CLI `--json` and text, and MCP `map_view("repo", targets=...)`;
  - nested functions and decorators;
  - the focus outweighing a hub on a 903-file graph;
  - absolute and `..` targets, and an unknown `--target` exiting 2;
  - `--max-tokens 0` and `-3` rejected;
  - MCP lowering the budget under a small cap, with counts equal to what is sent;
  - a moved definition not quoted and counted in `signatures_not_found`.
- tests/test_architecture_map.py: `VIEWS` includes `repo`, and it states its method and limits.
- tests/test_mcp.py (unchanged): passes with the new Literal value and a core menu under 4,500 characters.

## 84. Undocumented decisions (D111, 2026-10-01)

### 84.1 Why

Decision records only help when the choices that shape the code are recorded. Many are never written down:
storage that goes through one module, a library kept behind one file, configuration read in one place. The
code shows such a choice; nothing says it was one, and nothing keeps it. An ADR workflow that starts from what
the code already does lets the user record the choice (with a guard that keeps it) or say it is not one.

### 84.2 Decisions

- A new `decide` subcommand pair, no new MCP tool: `decide undocumented [--decisions-dir DIR] [--json]` lists
  the candidates, `decide dismiss CANDIDATE --reason "..." [--undo]` records the user's dismissal. The core MCP
  profile and its menu are unchanged; the tool count is unchanged.
- The facts come from `decision_brief`'s probes, not new scanners: P1 storage sinks (the guard engine's bound
  connection calls plus `SINK_PATTERNS`, comments and docstrings not read; the probe now also keeps each site's
  needle as `facts["sink_sites"]` so the evidence re-checks; a case-insensitive pattern's needle carries `(?i)`,
  so lowercase SQL re-checks too), P2 environment reads, P3 declared dependencies,
  plus `_Probe.py_imports` (imports from the syntax tree).
- Three candidate kinds, the smallest set the row names ("a single storage path, an exclusive library") plus the
  configuration reader the same probes give for free:
  - `single_storage_path` (`storage:<file>`): every sink line of a kind in one product file; at least two sink
    lines or a database connection;
  - `exclusive_library` (`library:<name>`): a declared runtime Python dependency whose modules (all of them:
    `attrs` is imported as `attr` and as `attrs`) are imported by exactly one product file; the guard's own
    pattern (`^\s*(?:import|from)\s+MODULE\b`) is run on the other product files' code (comments and strings
    removed, from the probe's cached text: no second scan of the repository) and must find none; a
    module that another product file names in a string literal of its code (`importlib.import_module("mod")`,
    a table of module names) gives no candidate;
  - `single_config_reader` (`config:<file>`): every environment read (two variables or more) in one file.
- Each candidate carries the fact (`statically_verified`, `path:line` evidence with the needle each line must
  hold, and the scope counted) and is itself `weak_inference`: that the fact is a decision is a guess. It gives
  the guard spec that would keep it when a guard kind can check it (`only_in sink=db-connection allowed=FILE`,
  `only_in pattern=... allowed=FILE`, the file quoted when its path holds a space; none for other sink kinds,
  whose `sink=` no engine checks), and the
  `decide record` and `decide dismiss` commands with placeholders for the user's own words. Nothing is recorded
  for the user.
- Coverage: a live record (status accepted or proposed, as for the decision reach of a review) or a hand-written
  ADR-like document (`decisions.adr_like_files`) covers a candidate when it names the candidate's file, or
  names the library (distribution or module name) or the database driver (`sqlite3`, `sqlite`) as one: in a
  code span, an import or a fenced block, or on a line with the word library, package, module, driver or
  dependency ("HTTP requests" names no library). A record also covers it when one of its `only_in` guards is
  about the same thing (a `sink=` for a storage path; `calls`/`pattern` naming the driver, the module, or
  `environ`/`getenv`) and allows only a glob that matches the file; edge, layer and public guards and
  `only_in` guards about something else cover nothing. Each covered candidate cites the matching `path:line`
  (for a guard, the guard's own line). Rejected,
  superseded and deprecated records cover nothing.
- Dismissals are local (`.verinoda/dismissed_decisions.json`, format 1, not committed: the directory gets its
  `.gitignore` even when `init` never ran; a byte-order mark is accepted): id, the user's reason,
  date, and the fact as it read then. Only a current candidate can be dismissed; a reason is required; a
  dismissal whose candidate has gone is listed with `current: false`; `--undo` removes one. An unreadable file
  is an error (exit 2), never an empty list.
- Fewer than three product code files give no candidate (one file holding everything is no choice).

### 84.3 Measured

- On Verinoda itself (325 product .py files, no records in the worktree), before the load-by-name rule: 16
  candidates, all `exclusive_library` (numpy, starlette, graspologic-native and 13 tree-sitter grammars). A grep
  of import statements confirmed each "imported by one file" fact (16/16). But the grammars of Go, Rust, Kotlin
  and PHP are also loaded by name through the module tables in `anchors.py` and `index.py`, so "kept behind one
  file" was wrong for 4 of them. The rule added afterwards (another product file names the module in a string
  literal of its code: no candidate) drops those 4, and also starlette, whose name is in
  `decision_brief.SERVER_DEPS` (a conservative miss). A grep for quoted module names gives 11 candidates
  expected: numpy, graspologic-native and 9 grammars. The command was not re-run on the whole repository after
  the rule (the load limits of this build allow one scan). No storage or config candidate: sinks and environment
  reads are spread over many files. The grammars are true facts but one choice in the user's eyes; they are
  dismissed one by one.
- Review round: ten findings, all confirmed and fixed. Lowercase SQL gave evidence that did not re-check (the
  needle lost `re.I`), so the candidate was dropped; any live guard glob (a `no_edge`, an `only_in` about
  subprocess) covered a candidate, citing the first line holding the glob; a distribution with two modules was
  counted per module; ordinary words ("requests", "SQLite") in an ADR covered libraries; a path with a space gave
  a guard `decide record` refused; the dismissal file could be committed (no `.verinoda/.gitignore` without
  `init`) and a BOM made it unreadable; each single-importer library re-listed and re-read the whole repository.
  Re-run on this repository after the fixes (419 product files): the 11 expected candidates (numpy,
  graspologic-native and 9 grammars), 32 s wall time under load (44 s before, as the reviewer measured it);
  most of the remaining time is the probes' own reading of the product files.
- The test project: storage, library and config candidates found; a library imported in two product files, a
  test file's import and a commented import give none.

### 84.4 Not done

- The candidate is a guess (weak_inference); only the fact under it is verified.
- Libraries: Python imports only; a module whose name differs from its distribution and is not in the small
  known list (`PY_MODULES`) is not matched; npm, Go, Cargo and JVM dependencies are not checked. Any string
  literal that equals the module name drops the candidate, even one that does not load it (a list of
  dependency names).
- Storage and environment facts are pattern-based (P1, P2): an ORM or reader the patterns do not know is not
  seen.
- Coverage is text: a record naming the file, or the library as one, covers the candidate whatever it says;
  one describing the choice in other words does not, nor does a plain sentence that names the library without
  a code span, an import or the word library/package/module/driver/dependency on its line. Broad documents (DESIGN.md, ARCHITECTURE.md) are not searched: they name
  nearly every file and would cover everything.
- Related candidates (a family of tree-sitter grammars) are listed and dismissed one by one.
- A run reads every product file (about 30 s on a 419-file project); `decide dismiss` runs the same search to
  check that the id is a current candidate.
- CLI only; not in any MCP profile.

### 84.5 Tests

`tests/test_undocumented.py` (14): the three kinds found on a small project, evidence that re-checks, guard specs
that `decide record` accepts, a two-file library, a test import and a commented import giving none; a library
loaded by name through `importlib` in another file giving none, while a comment naming it still does not; a record
(guard glob) and an ADR (names the library) covering candidates with the cited line; a rejected record covering
nothing; dismissal needing a reason and a current candidate, refusing a second dismissal, showing a dismissal
whose candidate is gone, `--undo`; an unreadable dismissal list is an error; a project under three files gives
nothing; the CLI's JSON and text output and exit 2 on an unknown id; lowercase SQL giving a storage path
whose evidence re-checks; a `no_edge` guard and an `only_in` guard about subprocess covering nothing; a
distribution imported as `attr` in one file and `attrs` in another giving no candidate; "HTTP requests" and
"SQLite" in a sentence covering nothing while `requests` in a code span does; a path with a space giving a guard
`parse_guard` accepts; a dismissal writing `.verinoda/.gitignore` and a BOM-prefixed list reading back. Touched modules' tests: `test_decide.py`,
`test_decide_lifecycle.py`, `test_decide_review3.py`, `test_cli.py`, `test_docs.py`, `test_line_endings.py`.

## 85. Change risk score (D112, 2026-10-01)

### 85.1 Why

`review` already measures a change from several directions: the findings it introduced (with the
introduced/preexisting differential), the public definitions it breaks, the dependents it reaches, the tests that
reach it, a coverage report's uncovered changed lines and what it could not tell. Nothing rolled these up, so two
reviews could not be compared at a glance and a reader had to add the sections up in their head. Greptile and
GitNexus show a single risk figure; ours must show how it was made and must never turn a low number into "safe".

### 85.2 Decisions

- No new command and no new MCP tool: the score is `review`'s `risk` key (`verinoda review --json`, the text
  output, the MCP `change_review` response). The tool count is unchanged; no new argument, so the core menu text
  is unchanged.
- New module `verinoda/risk.py`; it reads only the finished review result (no second analysis, no git call).
- The score is the sum over nine parts of `min(count x weight, cap)`; the caps add up to 100:

  | part | counts | weight | cap |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | findings_strong | introduced findings, statically verified or strong_inference | 10 | 30 |
  | findings_weak | introduced findings, weak_inference | 2 | 6 |
  | api_breaking | `api_changes` breaking (counted before the list cap) | 10 | 20 |
  | api_unknown | `api_changes` unknown | 2 | 4 |
  | dependents | `dependents_total` | 1 | 10 |
  | untested | `tests.no_test_reaches` | 5 | 10 |
  | reach_unknown | `tests.reach_unknown` | 1 | 5 |
  | uncovered_lines | changed lines a coverage report shows no test ran | 1 | 10 |
  | unknowns | the review's `unknown` entries | 1 | 5 |

  A tenth row, `preexisting` (the findings the base had too), is listed with weight 0: the base's findings are
  not the change's risk, but the reader sees they exist. With `findings=all` the preexisting findings sit under
  `concerns` and are still left out of the findings parts (`delta: preexisting`).
- Every part is listed, also at zero, with its value, weight, cap, points and up to three `file:line` locations
  (finding lines, API definitions, dependents, changed definitions, uncovered lines). The block's `evidence_at`
  is their union (at most ten), in the same shape as a review finding (`status`, `finding`, `evidence_at`).
- An input not measured is named in `not_measured` and its part has `value: null` and 0 points, never a zero
  count: uncovered_lines when no coverage report was read (the reason names an unreadable report given with
  `--coverage` apart from no report at all), when the report read measured none of the changed lines (the changed
  files are not in it, or match it ambiguously), or for a planned change; `preexisting` for a planned change (no
  base to compare findings with). Concerns left out by `concerns` and the review's `not_checked` are carried in
  `notes`, as are a per-concern list cut at its cap, a graph older than some files (`graph_stale`: dependents and
  the tests' reach may miss callers), a report that measured only some changed files, uncovered lines read from a
  report older than the file (weak_inference, counted at full weight), and, for a planned change, that the
  findings parts count findings in the targets' current code.
- A review with no changed definition scores 0 with no parts (an unknown raised without a change stays in
  `unknown`, not in the score), so the finding text, `--json`, the MCP response and the record agree.
- Status: `strong_inference` (the weights are a choice). `review` needs a graph (it stops with "run `verinoda
  scan` first" without one), so there is no no-graph case to score. Bands: low (< 20), medium (20-49),
  high (>= 50). The finding text, the summary sentence, the text output and the MCP
  note all say the score is a heuristic and a low one is never "safe".
- MCP: `risk.compact()` keeps the score, band, status and one `value x weight = points` string per part (354
  characters for a change with nothing found); `risk` is in `change_review`'s `keep` list, right after
  `counts`, so the response cap cuts other lists first.
- The review record stored in `analyses` keeps the score, band and status.

### 85.3 Measured

- The compact MCP block: 354 characters (every part at zero); the full block: about 2,300 characters.
- The tests' worktree fixture (one body change reached by one caller and no test): `dependents` 1 and
  `untested` 1 counted, the score equal to the sum of its parts, the same score in `--json`, the summary, the
  text output and the MCP response.
- No second analysis: the score reads the result dict only, so the review's time is unchanged within noise.

Review round: a coverage report that measured none of the changed files was scored as a measured zero; it is now
not measured, with the files it lacks named. The no-graph branch could not happen (`review` loads the graph or
stops) and was removed; a stale graph and a stale or partial report are said in `notes` instead. An unreadable
`--coverage` report no longer tells the user to pass `--coverage`. A review with no changed definition but an
unknown scored 1 while its text said 0; it now scores 0 with no parts everywhere. A planned change's `preexisting`
row is not measured instead of 0, and a note says its findings are the targets' current ones. End-to-end tests now
cover a real coverage report (counted, and read but not covering the changed file), an unreadable one,
`findings=all` with a preexisting finding, a planned change and the no-change unknown.

### 85.4 Not done

- The weights and caps are chosen, not fitted: no labelled set of risky and safe changes exists to fit them.
  The score orders changes by how much the review found, not by how likely they are to break.
- A count says how many, not how bad: one breaking change to a function with forty callers counts like one with
  a single caller (its dependents count separately, up to their cap).
- A `--run-tests` outcome is reported under `tests` and not scored.
- Per-concern lists are capped at 25 before scoring; the findings caps are reached long before that, and a cut is
  said in `notes`.

### 85.5 Tests

`tests/test_risk.py`: the caps add up to 100; a change with nothing found lists every part at zero and never says
safe; the parts, weights and caps add up (a capped part, a zero-weight preexisting row, locations, the compact
form under 600 characters); inputs not measured (no coverage report, an unreadable one, one that covers none of
the changed files, a planned change, a concern left out) are named and not counted; a stale graph, a stale report
and a partial report are noted; a worktree review carries the score in `--json`, the text, the summary and the MCP
response (placed after `counts`); a tree with no changed definition scores 0 and prints no score, also with an
unknown; a real review with a coverage report (counted; read but not covering the changed file; unreadable),
with `findings=all` (the preexisting finding is not scored) and of a planned change. Also run:
`tests/test_review.py`, `tests/test_review_delta.py`, `tests/test_reviewers.py`, `tests/test_decide_review3.py`,
`tests/test_mcp.py`, `tests/test_docs.py`, `tests/test_line_endings.py`.

## 86. Session dedup (D113, 2026-10-01)

### 86.1 Why

An agent asks `project_query` several related questions in one session; the same top passages come back each
time, and every repeat spends the answer's character budget (and the agent's context) on text it already has.
Probe and Ref skip passages a session already returned. Here the MCP server remembers what it printed.

### 86.2 Decisions

- **The session is the MCP server process** (one `AtlasTools`): an agent's session talks to one server. A new
  server, the CLI and `analyze` are not affected.
- **Text answers only, and only what was printed.** The server remembers, per file, the line windows its
  text answers printed (not an item's whole span: a long class shown by two windows is remembered as those two
  windows), and only the windows still in the answer when it was sent (a section the budget note pushed out is
  not remembered). In a later answer, an item whose whole span those windows cover is not printed again; within
  a longer item, a window printed before is not printed again (its header says so when nothing new is left). The
  JSON format is data and returns every item.
- **Never hidden without saying where.** The items not repeated are listed, grouped by file with their line
  ranges, near the top of the answer, before any section: the budget note at the end can never push the list
  out.
- **Changed files are new again.** Each remembered window carries its file's stat (mtime and size) when it was
  printed; a file that changed since is forgotten, and its passages are printed again. A file modified within the
  server's racy window (the one the answer memo uses) is not remembered at all.
- **The kept answer is the result, not its text.** The answer memo (D44-era) now keeps the retrieval result
  and renders it for each call with the session's memory, so a repeated question still costs no retrieval.
- **Off switch**: `VERINODA_QUERY_DEDUP=0` in the server's environment (tests that compare two answers use it).
  No new MCP argument: the core menu is near its size limit, and the listed locations already let the agent get
  the text again (by reading the file or `node_inspect`).

### 86.3 Measured

Tests: the same question twice in one session prints none of the first answer's sections the second time and
lists them; a second server prints them all; an edited file's passages come back.

Review round (two reviewers): fixed whole spans remembered for items printed in part, sections the budget note
pushed out remembered as returned, the "already returned" line dropped by the budget (now at the top, grouped by
file, never cut by the note), a list cut at twelve locations, and same-tick edits keeping their stamp.

### 86.4 Not done

- An agent whose context was compacted loses the passages it was given; the answer only lists their locations.
- The list of items not repeated is clipped at 700 characters on a very long session.
- The memory lives as long as the server process and grows with the number of items printed (a few bytes each).

### 86.5 Tests

`tests/test_mcp.py`: a repeated query in one session returns only new passages and lists the rest; a new server
returns them all; a changed file's passages are new again; JSON is not deduplicated; the stdio round trip's
second identical call; the memo tests with dedup off; only windows still in a budget-cut answer are remembered;
the list comes before any section; a long item seen in part is not hidden.

## 87. Incremental re-review (D114, 2026-10-01)

### 87.1 Why

An agent (or a CI job) reviews a change, fixes something, and reviews again: the second review repeats every
finding of the first, and the new one is hard to see. Bugbot and Ellipsis review only what changed since their
last review. Verinoda records each review already (the `analyses` table); `--since-last` compares with that.

### 87.2 Decisions

- **`verinoda review --since-last`** and MCP `change_review` with `since_last=true` (the core gateway's one-line
  text names it; the core menu stays under its limit). Off by default: a plain `review` is unchanged.
- **Which review is "the last".** The latest recorded review of the same base commit, the same mode (working
  tree or staged), the same concerns and the same findings mode (each record now keeps this scope): a review that
  checked fewer concerns would make the others look gone. A planned change (`--target`) is not compared, and a review without a store has nothing to
  compare with; both say so in `since_last.note`.
- **A finding is itself wherever its lines moved, and only there.** Findings are matched by concern, rule, file,
  their text with line numbers masked (`path:12`, `line 12`, `@12`; other numbers, such as a metric that got
  worse, are kept) and their place: the definition holding the line and that line's code. An edit above a finding
  keeps all of these; the same risky call moved into another function is a new finding. Repeated findings are
  counted per key, so a second copy is new.
- **What is shown.** `concerns` holds only the findings the last review did not list; `since_last` gives the
  review it compared with, `repeated` (left out), `gone` (findings of the last review not found now: fixed or
  changed), `new_changes` (changed definitions, by symbol and kind, the last review did not have) and the
  method. `counts.findings_new` and `counts.findings_repeated` (also when there is no earlier review: every
  finding new); the summary is rebuilt from the new findings and says the rest in one sentence; the text output
  has a "Since the last review" section. The exit code stays the whole review's: findings still there still
  count, so `--since-last` never turns a gate green with nothing fixed.
- **Every finding, not the shown ones.** The comparison and the record use every finding before the per-concern
  cap of 25, so a new finding sorting after 25 repeated ones is shown, and one pushed past the cap is not "gone".
- **The record is complete.** The review is recorded with all its findings (each with its place) and its scope
  before the repeated ones are left out, so the next `--since-last` compares with everything this one found.
- In the capped MCP response, `since_last` is a kept key (it says what was left out).

### 87.3 Measured

Tests on the orders example: a signature change gives 5 findings; reviewing again after an edit above it gives 0
new and 5 repeated; a new `os.system` call is the only new finding of the third review and its definition is
named as new; reverting the signature lists the 5 as gone.

Review round (two reviewers): fixed comparing only the 25 shown findings per concern, a new call in another
function taken for the old one, worse metrics hidden by masking every number, a gate turning green on an
unchanged tree, earlier reviews of other concerns or findings modes making findings look gone, and the summary
and counts disagreeing with the filtered list.

### 87.4 Not done

- Reviews recorded before this change have no scope or places: they are not compared (the first `--since-last`
  after upgrading says every finding is new).
- A finding whose wording changes with the code (a different callee name in its text) counts as new.
- "The last review" is the last one recorded, whoever ran it (an agent's or the user's) on this machine's store.

### 87.5 Tests

`tests/test_review_since_last.py`: the first review says every finding is new; the same change again after an
edit above it shows none, counted as repeated; a new finding is the only one shown and its definition is named
new; findings gone after a revert are listed and rendered; the CLI `--since-last --json` and MCP `since_last`;
a call moved to a new function is new and the exit code still counts the old one; a review of other concerns is
not compared; findings past the per-concern cap are compared; in a project path with a space and non-ASCII. `tests/test_mcp.py` lists the new MCP argument.

## 88. Glob-scoped context (D115, 2026-10-01)

### 88.1 Why

A rule about a part of the code ("the data layer is the only one that opens connections", "views never touch the
database") is written down once, in a decision record, a note or an editor's rule file, and then nobody sees it
at the moment it matters: when the agent opens a file it applies to. Kiro steering files and Cursor rules attach
such text to globs; Verinoda's decision records already name files in their guards. This puts all of them in
front of the agent when it reads or edits a matching file.

### 88.2 Decisions

- **`verinoda context FILE`** (CLI, `--json`) and MCP **`read_context`**, a hook call like D62's `grep_context`:
  reached through `run_tool`, not listed, not advertised in the gateway's text; its answer is a Claude Code
  PostToolUse hook output (`additionalContext`) or `{}` when nothing names the file or anything fails, so a Read
  is never held up. The hooks template gains a `Read|Edit|MultiEdit|Write` entry that calls it with the tool's
  `file_path` (opt-in, like the Grep hook). The server has one more tool: 40.
- **Decision records**: an enforced record's accepted guard whose glob fields match the file (only_in
  `allowed`, no_edge `from`/`to`, layers `order`, allow_edges `from`/`allowed`, public `module`/`api`; a
  `tag:NAME` read as its committed globs, with the same `guards.glob_match` the checks use), and governed symbols
  in the file. The item names the record, the guard and its record file. Whether the code keeps the record is
  `decide check`'s question; this only says the record is about the file.
- **Notes**: the user's notes anchored in the file, with their state (fresh, changed, gone); and notes scoped to
  globs: a Markdown file in the notes folder whose header has `scope: GLOB[, GLOB]` and no `file:` (such a file
  is not a regular note, so the notes view is unchanged).
- **Other tools' rules**: Cursor's `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` with `globs:` and Kiro's `.kiro/steering/*.md` with
  `inclusion: fileMatch` and `fileMatchPattern:`, in the project and, when the project is a folder of its
  repository, at the repository's top (matched against the repository path). Always-on rules (`alwaysApply:
  true`) are not listed: they are not about this file. Their globs are read as those tools read them: `**/` is no
  folder or any number, `{ts,tsx}` either; front matter lists (flow or block), quoted values, a closing `---`
  with trailing spaces or at the end of the file are read.
- **Quoted, not summarised.** Each note or rule quotes its first line of text (a heading only when nothing else is
  there; 160 characters) with `path:line`, and a decision guard is quoted as written (its spec), not with its tags
  expanded. Scoped notes and rules come first (they are written for files like this one), then notes on the file,
  then decision records; the hook's block is cut between items at 700 characters and says how many more `verinoda
  context` shows (the CLI shows them all).
- **Cheap on every Read.** The sources are parsed once and kept until one of their files changes (a stat of each
  rule, note and record file, and the config files, per call); `read_context` takes no server lock, so a Read
  never waits for an analyze.

### 88.3 Measured

Tests only.

Review round (two reviewers): fixed `**/` and brace globs (fnmatch read `src/**/*.ts` as needing a folder),
commas inside brace sets, quoted Kiro values, a closing `---` with spaces or at the end of the file, headings
quoted instead of the rule, always-on rules with globs listed, workspace-level Cursor and Kiro rules not read,
every source re-parsed on every hook call (0.5-0.8 s with 500 records), the server lock held by the hook, the
CLI's messages for a path outside the project, and rewritten historical upgrade notes.

### 88.4 Not done

- Only the first line of a note or rule is quoted; the agent reads the file for the rest.
- Decision guards are matched as `decide check` matches them (`guards.glob_match`), which can differ from the
  editors' dialect in corner cases; that is deliberate, so the two never disagree about a guard.
- Claims are not listed (a stale claim about the file shows in `verinoda update` and `analyze`).

### 88.5 Tests

`tests/test_scoped.py`: decision records (only_in and layers), a glob-scoped note, a Cursor rule and a Kiro
steering file found for the files they name, an always-on rule left out, nothing for a file nothing names, an
absolute path, a path outside the project; the text cap; the MCP hook output and `{}`, and the CLI, in a project
path with a space and non-ASCII. `tests/test_mcp.py`: the tool's parameters, the gateway's hidden tools and the
hooks template's Read/Edit entry.

## 89. SARIF in and out, CI check status (D116, 2026-10-01)

### 89.1 Why

GitHub code scanning, and most CI dashboards and editors, read SARIF. Verinoda's `review`, `check` and `decide
check` findings were only text or Verinoda's own JSON, so they could not show up next to CodeQL's or a linter's
results on a pull request; and a linter's or CodeQL's SARIF could not be read as evidence alongside Verinoda's own
claims. Copilot review and Code Pathfinder both speak SARIF.

### 89.2 Decisions

- New module `verinoda/sarif.py`; no new MCP tool and no new MCP argument (the core menu and the tool count are
  unchanged, so UPGRADING's tool count does not change).
- **Out**: `--sarif` on `review`, `check` and `decide check` prints one SARIF 2.1.0 log (one run) instead of the
  text or `--json`; the exit code is the command's own, so a CI step fails or passes as before, and the log is
  uploaded with `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif`. `automationDetails.id` is `verinoda/<command>/` so the three
  uploads stay separate categories in code scanning.
  - Rule ids: `review/<concern>/<rule>` (plus `review/tests/uncovered-changed-lines`), `decide/<decision>/<guard>`,
    `check/<verdict>/<site kind>`; `ruleIndex` set on every result.
  - Location: the finding's `file:line`, `file:line-end` or `file:line:col` as a relative `uri` (percent-encoded)
    under `%SRCROOT%`; a bare file path has no region. A finding cited at a symbol (`file::Name`) or at nothing is
    not written and is counted in the run's `properties.not_exported`, never silently dropped.
  - Level from the claim status: verified statuses `error`, `strong_inference` `warning`, `weak_inference` and
    `unknown` `note`. A review finding is something to read, not a defect, so it is a `warning` at most. `check`
    sites: `absent` is `statically_verified` (the closed-world rule plus the resolver) when the container is the
    standard library or the project's own code, else `strong_inference` (an installed package, a stub, a
    classpath or the environment's `sys.path`: what was installed or built here, which CI's may not match);
    `not_installed` `strong_inference` (CI's environment may differ), `unknown` `unknown`; `guarded` and
    `exists` are not written.
  - `review`: an `introduced` finding is `baselineState: new`, a `preexisting` one `unchanged`; findings past the
    review's per-concern cap are counted in `properties.not_listed`, the review's unknowns in
    `properties.unknowns`.
  - `properties` carry `status` and, when present, `evidence_at`, `basis`, `derived_by`, `delta`, `verdict`,
    `since`, `rank`.
  - `decide check`: with a base, a violation, possible violation or review is `baselineState: new` or
    `unchanged` as its own `since` says (new/touched or pre-existing); a
    violation the baseline lists or a waiver covers is written with an `external` suppression and its reason
    (still there, not failing). Governed symbols to review are notes when they have a file location; triggers
    have none and are counted as not exported.
- **In**: `verinoda sarif FILE... [--path P] [--limit N] [--json]` reads SARIF 2.1 files the way
  `coverage_import` reads coverage reports. Each result becomes a claim `<tool> reports <rule> (<level>): <message>`
  at its first physical location, with `stated_by`, `rule`, `level`, the innermost definition around the line
  (`coverage_import.facts_of`/`symbol_of`), and `evidence_at` = the location and the SARIF file. It is the named
  tool's statement, not checked here: `strong_inference` while the SARIF file is newer than the file it names,
  `weak_inference` when the file changed after it. Errors first, then warnings, notes.
  - Paths: a relative uri, one under a `uriBaseId` from `originalUriBaseIds`, an `artifacts[index]` entry, a
    `file://` uri under the repository or under one of the run's `originalUriBaseIds`; else, only for an absolute
    path that exists nowhere on this machine and has no third-party folder in it (`site-packages`,
    `node_modules`, `vendor`...), the longest suffix of the path that is a repository file (a CI runner's path).
    A suffix tie is a guess: the claim is `weak_inference` and names the original uri. A relative uri that is
    not a repository file, and a file that exists here outside the repository, are not in the repository. `..`
    never leaves the repository. Each distinct location is resolved once per run.
  - Rules: `ruleIndex` / `rule.index` in the driver, or in `tool.extensions[rule.toolComponent.index]` (CodeQL),
    else by id; the level is the result's when it is one of the four SARIF levels, else the rule's
    `defaultConfiguration.level`, else `warning`.
  - Messages: `message.text`, else the rule's `messageStrings[id]` with `{0}`... arguments filled in one pass
    (`{{` and `}}` are literal braces), else the rule's description; clipped to 300 characters.
  - Counted, not listed: suppressed results (a suppression with no status or `accepted`; `rejected` and
    `underReview` do not hide a result), `pass` / `notApplicable`, `baselineState: absent` (fixed), results
    without a physical location, results outside the repository (the first 20 uris listed), outside `--path`,
    and results that cannot be read (`unreadable`, with one example): a malformed result does not stop its run.
  - A file that is not SARIF 2.1, not JSON, missing or over 100 MB is an error entry, never a crash; exit 4 when
    no file was read.

### 89.3 Measured

- The review fixture (one changed function that gained a `subprocess.run`): `review --sarif` exits like
  `review --json`, every concern finding is either a result at `cart.py` or counted in `not_exported`, all levels
  `warning` or `note`.
- The logs pass a SARIF 2.1.0 schema subset written in the test (types, required keys, level, suppression kind
  and baseline state enums, region minimums, rule ids unique and `ruleIndex` consistent, relative posix uris).
- An exported log read back with `verinoda sarif` gives Verinoda's own findings as `stated_by: Verinoda` claims.
- A real `check --sarif` on `os.pathh` gives `source: stdlib`, `statically_verified`, `error`.

Review round: CodeQL's rules in `tool.extensions` are now found through `rule.toolComponent`, so their default
level and `messageStrings` apply (before, every such result was a `warning`). The suffix tie is limited to
absolute paths that exist nowhere here and lie under no third-party folder, and is `weak_inference` (before, a
relative uri or a sibling project's file could be tied to a repository file by its bare name, as
`strong_inference`). `decide check` takes `baselineState` from each finding's `since` (a pre-existing possible
violation was `new`); `review` sets it from `delta` and counts findings past its per-concern cap and its
unknowns. An `absent` check site is verified only against the standard library or the project's own code.
Rejected and under-review suppressions no longer hide a result. A non-string level, a boolean `startLine` and a
malformed result no longer crash or cut the run short (one malformed result among three: two claims and
`unreadable: 1`, where the rest of the run used to be lost). Message arguments are filled in one pass. Each
location is resolved and stat'ed once per run (50 results on one file: one lookup).

### 89.4 Not done

- Not uploaded or validated against GitHub here (no network): the shape follows the SARIF 2.1.0 schema and the
  fields GitHub documents; a file-level location (no line) is valid SARIF but code scanning shows it at the file.
- No `partialFingerprints`: `upload-sarif` computes them from the file contents.
- Import reads the first physical location of a result; related locations, code flows and logical locations are
  not read; `review` does not yet take imported SARIF results on its changed lines (a next step: a `--sarif-in`
  like `--coverage`).
- Levels follow how sure a statement is, not how severe it is; no `security-severity` is set.
- A path from another machine that matches two repository files by suffix takes the longest suffix that exists;
  with equal suffixes the first one found wins. The suffix can be the bare file name (a file at the repository
  root), which is why such a claim is `weak_inference`.
- The test of a real `review --sarif` checks that at least one result is written and that the log passes the
  schema subset; it is not checked against GitHub's own SARIF validator (no network).

### 89.5 Tests

`tests/test_sarif.py`: a schema subset validator (and that it rejects a broken log); review findings at their
lines, a warning at most, a symbol-cited finding counted in `not_exported`; `decide check` violations as errors,
possible ones as notes, `baselineState`, baselined and waived ones suppressed; `check` verdicts to levels with
columns, guarded sites left out; a path with spaces and non-ASCII as a valid uri; `check --sarif` through the CLI
with its exit code; ruff-like and CodeQL-like SARIF read as claims (rule by index, `messageStrings`, artifacts,
`originalUriBaseIds`, suppressed, pass, absent, no location, outside the repository); a file changed after the
SARIF is weak; an absolute CI path tied by suffix and `--path`; an exported log read back; broken files as errors;
`verinoda sarif` CLI (`--json`, text, exit 4); a real `review --sarif` in a git worktree with at least one
result. Review round: the review cap and unknowns counted and `delta` as `baselineState`; a pre-existing possible
violation `unchanged`; an installed-package `absent` site `strong_inference`; CodeQL extension rules (level and
message); suffix ties limited (a file here, a `site-packages` path, a relative uri: not tied; a CI path: weak);
rejected and under-review suppressions; an invalid level, a boolean line and a malformed result in one run;
one-pass message arguments with escapes; one path lookup per location. Also run:
`tests/test_cli.py`, `tests/test_docs.py`, `tests/test_line_endings.py`, `tests/test_decide.py`,
`tests/test_codecheck.py`.

## 90. Flaky test history (D117, 2026-10-01)

### 90.1 Why

`debug rerun` measured a pass rate for one series and one repro command, then the per-test picture was gone:
the next session could not say which tests had flipped before, a user had nowhere to keep "this test is known
flaky", and nothing said when a failing test's change had held long enough to trust. Test-optimization tools
(Datadog Test Optimization) keep per-test history across runs, a quarantine list and "fixed after N reruns". This
decision keeps that history locally, from the runs the debug ledger already makes.

### 90.2 Decisions

- **Where the rows come from.** Every debug-ledger attempt Verinoda runs itself (`debug start`, `try`, `rerun`,
  `differential`, `bisect`, `observe`) that passed or failed writes one `test_runs` row per test, from the
  per-test outcomes the failure-signature plugin already records (`passed`/`xpassed` -> pass, `failed`/`error`
  -> fail; skipped and xfailed tests are not rows). A runner without per-test outcomes (Go, Cargo, a script)
  writes one row for the command (`$ <command>`, pytest's output-only options left out). Agent-reported runs
  never count (as in `debug rerun`), and timeouts and inconclusive runs leave no rows: their per-test outcomes
  may be partial.
- **Schema v7** (`store.py`): `test_runs` (attempt, session, test, outcome, kind, tree hash, evidence id;
  unique per attempt and test, so recording twice adds nothing) and `test_quarantine` (one row per add or
  remove; the latest row per test is its state). Both are append-only (delete/update triggers). Attempts
  recorded before v7 are added the first time the history is read (`sync`), so an upgraded project keeps its
  ledger's history; runs are read in the attempts' order (time, then attempt row), not the rows' insertion order.
- **Flaky** = one tree (the ledger's tree hash) has both a passing and a failing run of the test. Failures on one
  tree and passes on another are a change, not flakiness.
- **Held** (the row's "fix verified by N reruns") = the test passed the last N recorded runs of the working tree
  in a row since its last failure there, each on a tree no run of it ever failed on. A pass on a failing tree
  makes the test flaky there, not fixed. Runs of other commits (`bisect`, `differential`, any run copied from a
  commit) never count toward held: an older commit passing says nothing about the newest one. N is
  `debug.rerun_times` (5), `--runs N` (1 or more; 0 or less is an error) overrides. Fewer passes are listed as "not yet held
  (k of N)". The word is "held", never "fixed": the debug ledger's rule that Verinoda never says fixed stands.
- **Quarantine is the user's list.** `verinoda debug quarantine TEST [--remove] [--reason]` logs the decision;
  `debug flaky` shows each quarantined test's state (flaky, held, passing, failing, no runs) and lists flaky
  tests not on the list as candidates. Verinoda never skips, deselects or reruns a test because it is quarantined.
- **Claims.** Flaky and held entries carry `status: strong_inference`, the finding in words, `evidence` (up to
  three evidence ids of the runs: a failing and a passing run of the flaky tree; the last failure and the last
  pass of a held test) and `at` (the test's `path:line` in the working tree, found by its `def`). Pass rates and
  counts are counts of recorded rows.
- **Surfaces.** CLI only: `debug flaky [--runs N] [--test ID] [--json]` and `debug quarantine`. `debug rerun`
  adds `tests_both_outcomes` (the tests that passed and failed within that series) when there are any. No MCP
  tool or argument was added (the core menu is unchanged).
- **Lists** (flaky, held, pending, quarantine, candidates) are capped at 20 (`truncated: true` when cut);
  `--test ID` adds that test's last 20 runs. `at` is looked up only for the entries shown, each file read once.
- **`debug quarantine --json`** has one shape on every path: `test`, `quarantined`, `changed`, `recorded_runs`,
  `reason`, `since`, and a `note` for an unknown id or a new reason given for a test already on the list (the
  logged reason stays; remove and add again to change it).

### 90.3 Measured

- Synthetic store (scratch script, this machine under load): 2,000 tests x 10 runs. Recording one run's 2,000
  rows: 22 ms. `report` over 20,000 rows: 201 ms. The JSON answer with every list at its cap: 6,890 characters.
- End to end (`tests/test_testhistory.py`): a copy of `examples/orders_app` with a test that fails every second
  run; `debug start` + `debug rerun --times 2` give pass, fail, pass; `debug flaky` lists exactly that test,
  pass rate 0.67, at `tests/test_flip.py:4`, with two evidence ids; the always-passing `test_pricing.py`
  tests of the same runs are not listed.
- Not measured: a real flaky suite over weeks of sessions.

Review round: a review found that bisect and differential passes on older commits could make a test still
failing at HEAD "held", that attempts added by `sync` sorted after newer live ones (a false "held" after an
upgrade), that `at` read the test file again for every flaky test before the cap (5.12 s for one 2,000-test
file), that the quarantine list was not capped, that `--runs 0`/`-3` were silently replaced, and that the
`quarantine --json` keys changed with the path. All six are fixed, each with a test. Re-measured: one 2,000-test
file, 4 runs on one tree with every test flipping, in a directory with spaces and non-ASCII characters:
`report` 162 ms, 20 entries, 7,254 JSON characters.

### 90.4 Not done

- Only runs made through the debug ledger are recorded; `experiment run`, `analyze --run-tests` and
  `review --run-tests` do not write per-test rows (they do not load the failure-signature plugin).
- Flaky needs both outcomes on one tree: a test that failed once on a tree run only once is not flaky yet.
  N passes never prove a cause is gone; the history is this machine's.
- "Held" reads the working tree's runs in the order they ran; a `bisect` or `differential` run neither counts
  toward it nor restarts it, but a failure it records on a tree makes a later pass on that tree no held fix.
  Two attempts made in the same second in different sessions are ordered by when they were stored.
- A pytest id parametrised over absolute paths is normalised by the failure signature; other run-to-run id
  changes (a renamed test) start a new history.
- The quarantine list is not consulted by the debug ledger's loop rules, `close` or any run.

### 90.5 Tests

- `tests/test_testhistory.py` (14): flaky on one tree vs a change across trees; held after N passes on a changed
  tree, pending below N, undone by a later failure; a pass on the failing tree is flaky, not held; only
  Verinoda's pass/fail runs are recorded and a runner without per-test ids counts as its command (output-only
  pytest options ignored); recording twice adds nothing, older attempts are added on read, both tables are
  append-only; the quarantine log (add, already, remove, unknown id note, errors, state, candidates); a test's
  `path:line`; a v6 database migrates to v7; bisect and differential passes never hold a fix; a pass on a tree
  that failed before is not held; attempts added on read keep their run order; every list including the
  quarantine is capped and files are read only for shown entries; `--runs` below 1 is an error; end to end a real `debug rerun` series plus the CLI (`debug
  quarantine`, `debug flaky` text and `--json --test`).
- Run: `tests/test_testhistory.py`, `tests/test_debug.py` (48), `tests/test_cli.py`, `tests/test_buildinfo.py`,
  `tests/test_store.py`, `tests/test_docs.py` (one expected failure: UPGRADING.md lacks v7, see above),
  `tests/test_line_endings.py`.

## 91. Named flow maps (D118, 2026-10-01)

### 91.1 Why

A trace or a map view an agent worked out ("how an order request reaches the repository") is gone when the
session ends; the next agent, or a reviewer, runs it again or trusts a copy pasted into a note that nobody
checks. Windsurf/Devin Codemaps keep such maps by name. Here a saved map is citable by name, and reading it back
says whether the code it describes is still the code: an old map is never presented as current.

### 91.2 Decisions

- **No new command or tool: `map` gets three actions, MCP `map_view` one view.** `verinoda map save NAME
  [--trace SOURCE TARGET [--mode] | --view V [--target ...] [--base] [--max-tokens]]` (neither: the default
  views), `map show NAME`, `map list`. The first positional of `map` is the project folder; `save`, `show` and
  `list` there are the actions (a project folder with such a name is passed as `./save` or `--repo`). The MCP
  read is `map_view` with `view: saved`, `targets: [NAME]` (none: the list), reached through `run_tool` in the
  core profile: the core menu grows by six characters (`|saved`), no tool and no argument is added, the tool
  count stays as it is.
- **What is saved is the `--json` result the command prints**, with the arguments that made it, under
  `.verinoda/maps/NAME.json` (`verinoda.named_map/1`), the index's latest snapshot id and commit, and for each
  file the result cites the sha256 **the snapshot recorded** - not the file on disk: the result describes the
  indexed version. A file is cited when a string or key of the result names a snapshot path, alone or as
  `path:LINE`, `path:A-B` or `path::Symbol`, as the whole string or as a word of a longer one (the tests view
  writes `"apply_discount() (orders/pricing.py:11)"` and `"orders/repository.py:9 .__init__()"`). The
  index-freshness keys of the result (`stale_count`, `stale_files`, `index_freshness`) are dropped before the
  citations are read and are not saved: a file is never cited because it changed since the index; a cited file that had changed since the
  index when saving is recorded as `stale_at_save` and makes the map read back stale at once.
- **Reading back hashes the cited files again** (stat-cached, `snapshot.hash_files`): `current` when each has the
  recorded hash, `stale` when one changed or is gone, `unknown` when the map cites no file (an empty cycles or
  sides view, an impact view of a clean tree): nothing was compared, so the claim is `unknown`, not
  `primary_source_verified`, and the next step is the command that makes the map from the code now. The answer carries `as_of` (snapshot, commit, saved_at),
  the changed files (up to 20, with the exact count), one `primary_source_verified` claim stating the hash
  comparison (evidence: each changed file with its saved hash prefix and `modified`/`removed`), the command
  that makes the map again, and `limits`. The saved result is returned as it was, under `result`, after those
  keys; in the MCP answer `status`, `name`, `as_of`, the changed files, the claim and the next step are kept
  first and are never cut before the saved result.
- **Refused, not saved**: a trace that is not `found`, a view whose `--target` did not resolve (exit 2), a name
  that is not 1-64 letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-` starting with a letter or digit (no path can be formed from
  it). Saving under an existing name replaces the map (written to a temporary file, then renamed).
- **Exit codes of `map show`**: 0 current, 1 stale (for CI: a map cited in a document that no longer holds),
  1 also for unknown (it cannot be shown current), 2 not found, invalid name, or a map file that is not a
  valid saved map (not JSON, `files` not a map of repository-relative paths to sha256 hashes); such a file is
  listed as `invalid` and never stops the other maps from being listed.
- **Names are exact, and names that differ only in case are refused**: `maps/` ignores case on Windows and
  macOS, so `map save T1` beside `t1` would replace it; it is refused (exit 2) and `map show T1` finds only a
  file named exactly `T1.json`.
- **An impact or repo view saved without `--target`** took its targets from the working-tree changes; the
  targets it used are saved as its `target` argument, so the re-run command makes the same map.
- **Arguments that would be ignored are refused** (exit 2), as plain `map` does: `--trace` with a view
  argument, `--mode` without `--trace`, any view or trace argument with `show` or `list`, a name with `list`.
- **Sharing**: `.verinoda/` is git-ignored as a whole (`.verinoda/.gitignore` is `*`), so a map is shared by
  committing it explicitly: `git add -f .verinoda/maps/NAME.json` (printed by `map save`); once tracked, later
  saves show up as changes.

### 91.3 Measured

On a scanned copy of `examples/orders_app`: the trace `create_order_handler -> OrderRepository.save` saves as
1,821 bytes citing 3 files; the default views (`map save all`) as 21,953 bytes citing 11 files. Reading either
back took about 0.04 s. The MCP answer for the trace is 1,828 characters, for all default views 11,678 (cut
to the 12,000 cap with the status keys first). Core menu: 4,444 characters (limit 4,500).

Review round: the citations were read as whole strings only, so a saved tests view cited 0 of the 6 files
it names and read `current` after any edit; it now cites them (per view on the scratch copy: hierarchy 11,
dependencies 7, dataflow 3, config 5, tests 6, history 11, repo 7, dead 2, hotspots 5; cycles, sides and a
clean-tree impact view 0 and read `unknown`). The freshness keys decided the citations before being dropped
(a cycles view saved beside an edited `orders/pricing.py` read stale); they are now dropped first. Also fixed:
a map citing nothing read `current`; an impact view without `--target` did not keep its targets; `T1` replaced
`t1`; a broken map file crashed `map show` and `map list`; an unreadable index gave a traceback with exit 1;
ignored arguments passed silently. `git add -f` on a saved map stages it (checked on the scratch copy).

### 91.4 Not done

- `current` means only that the files the map cites are as they were. A file it does not cite can change what
  a new run returns (a new path through a new file, a new dependent of an impact target, a new folder in the
  hierarchy); the read says so in `limits`. A whole-project view cites most files and goes stale with almost any
  change.
- A file is cited only when a string of the result names it; a view that names a folder or a package (the
  hierarchy's folder rows) is checked through the files it does name.
- The saved result is not re-run or migrated: a map saved by an older Verinoda keeps that version's shape.
- An impact view saved without `--target` cites the changed files it was computed from, so it reads back
  stale until the change is indexed and the map saved again.
- A map file is checked for shape when read, not for having been written by Verinoda: a hand-edited hash
  only makes the map read stale.
- Saving is CLI only; agents read maps by name but do not write them (no write tool behind the core menu).

### 91.5 Tests

`tests/test_named_maps.py`: citation of `path:LINE`, `path:A-B`, `path::Symbol` and keys; name checks; a trace
saved through the CLI reads current, stays current when an uncited file changes, goes stale (exit 1, the file
named, the claim's evidence, the re-run command, the result kept) when a cited file changes or is removed; a
view saved, listed, shown and replaced; a map saved from a file changed since the index reads stale; refusals
(unresolved trace, bad name, missing name, stray argument, unknown map, empty list); MCP `map_view` saved view
(read, list, two targets, bad name, unknown name, a small response cap keeping the status first).
Review round: citations inside longer strings; a saved tests view cites the files it names and goes stale on
an edit to one; a view saved beside an unrelated stale file cites nothing from it and reads `unknown` (exit 1);
an impact view without `--target` keeps its targets; a name differing only in case is refused; broken map
files (list `files`, a `../` path, not JSON) read `invalid` (exit 2) and are listed without hiding the
others, also through MCP; an unreadable index does not crash a read and refuses a save; ignored arguments are
refused.
Also run: `tests/test_mcp.py` (view enum, core menu under 4,500), `tests/test_docs.py`, `tests/test_cli.py -k
"map or trace or help"`, `tests/test_architecture_map.py`, `tests/test_line_endings.py`.

## 92. Crash diagnosis rules and suspect scoring (D119, 2026-10-01)

### 92.1 Why

`verinoda trace-log` maps a log's stack traces onto the project, but a player's crash report is mostly about other
mods: sixty frames of the game with three of some storage mod in between, or no trace at all, only a loader line
saying a dependency is missing. Tools such as mclo.gs Codex, mc-crash-doctor and NotEnoughCrashes name the known
pattern and the mod to blame; `trace-log` said neither.

### 92.2 Decisions

- **Rules are data** (`verinoda/crash_rules.py`, `RULES`): an id, the line patterns that show it, what it means.
  Six rules: `out_of_memory`, `watchdog` (the tick took too long; `Description: Watching Server`),
  `missing_dependency` (Fabric's "requires [version X or later | any version | any version between A and B] of ...
  which is missing / but only the wrong version", Forge's "Missing or unsupported mandatory dependencies" and its
  "Mod ID: ..., Requested by: ..." lines), `missing_class` (`NoClassDefFoundError` / `ClassNotFoundException`, but
  not on a line logged at WARN, INFO, DEBUG or TRACE, nor a Mixin "Error loading class:" warning: optional compat
  classes), `mixin_apply` ("Mixin apply for mod X failed", `MixinTransformerError`, `InvalidInjectionException`) and
  `wrong_java` (`UnsupportedClassVersionError`, ASM's "Unsupported class file major version NN", the launcher's
  "LinkageError occurred while loading main class"; the class file versions turned into Java releases: 65 -> 21).
- **A rule names its evidence**: the first matching log line (the logger's prefix stripped), how many lines matched,
  and what the pattern captured (`found`: the mod id, the Mixin and its target, the seconds of the tick, the Java
  versions; each value cut to 200 characters). A rule hit carries `status: strong_inference`: the line is
  observed, what it means is an interpretation. When the first line is a bare header
  (`Description: Watching Server`) and a later one names more, the
  later line's captures are kept with `found_at`.
- **A suspect** is the owner of frames outside the JDK, the game, the loaders and common libraries: a mod named by a
  Mixin handler's name (`handler$bfk000$lagfix$afterTick`, a mod id with a dash included) or by a modern Forge
  frame's module (`TRANSFORMER/bigstorage@2.4.1/...`), the mod jar a Forge frame names
  (`~[bigstorage-2.4.1.jar%23188!/:2.4.1]`), else the class's package (its first three parts). A class with no
  package (an obfuscated game class, `dzv.a(SourceFile:123)`) is never a suspect; a hidden lambda class
  (`Foo$$Lambda$12/0x...`) is its outer class. A mod named by a handler or module, its jar (the name before the
  version) and every package that has the mod id as a dotted part are one suspect, led by the jar, else the
  package; a mod id too common to tell (`core`, `api`, `common`, `client`, ...) ties nothing.
- **The score** is the sum of `1 / (1 + position)` over the suspect's frames, position 0 being the top of a trace or
  of a `Caused by` (the parser now records each frame's position, Forge jar and module). A crash report section's
  `Stacktrace:` (`-- Head --`, `-- Block entity being ticked --`, ...) whose frames are a run of an earlier trace's
  frames is not counted again, nor a trace printed twice (the same header and frames); another exception thrown
  at the same place is counted. The score is a heuristic:
  every suspect is `strong_inference`, with its inputs (frames, traces, positions, frames at the top, the first
  frame, how it was named, whether the project's own code). At most five suspects are shown.
- **Output**: `trace-log` (text and `--json`) gains `diagnosis` and `suspects` (with `score`, the formula once),
  each key present only when non-empty. A log with a diagnosis but no trace and no test result exits 0, not 2
  (nothing found). Fabric's own log lines (`[time] [main/ERROR] (FabricLoader) ...`, no colon) now lose their
  prefix too. No new command, no MCP change; nothing is stored beyond what `trace-log`
  already stored.

### 92.3 Measured

Five hand-written fixtures in the shape of real logs (`tests/fixtures/crash/`): a Forge out-of-memory crash report
(rule `out_of_memory` at line 7; suspects `bigstorage-2.4.1.jar` 0.78 from positions 2, 3, 4 and
`tinyhud-1.0.3.jar` 0.1; the `-- Head --` repeat not counted), a Fabric watchdog report (rule `watchdog`, 60.00
seconds; suspect `dev.lagfix.chunk (mod lagfix)` 1.83 from two package frames and one Mixin handler), a Fabric
Mixin apply failure (rule `mixin_apply`: mod `guardmod`, `guardmod.mixins.json:LevelMixin` on
`net.minecraft.class_1937`; no suspect, every frame is the loader's), a missing `fabric-api` and a class file 65 run
on Java 17. Not measured on real players' logs.

Review round: a crash report's category sections (`-- Block entity being ticked --`) repeat a run of the main trace
and were counted again (a mod at position 2 scored 0.83 over 2 traces instead of 0.33): now skipped, and only
`Stacktrace:` sections are skipped as runs, so a second exception at the same place counts (2.5, was 1.5); the
check is indexed by frame (4,000 traces in 0.03 s; 2,000 took 0.76 s before, growing quadratically). A Mixin "Error
loading class" warning no longer comes first as `missing_class`; Fabric's "any version between" wording, the
Forge "Mod ID / Requested by" line, "Unsupported class file major version" and the launcher's LinkageError now
match; `found` values are capped; rule hits carry a status; `trace-log` exits 0 on a diagnosis alone; a dashed
Mixin handler mod id, a Forge module prefix, an obfuscated class with no package and a hidden lambda class are
handled; jar, module, handler and package rows of one mod merge, a generic mod id never does.

### 92.4 Not done

- The rules match single lines; a message wrapped across lines matches only on its first line.
- Package attribution takes the first three parts: two mods sharing them (`com.example.a`, `com.example.b` at depth
  two) are one suspect, and one mod spread over packages that differ in the first three parts is several.
- `missing_class` is skipped on WARN / INFO / DEBUG / TRACE lines: a mod that logs a real missing class at WARN is
  missed (its stack trace's own `Caused by` line, which has no prefix, still matches).
- A module prefix with no `@version` is not read as a mod; a mod id that is not a dotted part of its packages
  (`big-storage` vs `com.bigstorage`) keeps the jar and package apart.
- Obfuscated or remapped frames are not named back to a mod beyond the Mixin handler's mod id; a Fabric mod list
  (`Fabric Mods:` in a crash report) is not read to turn a package into a mod id.
- A Mixin apply failure's mod is in the rule's `found`, not among the suspects (its frames are the loader's).
- No claim is stored for a rule or a suspect: they describe the run and the installed mods, not the project's code.

### 92.5 Tests

- `tests/test_crash_rules.py`: each rule on its fixture (first line, captures), a bare header taking a later line's
  captures, suspects by jar with their score and the `-- Head --` repeat skipped, a Mixin handler merged with its
  package, platform frames never suspects, `Caused by` restarting the position, a missing class and a clean log;
  crash report sections not counted again, another exception at the same place counted, a trace printed twice
  counted once and 2,000 traces fast, an optional class warning not a `missing_class`, the Fabric range and Forge
  dependency wordings, a dashed handler mod id, a generic mod id tying nothing, a Forge module tying its jar and
  package, obfuscated and hidden lambda classes, the other wrong-Java wordings, `found` capped and the status, a
  Fabric line's prefix stripped.
- `tests/test_trace_log.py`: the CLI (`--json` and text) names the rule and the suspect with its score, the project's
  own frames marked; a log without a crash pattern has no `diagnosis`; a log with only a missing-dependency line
  (in a folder with a non-ASCII name) exits 0 with that diagnosis.

## 93. Rationale nodes (D120, 2026-10-01)

### 93.1 Why

An agent that inspects a symbol sees its source, its edges and the backlog items its comments cite, but not the
comments where the author says why the code is the way it is (`# WHY: ...`, `// NOTE: ...`, `HACK:`, a citation
of an ADR). Those comments are the shortest path to the reason, and an agent reading only the excerpt can miss one
that sits above the definition, or deep inside a long body past the excerpt's cut. Graphify and
codebase-memory-mcp turn such comments into graph nodes linked to the code; this decision gives Verinoda the same
reach without changing the graph.

### 93.2 Decisions

- New module `verinoda/rationale.py`; a new CLI command `verinoda rationale [symbol|path] [--limit N] [--json]`;
  MCP `node_inspect` gains a `rationale` list. No new MCP tool, no new argument: the core menu is unchanged.
- What counts: a comment whose words start with `WHY:`, `NOTE:`, `NB:`/`N.B.:`, `HACK:`, `IMPORTANT:` or
  `RATIONALE:` (any case, an optional `(who)` before the colon, `@`-prefixed in Javadoc), with the comment
  lines right after it (up to 6, until a blank comment line or a new marker); and a comment that cites a decision
  record anywhere in it: `ADR-12` / `ADR 12`, a document (`.md`, `.rst`, `.txt`, `.adoc`) under `adr/`, `adrs/`,
  `decisions/` or `decision-records/` (a source file under a `decisions/` folder is not one),
  `<file>.md D50` (this repository's own form), or the words "decision record". The citations are listed in
  `cites`. "Note that ..." without a colon is prose, not a marker.
- Comments are found with `tokenize` for Python (a `#` inside a string is not a comment; trailing comments count)
  and line by line elsewhere (`//` and `/* ... */` blocks for C-family languages, `#` for shell, Ruby, YAML,
  TOML, `--` for Lua and SQL); only whole-line comments outside Python. Markdown and other prose are never read
  (a `# WHY` heading is not a comment).
- Attachment, by position: a comment directly above a definition (only comment, decorator or annotation lines
  between; a blank line breaks it) is `above` that definition; a comment between a decorator and its `def` is
  `above` it too; otherwise the innermost definition around it (`inside`); otherwise `module`. Definitions come
  from `anchors` facts (Python, TypeScript/JavaScript; graph symbols the TS/JS facts miss, such as
  `const f = () => ...`, are added from the graph's spans) and, for other languages, from the graph's symbol
  spans. A Python comment after a body's last statement (past the ast end) is `inside` the definition just above
  it whose `def` line is indented less than the comment. Lines are counted on `\n` only, as editors and git do.
- Side table, not graph nodes: nothing is stored. The comments are read from the file as it is when asked, so the
  index build, `graph.json` and the snapshot are unchanged and the quoted text is never stale. For a symbol the
  definition is found by the node's indexed line, so a symbol whose file changed since the index gets no rows
  (`node_inspect`: `rationale_note` says to run index_update; the CLI: status `stale`, exit 2). A file is parsed
  for its definitions only when its comments hold a marker (a cheap text check first, then the comment scan).
- Status: each row is `statically_verified` that the comment is at that `file:line` (the text is quoted as
  written); what it says is the author's statement and is not checked; which definition it explains is read
  from its position and has its own `attach_status`, `strong_inference`. The note says so in one sentence (`rationale_note` in `node_inspect`, `note` in the CLI).
- `node_inspect` adds `rationale` only when the node has some: at most 5 rows of `at`, `tag`, `text` (at most 200
  characters, ending in `...` when cut), `attach`, `status`, `attach_status`, plus `rationale_total` when there are more, so it stays far from the
  12,000-character cap. A file node gets the module-level rows.
- The CLI: a symbol (resolved as `backlog` and `node_inspect` resolve names) gives its rows; a file or folder,
  or nothing (the project's tracked and untracked-not-ignored files, `git ls-files -z`), gives every row there
  with counts per tag. A path is resolved against the repository (`.`, `./pkg`, an absolute path inside it); a
  path outside it is `not_found`. An index that exists but does not load is reported with its error. Exit 0 when something is
  found, 2 otherwise (none, not found, ambiguous with candidates).

### 93.3 Measured

On this repository (2,666 listed files): 74 rationale comments (ADR citations 66, NOTE 7, IMPORTANT 1; 41 at
module level, 29 inside a definition, 4 above one) in about 13 s for the whole project on the loaded test PC
(a first version that parsed every Python file for its definitions took 41 s). Most hits are this repository's
`(docs/DESIGN.md Dnn)` citations; section-divider comments that cite a decision (`# -- decisions (docs/DESIGN.md
D33) ---`) attach to the module or to the definition right below them.

Review round: the project run now lists untracked files and non-ASCII names (2,669 files, 72 comments: ADR 64,
NOTE 7, IMPORTANT 1, in about 21 s on the loaded PC); two former ADR rows were source paths under a `decisions/`
folder. A 64 KB comment line of `a.a.a...` took 30.8 s in the citation regex before (a match could start after
every `.`); the citation patterns now start only at the start of a path, and the same line takes well under a
second (the test bounds it at 2 s).

### 93.4 Not done

- Outside Python a comment after code on the same line (`x = 1; // NOTE: ...`) is not read.
- Docstrings are not comments: a `Note:` section of a Python docstring is not listed (the excerpt shows it).
- Attachment is by position only; a section-divider comment directly above a function is attached to that
  function.
- Without facts (Java, Kotlin, Go ...) the definitions are the graph's spans, which may be heuristic (next
  symbol, capped); a comment past a heuristic end is attached to the module.
- `node_inspect` on a Java/Kotlin node matches the node's own span; a comment above an annotated method is
  attached when only comment and annotation lines come between.
- A whole-project run reads every listed file; there is no cache.

### 93.5 Tests

`tests/test_rationale.py`: markers, a continued block and an ADR path in Python; a trailing citation after code;
a `#` inside a string ignored; a comment above a decorated property and one between a decorator and its `def`
attached `above`; Javadoc past an `@Override` and a `//` line comment with a `DESIGN.md D50` citation, attached
with given spans; prose (`Note that`, a Markdown heading) skipped; `node_inspect` quoting the rows of a method and
none for a function without; a Java node through the graph's spans; the CLI for a symbol, a folder (`--json`), the
project with `--limit`, none and not found. Review round: an arrow-function constant in TypeScript gets the
comment above it (node_inspect and file); a stale file gives no rows (node_inspect note, CLI `stale`); rows carry
`attach_status`; a comment after a Python body's last statement is `inside`; a source folder named `decisions/`
is not a citation; a 64 KB comment line scans in under 2 s and cut text ends in `...`; U+2028 does not shift
line numbers; `.`, `./pkg`, an absolute folder and the project find a committed non-ASCII file and an untracked
one, a path outside the repository is not found; a broken index is reported with its error. Also run: `tests/test_mcp.py`, `tests/test_docs.py`,
`tests/test_line_endings.py`, `tests/test_backlog.py`, `tests/test_cli.py`, `tests/test_exact_and_fresh.py`.

## 94. Structural (AST pattern) search (D121, 2026-10-01)

### 94.1 Why

Text search finds spellings; it cannot say "every call of `foo` with at least one argument" or "every `return`
of a Java method" without a regex that breaks on line breaks, comments and nesting. ast-grep, Semgrep, Comby and
Sourcegraph's structural search answer such questions with code-shaped patterns and metavariables. Verinoda
already has the tree-sitter grammars the index reads, so the same kind of search costs no new dependency.

### 94.2 Decisions

- **Pattern = code with metavariables.** `$A` (an upper-case name) is one named node and captures its text; the
  same name twice must capture the same text; `$_` matches one node without capturing. `$$$REST` is zero or more
  nodes in a sequence of children (`$$$` alone: without capturing). The metavariables become placeholder
  identifiers (`VNMV_A`, `VNMVS_REST`) so every grammar parses them where an expression, a name or a statement
  may stand.
- **Parsed per language.** The pattern is parsed with the grammar of each language searched (the grammars of
  `anchors.TS_LANGS`, plus Python's). A fragment that is not a whole program on its own (a Java call or `return`)
  is parsed inside the smallest wrapper that parses without an error (a statement with `;`, a class body, a method
  body); the pattern's node is the innermost one spanning exactly its text (or its text plus the `;` the wrapper
  added). A language whose grammar cannot parse the pattern is not searched and is named
  (`not_searched.pattern_not_parsed`); a pattern that parses nowhere, or is only a metavariable, is refused
  (exit 2).
- **Matching.** Same node kind and the same children, a leaf the same text; commas and semicolons between
