when the code behind them changes and stay stale until someone runs `verify`, even when the change was undone;
and two analyses can record the same statement twice.

### 107.2 Decisions

- **`verinoda consolidate [--limit N] [--budget S] [--merge] [--dry-run]`**, CLI only. A negative `--limit` or
  `--budget` exits 2.
- **Stale claims are re-verified** with `verify` (static: cited lines and the files behind each claim) on the
  current tree, at most `--limit` (50) within `--budget` seconds (60): one whose code is back as it was, or
  whose cited lines re-check, is restored up to its recorded ceiling and rebound to the current snapshot; the
  rest stay stale. No test is run: `verify --run` stays the user's call. One claim failing never stops the
  others (it is listed, exit 1). `restored` counts a claim back at its status before it went stale (or
  higher); `changed_status` one that left stale for a lower status or contradicted.
- **The queue rotates.** Each attempt is recorded in the claim's `spec.consolidate_tried`; claims never tried
  come first (newest stale first), then the one tried longest ago, so a limit of N reaches every stale claim
  over a few runs instead of the same N each time. A folded duplicate is not re-verified. The bookkeeping keys
  (`duplicate_of`, `consolidate_tried`) are never copied into a new claim (a correction copies the spec).
- **The budget bounds the run.** When the tree changed since the last snapshot the index is refreshed once
  first, waiting for another build at most the budget (busy: nothing is re-verified, the reason is reported);
  each `verify` then runs with `wait=0`, so none blocks on a build lock.
- **Duplicates.** Claims with the same claim key (kind and semantic spec, subjects, else the normalised text),
  the same project and the same `valid_env`, not superseded, not already folded and neither stale nor
  contradicted form a group. The snapshot and `valid_version` are not part of the key: they default to the
  commit at creation, and a claim that is not stale holds on the current tree as far as invalidation knows; a
  stale claim is folded only once a re-verification restores it. `--merge` keeps the one with the best status,
  then the latest verification (the time of the snapshot `verified_at` names), and folds each other one into
  it in one transaction (`store.tx()` now nests: the outermost block commits): its supporting and qualifying
  evidence is linked to the kept claim (note `merged from`, its evidence group renamed `<duplicate>:<group>`
  so two claims' groups never merge), its refuting evidence is not carried, and the duplicate keeps its row and
  status with `spec.duplicate_of` and a history entry naming the kept claim. The kept claim's status is not
  changed: the next `verify` applies the rules to the union (re-assessing in the fold would lift a claim
  without verify's change check and rebind). Nothing is deleted, and a folded claim is not marked superseded
  (that would make it contradicted). `--merge` is not bounded by `--limit` or `--budget`: a fold is a few
  writes, and only an explicit `--merge` folds.
- **Conflicts.** A statement (key, project, `valid_env`) that is contradicted in one claim and not in another
  is reported separately and never folded: folding would hide the refutation.
- **After an update.** `update --consolidate`, or `claims.consolidate_on_update: true` in
  `.verinoda/config.json` (off by default), re-verifies up to 20 stale claims within 20 s after a complete
  update and reports the counts (errors included); it never merges. So the updates the git hooks start re-check
  stale claims too; `ui --watch` calls the update directly and does not. It is skipped when the update failed
  or was busy, and when `--fast` left the graph to a background build (no snapshot of the tree yet: each verify
  would start that build). A failure there never fails the update.

### 107.3 Measured

Tests only.

Review round: two reviews found that a fold re-assessed the kept claim (lifting a stale or changing a
contradicted one without verify's checks), that the stale queue picked the same newest N claims every run, that
a contradicted claim could be folded into a supported one with its refutations, that grouping ignored project
and environment, that evidence groups of two claims could merge, that `update --fast` followed by consolidation
could wait up to 600 s on the build lock, that the docs claimed `ui --watch` consolidates, that the tiebreak read
a snapshot id as a time, that a fold was not atomic, and that `restored` counted any non-stale result. Each is
fixed as described above and covered by a test.

### 107.4 Not done

- Only stale claims are re-verified; a claim that is merely old is not re-checked.
- Duplicates are exact on the claim key: two wordings of one fact are not found.
- The one index refresh before re-verifying is not interruptible: the budget bounds its wait for the lock, not
  the build itself; a tree edited during the run can still make a verify refresh the index (without waiting
  for a lock).
- A conflict is only reported; settling it (`verify`, a correction) stays the user's call.

### 107.5 Tests

`tests/test_consolidate.py`: a stale claim stays stale while its code differs and is restored when the code is
put back (a dry run changes nothing); the limit and the time budget; the queue rotates across runs; two claims
with one statement are folded (evidence linked, the group renamed, the duplicate marked and not superseded, the
group gone) and another claim untouched; a fold never changes the kept claim's status; a stale claim is not
folded; a contradicted claim and a supported one are a conflict, never folded, and refuting evidence is not
carried; claims of different projects or environments are not grouped; the tiebreak prefers the later
verification; a fold that fails part-way leaves nothing behind; `update` consolidates only with the setting and
with `--consolidate` (`restored == 1`), skips after a deferred `--fast` update, and reports an error without
failing; the CLI (a negative limit or budget exits 2). `tests/test_store.py`: nested transactions commit once
and roll back together.

## 108. Error and trace import (D135, 2026-10-01)

### 108.1 Why

`trace-log` maps the stack traces of a log onto the code, but production errors usually live in an error tracker
or a tracing backend, not in a log on disk. Sentry's event JSON and an OpenTelemetry trace in OTLP JSON carry the
same thing in a structured form: frames with a file, a line and a function. Reading them from an exported file
gives the same kind of evidence - what one run recorded - without a network call or an account.

### 108.2 Decisions

- No new command: `verinoda trace-log FILE` reads a JSON export as well as a log. A file whose text starts with
  `{` or `[` and parses - as one document, or as JSON lines where most lines parse or only the last one does not -
  and holds a Sentry event or a span with frames is an export. A file named `.json` / `.jsonl` / `.ndjson` that
  does not parse, or holds no event or span, is refused (exit 1) with the line and column; any other file that
  does not parse (`{main} starting`, `[14:02:08] [Server thread/INFO] ...`, a JSON log line followed by a
  traceback) or holds no event (a structured log) goes to the log reader as before. `--json` says which with
  `mode`: `export` or `log`.
- Formats: a Sentry event (`exception.values[].stacktrace.frames`, the API's `entries` form, a list of events,
  `{"data": [...]}`, JSON lines) and OTLP JSON (`resourceSpans` / `scopeSpans` or the older
  `instrumentationLibrarySpans` / `spans`). From a span: its `code.filepath` / `code.lineno` / `code.function`
  (and the newer `code.file.path` / `code.line.number` / `code.function.name`; with only `code.namespace`, the path
  is built from the class or module and the row says so - a namespace without a package, such as `Foo` or `a.`,
  builds none and the frame is "not in the repository") and the `exception.stacktrace` text of its `exception`
  events, read for Python, JVM and Node frames with the failure-signature reader's patterns. Frames are kept
  innermost last for every source; a JVM text's `Caused by:` blocks are each reversed on their own, so the root
  cause's throwing frame comes last. A line number is at most 9 ASCII digits; a text frame with anything else is
  skipped, a structured one has no line.
- Paths: whole-suffix matching over the indexed files, the rule `failsig.PathResolver.resolve` already used.
  `PathResolver.matches()` now returns every file that ties for the longest suffix, so an ambiguity is reported
  with its candidates (and the ones whose function fits the line) instead of silently giving nothing; `resolve()`
  keeps its behaviour. Backslash Windows paths, `file://` URLs and the repository's own absolute root are handled
  there; a Windows path that matches nothing as written is compared again with case folded. A Sentry JVM frame
  (`Foo.java` with `module: com.example.Foo`) is matched as `com/example/Foo.java` only, never as any other
  `Foo.java` of the project.
- A frame is `mapped` only when the file exists, the line is inside it, a recorded `context_line` equals the
  current line, and the frame's function is one of the definitions the index puts around that line (lambdas,
  `Object.handle`, `lambda$tick$2`, Go's `.func1`, `<init>` are reduced to the name compared; a name over 512
  characters is not compared). What a mapped frame was not compared on is named in `not_checked`: `source line`
  when the frame records none, `function name` when it has no name to compare (`<anonymous>`, `?`) or the file has
  no indexed definitions. A frame checked on nothing but its line's range says so on its row ("only the line's
  range was checked") and in the stored claim's text. Otherwise the row is `stale` (file missing on disk, line
  beyond the end, the recorded source line differs, the function name is not at that line - with what is there),
  `ambiguous`, or `not_in_repo` (no indexed file ends with the path: "file missing" for an `in_app` frame, "origin
  unknown" for a frame the export does not mark, which includes every frame of an OTLP export).
- Library frames are folded into a count with the first and last name: `in_app: false`, or a `site-packages` /
  `node_modules` / stdlib path on a frame the export does not mark `in_app: true`. A frame marked `in_app: true` is
  matched whatever its path looks like (a Go project's `internal/`, a checkout under `/lib/python...`).
- A mapped row carries `status: observed` and the event's scope: what that event recorded, not what always
  happens. `store()` records one claim per mapped frame (at most 50 a run) whose evidence is the frame as read,
  kept under `.verinoda/logs/<name>-<hash>.frames.json`. Only the frames are kept, redacted, not the export: a
  Sentry event also carries request headers, the user and local variables. The same export imported again adds
  no claim: one with the same kept file, event and frame that is not stale is reported as `existing`. `--json`
  carries a `claims_note`: a stored claim's evidence never verifies.
- Limits are applied while reading: at most 200 events (an OTLP document stops building spans at the limit), the
  innermost 200 frames of each, 5,000 lines of one `exception.stacktrace` text.

### 108.3 Measured

- The fixtures (`tests/fixtures/trace_import/`): a two-event Sentry export (Python and JVM, the `entries` form)
  gives 3 mapped, 3 stale (line beyond the end, another function at that line, a changed source line),
  1 ambiguous, 1 not in the repository, 2 library frames; an OTLP export with two spans gives 5 mapped frames and
  one JDK frame (`java/lang/Thread.java`) reported as not in the repository, origin unknown.
- A 5,000-frame event reads the innermost 200 frames and says so (tested with three such events).
- Review round: a `{`-led log that is not JSON was refused; it is read as a log again unless named as JSON. A
  5,000-digit line number or a superscript `2` aborted the run; such a text frame is now skipped and a structured
  one has no line. Function-name reduction used two backtracking patterns (the reviewers timed 27 s and 2.9 s on
  long names); it is string operations on a name capped at 512 characters, and the test bounds pathological names to
  under 0.5 s. A frame checked on nothing but its line's range was reported like a checked one; it is labelled.
  Unmatched frames of unknown origin were folded as library frames, and `in_app: true` was overridden by a
  library-looking path; both fixed. A small JSON-lines export whose only other line was cut was refused; it is read.
  A repeated import duplicated its claims. JVM `Caused by:` blocks were reversed as one list. `code.namespace`
  values without a package built paths that matched any file of that name. An OTLP document built every span before
  the event limit applied.

### 108.4 Not done

- Stored claims have the status the claim rules allow for evidence Verinoda did not produce (`agent_report`
  never verifies): in practice `weak_inference`, as for `trace-log`. The report's rows are `observed` for their
  event; the stored claim does not claim more than its evidence allows, and the command and `claims_note` say so.
- A mapped frame without a `context_line` (every OTLP frame) was not compared with the source line, only placed
  inside the file and, when it has a name, inside a definition of that name.
- Path matching is case-sensitive except for a Windows-looking path (a drive letter or backslashes) that matches
  nothing as written: it is compared again with case folded. A macOS path in another case is not.
- Only the indexed files are candidates: a frame in a file the index does not hold is "not in the repository".
- `exception.stacktrace` text is read for Python, JVM and Node frames; Go, Rust, .NET and Ruby text stacks are
  not (their span `code.*` attributes are).
- A file over 32 MB is refused when named `.json` / `.jsonl` / `.ndjson`, otherwise read as a log; at most 200
  events, the innermost 200 frames of each and 50 stored claims a run. Nothing is fetched from Sentry or a
  collector: the export must be on disk.
- A JSON-lines file where half the lines or more do not parse is not JSON lines, unless the only line that fails
  is the last one.
- Frames are not linked to the callers and callees in the graph, nor to GameTests (`trace-log`'s log path does
  that for JVM logs).

### 108.5 Tests

`tests/test_trace_import.py`: telling an export from a log (JSON lines with a cut last line, a single event and a
cut line, UTF-16, bytes that are not UTF-8, broken and deeply nested JSON, a `{`-led log and a JSON log line
followed by a traceback read as logs, a named file with half its lines broken refused); line numbers that are not
numbers (a superscript `2`, 5,000 digits in Python, JVM and Node text) skipped without aborting; function-name
reduction in
bounded time on pathological names; JVM `Caused by:` order; `code.namespace` without a package; the OTLP event
limit applied while reading; `PathResolver.matches()` naming every file of a shared suffix while `resolve()` still
picks none; the Sentry fixture's mapped, stale, ambiguous, missing and library frames (a Windows absolute path, the
`entries` form, a JVM frame); the OTLP fixture's `code.*` attributes and Python and JVM `exception.stacktrace`,
its JDK frame of unknown origin; the CLI storing one claim per mapped frame with only the frames kept, `mode` and
`claims_note` in `--json`, and a repeated import adding none; the CLI refusing broken or empty named exports and
leaving a structured log and a `{`-led log to the log reader (`mode: log`); hostile frames (a `site-packages` path
whose tail is a project file, a library class sharing a project file name reported as not in the repository, a
Windows path in another case, an `in_app` frame under `/lib/python` mapped, a frame checked on nothing but its
line's range labelled, an unmarked unmatched frame not folded, line 0, a boolean line, a non-object frame, 5,000
frames).

## 109. Specs traced to code and tests (D136, 2026-10-01)

### 109.1 Why

Kiro specs, GitHub spec-kit and Tessl keep requirements next to the code, but nothing checks that a
requirement is still backed by anything: a test gets renamed, a claim goes stale, a function moves, and the
spec keeps saying the system does X. Verinoda already has the pieces (claims with a status, file:line
evidence, symbol facts per file, test detection); this decision joins them to requirement criteria and makes
the unbacked ones visible, with an exit code a CI job can read.

### 109.2 Decisions

- **Format.** A spec is a Markdown file (`.md`, `.markdown`) under the specs folder. A criterion is a line that
  starts, after an optional list marker, task box (`- [ ] [R21] ...`) or bold, with an id in brackets holding a
  digit (`[CART-1]`, `[R1]`, `[AC-2.3]`; a task box `[x]` alone is not one; the id is at most 64 characters).
  The EARS style is recommended, not required: the criterion's EARS pattern is named (`event` WHEN, `state`
  WHILE, `unwanted` IF, `optional` WHERE, `ubiquitous`), or null without a SHALL. `evidence:` lines under a
  criterion (any number, until the next criterion, heading, or another list item or paragraph at the
  criterion's indent or less) list references separated by commas or spaces; one with spaces goes in backticks.
  Not read: fenced code at any indent (inside list items too), indented code (four columns past the enclosing
  list item, after a blank line), HTML comments (one line or several) and link reference definitions
  (`[v2]: https://...`, `[RFC2119]: ...`).
- **Folder.** `.verinoda/specs/` by default, like the decision records; a committed folder for CI through
  `[specs] dir` in `verinoda.toml` or `[tool.verinoda.specs] dir` in `pyproject.toml` (read with the same
  helper as the decisions folder), `specs.dir` in `.verinoda/config.json`, or `--specs-dir`. A folder outside
  the repository is an error, and so is a setting that cannot be known: a `verinoda.toml`, `pyproject.toml` or
  `.verinoda/config.json` that does not parse, a `specs` that is not a table or object, a `dir` that is not a
  string (exit 2, never the default folder). The folder is walked without following links or junctions (they
  are listed as skipped), dot folders and vendored folders (`node_modules`, `venv`, `dist`, `build`, ...) are
  left out, and a file whose real path is outside the repository is not read.
- **References are written, never guessed.** A claim id (`clm_...` or `claim:ID`); a test id `path::name` or
  `path::Class::name` in a test file, or `test:ID`; `path::Name` in other code; `path:12` / `path:12-30`; a
  bare path; `code:` forces a path. Nothing is matched by text similarity: a criterion with no reference is
  unevidenced, and no suggestion is made.
- **What counts as a test.** Python: a `test*` function, or a `test*` method of a `Test*` or `TestCase` class,
  not a pytest fixture; a test class stands for the tests it holds (listed). Go: `TestX`, `BenchmarkX`,
  `ExampleX`, `FuzzX`. Java, Kotlin, C#, Rust: a function with a test annotation or attribute (the rules of
  `testcode`). These are definitions read from the file's facts (`statically_verified`). JavaScript and
  TypeScript: the title as the first argument of an `it(` / `test(` call, found by a text pattern, so
  `strong_inference`; a `describe(` suite or an `it.skip` / `todo` is not a test. A helper, fixture, a class
  with no test, or a method of a non-test class is a code pointer; a quoted string anywhere else, and any
  string in a Python file, is never a test. A parametrized id is checked by its function name; the parameters
  are not checked, and the reference says so.
- **What counts as evidence.** A claim whose recorded status is verified (observed, experiment, static,
  primary source) and whose cited file lines (source code, documents, dependency or reference sources, static
  resolutions) still hold the content recorded for them (`evidence.check_source`: the content hash, or the
  anchored symbol for a block that moved); a test as above. A code pointer (`path::Name`, `path:lines`, a
  bare path) is labelled `pointer`: checked to resolve, it only shows where the behaviour lives, never that it
  holds; an inference claim is not evidence.
- **The store is read-only.** It is opened only when a claim is cited, with `sqlite3.connect("file:...?mode=ro",
  uri=True)` (the path URI-quoted, so spaces and non-ASCII names work on Windows), no migration, no journal
  setting, nothing written. A missing store, a file that is not a database, or a schema version other than this
  build's leaves the claims `unchecked` with the reason; a corrupt store is never opened when no claim is cited.
- **How a reference resolves.** Paths compare with their case on disk (a case-insensitive file system would
  accept `SRC/a.py`), names in NFC (macOS may store them decomposed), and a link leading outside the
  repository does not resolve; a definition is found in the file's facts (`anchors.facts_for_path`: Python and
  the tree-sitter languages). Where a language has no facts the name is searched as a word, which is
  `strong_inference` and says so. Lines must be inside the file.
- **Criterion status**, strongest problem first: `broken` (a reference does not resolve, cites a stale or
  contradicted claim, or a verified claim whose cited lines changed), `verified`, `tested`, `tested_inferred`
  (a test found only by a text pattern or a word search), `unchecked`, `unevidenced`. A stale claim's
  supersession is followed (`superseded_by`, else the newest claim that `supersedes` it) to the live claim,
  which the reference names.
- **Exit codes**, as the other checks: 1 while a criterion is broken or unevidenced or a spec line has a
  problem (a SHALL line with no id, an evidence line with no criterion above it or with nothing on it, an id
  used twice: compared case-insensitively, across files), with status `failed` when something is broken or
  malformed and `unevidenced` when that is the only cause; else 3 when something was not checked (unchecked
  claims, a spec file too large or unreadable, a configured folder that does not exist); 2 on an error; 0
  otherwise (`ok`, `no_criteria`, or `no_specs` when the default folder does not exist).
- **Output.** The text lists every criterion with its references, a cited claim's evidence locations with
  what the re-read found, the problems, the limits and, when claims were read, the last index time and its age.
  The JSON adds the spec `line` of each reference, the claim's evidence `at`, and problems as
  `{at, kind, message}`.
- **Lines** are split at LF only, a CR before it dropped, so a CRLF file or a Unicode line separator inside
  a sentence keeps the line numbers an editor shows (spec files and the files a test is searched in alike). A
  criterion's sentence may wrap onto the following lines; `none`, `tbd` and `todo` on an evidence line are no
  reference. A closing fence must be as long as the opening one. The line patterns are linear: an id is
  bounded, the text is taken greedily and trimmed in code, `path:lines` is split in code.
- CLI only (`spec check [--specs-dir DIR] [--json]`); no MCP tool, so the core menu does not change.

### 109.3 Measured

- A five-criterion spec over this repository's own tests and code: 1 tested, 2 unevidenced (a helper cited as
  a test, now a pointer; lines only), 1 broken (a test name that does not exist), 1 unchecked (a claim with no
  store), a link reference definition not read, status `failed`, exit 1, in 0.75 s wall time including the
  interpreter start.
- Review round: two reviews found fourteen issues, all confirmed and fixed. A helper, fixture or class counted
  as a test, and a quoted string anywhere (Python files included) matched a test title; a link reference
  definition was read as a criterion; a verified claim whose cited code had changed passed; the id and text
  patterns backtracked (`"[a" + "1" * 20000` took 11 s, now the six long-line cases of the timing test take
  0.07 s together); the store was migrated and given a `.gitignore` by a read-only check, and a corrupt store
  failed the check even with no claim cited; a broken `verinoda.toml` silently fell back to the default
  folder; links and junctions were followed and dot or vendored folders read; indented code, fences in list
  items and HTML comments were read; references had no spec line; code pointers were labelled
  `statically_verified`; an evidence line under an unrelated item attached to the criterion above; a
  supersession chain stopped after one step; a task box before an id hid the criterion.
- 30 tests in `tests/test_specs.py` cover each status, each reference kind, real tests against helpers,
  fixtures and classes, JS titles, CRLF, a non-ASCII repository path, duplicate ids, fences, indented code,
  comments, link definitions, task boxes, wrapped sentences, path case, paths outside the repository, an unread
  file, the folder settings and broken ones, links and junctions, dot and vendored folders, the read-only store
  (empty, corrupt, another schema), changed claim evidence, a supersession chain and the timing of long lines.

### 109.4 Not done

- Whether the cited claim or test really covers the criterion is the author's statement; it is not judged.
- Claim statuses are read as recorded; the claim's cited file lines are re-read, but other evidence (an
  experiment, a URL) is not re-run, so `verinoda update` is still the way to refresh claims.
- A test is checked to be defined, not run, and its last outcome is not read; the parameters of a
  parametrized test id are not checked.
- A JS/TS test is found by a text pattern on its title (a commented-out call would match); it is
  `tested_inferred`, never `tested`.
- The Markdown reading is line based: lazy continuation lines, block quotes holding criteria and list items
  nested in other containers are approximated.
- Kiro's and spec-kit's own files are not read as they are: their criteria need an `[ID]` added.
- No suggestion of tests or code by name for an unevidenced criterion.

### 109.5 Tests

- `tests/test_specs.py` (new).
- `tests/test_docs.py` (README Commands row, ARCHITECTURE module row), `tests/test_cli.py`,
  `tests/test_line_endings.py`.

## 110. Trigram regex index (D137, 2026-10-01)

### 110.1 Why

Verinoda had ranked retrieval (`query`), structural search (`grep-ast`) and the MCP Grep hook, but no plain exact or
regular-expression search: an agent or a user looking for every `TODO`, every `cap_response(` or every `class
\w+Error` had to walk every file. Zoekt, Cursor and Moderne answer such searches from a trigram index. On a
repository of a few thousand files a walk costs seconds; most of that is reading files that cannot match.

### 110.2 Decisions

- New command `verinoda search PATTERN [PATH ...] [-i] [-F] [--max-results N] [--timeout S] [--rebuild] [--json]`, module
  `verinoda/trigram.py`. No MCP tool (the Grep hook and `query` cover agents; a tool can follow).
- **The index** is `.verinoda/index/trigram.db` (SQLite, derived and disposable like `search.db`): for every text file
  (git's tracked and untracked-not-ignored files, or a walk outside git; no NUL byte in the first 8 KiB; at most
  2 MB) its sorted array of distinct byte trigrams with ASCII letters lowered (24-bit integers), and for every
  trigram the sorted list of files holding it. Trigrams are computed with numpy (already a dependency).
- **Freshness without a daemon:** every search lists the files (`git ls-files -co --exclude-standard`), reads their
  sizes and modification times a directory at a time (`os.scandir` on 8 threads: on Windows the listing carries
  both, so no file is opened) and re-indexes the files that differ, dropping the ones gone. A changed file's new
  trigram array is diffed with the stored one and only the postings that differ are rewritten, in one transaction.
  The first search builds the whole index.
- **What a pattern requires** (`required`): the parsed expression (`re._parser`) becomes an AND/OR tree of literal
  runs of at least three bytes that every match must contain: a sequence ANDs its parts, a repeat with a minimum of
  one requires its body, an alternation requires one of its branches (nothing when any branch requires nothing),
  and classes, `.`, anchors, backreferences and lookarounds break a run. Candidates are the files whose postings
  hold every trigram of a required literal.
- **Soundness over speed:** the expression, not the index, decides every match; the index only picks the files to
  read. Case-insensitive patterns (`-i`, `(?i)`, `(?i:...)`) require only ASCII runs without `i`, `k` and `s`,
  because Python's case folding matches those to `İ`, `ı`, the Kelvin sign and the long s (measured on Python 3.13
  over every code point); a non-ASCII character or U+FFFD breaks a run under any flags where its bytes may differ.
  Files are read as UTF-8 with replacement; `^`/`$` work per line (multiline).
- **Output:** each match is `path:line` with the line's text (cut at 300 characters), `status: observed` - what the
  file says now, like a grep - plus the number of files indexed and read, whether the pattern narrowed the files,
  and the time spent per stage. Exit 0 with matches, 1 with none, 2 on a bad pattern or argument.

### 110.3 Measured

On this repository (2,710 files, 45 MB of text), with the full test suite and three review agents running on the
same machine:

- building the index: 11 s (the first version, with Python sets, took 65 s); `trigram.db` is 56 MB;
- a search with nothing changed spends 0.35 s keeping the index fresh (git's file list about 0.18 s, the directory
  scan 0.08 s);
- `def changes_vs_base`: 10 of 2,710 files read, 0.39 s in total (a walk: 2.7 s);
- `cap_response|MAX_FILE_BYTES`: 58 files read, 0.55 s (walk 3.3 s);
- `todo|fixme` with `-i`: 56 files read, 0.68 s (walk 6.0 s);
- `class \w+Error\b`: 731 files read (`class ` and `error` are common), 1.1 s (walk 2.7 s);
- `sipariş` with `-i`: only `par` is required (`i`, `s` and `ş` fold), 1,683 files read, 3.9 s (walk 4.8 s);
- `\w+`: nothing required, every file read, 9.6 s (walk 7.9 s).

Every pattern returned exactly the matches the walk found (the benchmark compared the totals; the tests compare
the sets of `path:line`).

Review round: two reviewers (soundness, with an 8,300-pattern differential fuzz against a walk that found no
missed match; robustness and performance) found a failed read cached forever, two first searches at once failing on
the files table, a damaged database crashing with exit 1, no time limit, the incremental update slower than a
rebuild after many edits, file names SQLite cannot hold, paths matched as raw strings, a same-size same-time rewrite
missed, surrogates in a pattern crashing, and the file list and postings read in two snapshots. All fixed: unreadable
files are stored without a time and read by the search, writers compare under the write lock (ids never reused),
a damaged index is rebuilt, `--timeout` with an `incomplete` status and exit 3, a rebuild past a fifth of the files,
such names skipped, paths resolved against the current directory (outside or missing: exit 2; any case on Windows),
the racily clean rule, surrogates break literals, and one read transaction. Each has a test
(`tests/test_trigram_robust.py`).

### 110.4 Not done

- Text files only: binary files and files over 2 MB are neither indexed nor searched.
- A pattern without a literal run of three characters every match must hold reads every file: correct, and slower
  than a walk by the freshness check. Case-insensitive searches narrow less (the folding letters break runs).
- "Under a second on 2,000 files" holds for selective case-sensitive literals; `class \w+Error` (733 files read)
  took 1.2 s, `-i sipariş` 3.8 s.
- The freshness check costs about 0.35 s on 2,700 files each search. Size and modification time decide whether a
  file changed: a rewrite that keeps both is caught while it is within 3 s of the last refresh (git's racily clean
  rule), not later.
- The time limit is checked between files; one catastrophic expression on one file is not interrupted (Python's
  `re` cannot be).
- The full build holds every file's trigram array in memory (about 60 bytes per posting: 300 MB for this
  repository's 5 million postings); the index takes about 1.2 times the text it covers.

### 110.5 Tests

`tests/test_trigram.py`: the requirement tree (sequences, classes, alternations with and without a requirement-free
branch, optional and repeated groups, short literals); case folding (`i`, `k`, `s` and non-ASCII letters break
literals under `-i`, `(?i)` and not without it, with the folding matches themselves checked); search results equal
a walk's `path:line` set for literal, class, case-insensitive, non-ASCII, alternation, anchored and unnarrowed
patterns in a repository whose path has a space and `ş`; binary and git-ignored files left out; path scope; an
incremental update after an edit, a delete and a new file (the old content leaves the postings); a rebuild; CLI exit
codes; pathological patterns stay bounded. `tests/test_trigram_robust.py`: the racily clean rewrite, an unreadable file
tried again, three searches at once, a damaged database rebuilt, a rebuild after many changes, surrogates and
zero-length matches, path resolution (absolute, relative to the current directory, outside, missing, case), the time
limit and its exit code.

## 111. Mutation testing scoped to the diff (D138, 2026-10-01)

### 111.1 Why

The change review says which tests reach a change (the test map, static reach), and `review --run-tests` says whether
they pass. Neither says whether those tests *check* the change: a test that calls a changed function and asserts
nothing about the changed branch passes before and after any edit to it. Mutation testing answers that directly
(mutmut, cosmic-ray, PIT, cargo-mutants, Stryker), but run over a whole project it costs hours. Scoped to the lines
a diff changed and to the tests that reach them, it costs one test run per mutant and answers the question a
reviewer has: is this change tested, or only executed?

### 111.2 Decisions

- New command `verinoda mutate [--base REF] [--tests TEST_ID ...] [--file PATH] [--max-mutants N] [--timeout S]
  [--json]` (module `verinoda/mutate.py`). Python only; no MCP tool (each mutant is a test run: too slow for an
  agent's turn by default).
- **Changed lines:** the added and replaced lines of the working tree against the base (default HEAD), in `.py`
  files that are not tests or test support, from `treestate.changes_vs_base`. Deleted lines have nothing to mutate.
- **Operators**, one mutant per site on a changed line: comparison swaps (`<`/`<=`, `>`/`>=`, `==`/`!=`,
  `in`/`not in`, `is`/`is not`), `+`/`-`, `*`/`/`, `//` -> `*`, `and`/`or` (two operands), `True`/`False`, an
  integer `n` -> `n+1`, `not x` -> `x`, an `if`/`while` condition negated (single-line conditions), `return x` ->
  `return None`. A fixed, small set chosen for the faults reviews miss (off-by-one, inverted conditions, ignored
  results), not completeness.
- **Splicing, not unparsing:** each mutant replaces one span of the source text at the AST's offsets (UTF-8 columns
  converted to characters), so the rest of the file is byte for byte the same and line numbers in failures match.
  An operator is located in the text between its two operands with comments blanked, and only when exactly one
  match is there. Docstrings and comments are never mutated. A mutant that does not compile is dropped; identical
  texts are one mutant. At most `--max-mutants` (default 25, cap 500) are run, in source order; the rest are
  counted (`not_run_over_limit`), never silently dropped.
- **Tests:** the change review's `affected` block (the test map's observed tests, tests the change edits, static
  reach), or `--tests`. No test: status `no_tests` with a next step.
- **Runs:** every run is an experiment (`experiments.run`) on a copy of HEAD with the working tree's changed files
  replayed on top (deleted ones left out), and the mutant on top of that: the same command policy, trust rule and
  isolation as any test run (an untrusted project runs only in a container). The command is `python -m pytest -q
  -x -p no:cacheprovider <test ids>`.
- **Baseline first:** the selected tests run once on the unmutated change. When they do not pass, no mutant can be
  judged and none is run (`baseline_failed`, or `not_run` when the run was refused or inconclusive).
- **Verdicts:** `killed` (the tests failed), `survived` (they passed), `timeout` (counted apart: nothing failed),
  `not_run` (refused or inconclusive). Each row carries its experiment id and `status: observed` (what that run
  showed). A survivor carries a `strong_inference` claim "the selected tests do not check path:line": never
  verified, since the mutant may be equivalent and the selection may have left out a test that kills it.
- **Exit codes:** 0 when every mutant run was killed and none was left out, or no mutant could be made; 2 on an
  error (bad arguments, not a git work tree); 3 otherwise (survivors, a timeout, a run not made, mutants over the
  limit, no test, a failing baseline).

### 111.3 Measured

- A scratch repository with `price(n, vip)` changed to `if vip and n > 5: return n - 1` and one test that calls
  `price(10, False)`: 7 mutants, 2 killed (`and` -> `or`, the negated condition), 5 survived on lines 2 and 3 -
  the test never takes the `vip` branch. About 20 s in total (8 runs of one test, each a copy of the repository),
  so about 2.5 s per mutant on that repository; a run costs what copying the repository and one pytest start cost.
- With no `--tests`, the change review selected the one test by static reach.

### 111.4 Not done

- A surviving mutant may be equivalent to the original; it is a lead, not proof.
- Only the selected tests run. A test the selection left out may kill a survivor; name more with `--tests`.
- Python only; a fixed operator set; no mutants on deleted lines or in non-Python files; multi-line conditions are
  not negated; comparisons with more than one operator (`a < b < c`) and `and`/`or` with three or more operands are
  left alone.
- Each mutant is one full run of the selected tests in a fresh copy of the repository: large repositories pay the
  copy every time. Mutants run one after another.
- `-x` stops at the first failing test, so a killed mutant names no test that killed it beyond its experiment's log.

### 111.5 Tests

`tests/test_mutate.py`: mutants only on changed lines, never in docstrings or comments, the rest of the file
unchanged, every mutant compiles; the operator set and deduplication; non-ASCII offsets; unparseable text gives no
mutant; changed-line detection; an end-to-end run on a scratch repository (a path with a space and `ş`) where the
negated condition is killed and the untested branch's mutants survive with their line, experiment and a
`strong_inference` claim, with the over-limit count; a failing baseline runs no mutant; CLI exit codes (0 nothing
to mutate, 3 when mutants exist but were not run, an argument error).

## 112. Guards written as programs (D139, 2026-10-01)

### 112.1 Why

The guard kinds of a decision record (`only_in`, `no_edge`, `layers`, `allow_edges`, `public`, `dependency`)
cover the rules that fit one line of `key=value`. A team's rule often does not: "every handler in `api/` that
writes calls `audit()` first", "no module under `core/` reads a setting that is not in `settings.py`". Archgate
lets an ADR carry its check as a small program with access to the code. Here the same thing runs inside
`decide check`, so its result sits beside the other guards' (file:line, exit codes, baseline, waivers, SARIF,
`--changed`), instead of in a separate CI step nobody connects to the decision.

### 112.2 Decisions

- **A new guard kind `script path=FILE.py [timeout=SECONDS]`.** The file is a Python file inside the repository
  (relative, no `..`; `decide record` / `decide guard` also want it to exist) that defines `check(guard)`.
  `timeout` is 1-600 seconds, default 60. The spec is checked again when a record is read, so a hand edit
  that points it at `/etc/x.py` or gives `timeout: true` makes the record unreadable (not enforced, reported),
  never a guard that runs something else.
- **What the script gets** (`GuardAPI`, read-only): `repo`, `spec`, `files()`, `nodes(file=None)`, `node(id)`,
  `edges(relations=None, from_file=None, to_file=None)` - each edge in its true direction with the file and
  line the index cites -, `claims(status=None, limit=1000)` - the stored claims, newest first, with their
  supporting evidence as `path:line` -, and `read(path)`. It reports with `guard.violation(path, line, why)`
  and `guard.possible(path, line, why)`; the return value is not read. The graph is `.verinoda/index/graph.json`
  as the index last wrote it, without the receiver-call edges `index.load` adds from `receiver_calls.json`
  (said in `GuardAPI.edges`, the README and each result's limits); `decide check` refreshes the index first
  when a script guard is enforced, as it does for edge guards. The file filters of `nodes` and `edges` are
  exact strings (`/`-separated, case-sensitive on Windows too). The claims are read by Verinoda before the
  child starts - the newest 20,000, with a limit naming how many older ones were left out - and handed to it
  as data: the child has no database connection.
- **Its result is evidence like the other guards'.** Every finding must cite a line of a file of the
  repository: the file is read again and the line must exist; the line's text is shown as for any guard, and
  the path is the file's own spelling (`APP/VIEWS.PY` on Windows is cited as `app/views.py`). A citation
  outside the repository (a link or junction that leads out of it too), past the end of the file, without a
  line or of a missing file is listed under `unknown` (so the check exits 3), never dropped and never counted
  as a violation. A VIOLATED of a script guard has the status `strong_inference`, not `statically_verified`:
  the script's own logic is not verified here, only its citation. A POSSIBLE is `weak_inference`. A finding
  counts as new under `--changed` / `--base` when its file or the script changed; a pre-existing one says
  "pre-existing: FILE and the guard's script SCRIPT unchanged since REF". The first 500 findings are listed,
  the rest counted under `unknown`. `decide check`'s text output prints a script finding's limits under it.
- **A script that does not end well is `unknown`, never ok.** An exception (with its type, message and the
  script's line), `sys.exit` (any code, 0 too), `os._exit`, no `check` function, a syntax error, a timeout,
  a child that prints no result: each is `unknown` with the reason, and `decide check` exits 3. An ok means the
  script ran `check` to its end; its scope is `{"script_runs": 1}` and its limits say what that does not
  prove. What the script printed is kept (its last 2,000 characters; 400 in the limits).
- **The result channel.** Before the script loads, the child reads the whole request from stdin (nothing is
  left there to read again), takes the per-run nonce out of it, keeps a private copy of the stdout pipe
  (`os.dup(1)`), points file descriptor 1 at the null device and `sys.stdout` / `sys.__stdout__` /
  `sys.stderr` at the in-memory tail of what the script prints. The result is written only to the private
  copy and carries the nonce; the parent takes the line with this run's nonce. A script that prints a fake
  result line, writes it to `sys.__stdout__` or `os.write(1, ...)` and calls `os._exit(0)` leaves no result
  (`unknown`); one that writes result-like lines to every descriptor, the private one included, makes the
  run an error even when the real result says ok.
- **Where it runs.** Only from the CLI's `decide check` and `decide baseline` (`guards.check(run_scripts=True)`);
  `update`'s summary line, `what-if` and MCP `decision_check` report a script guard as `unknown` ("runs only
  from the CLI"). `update` counts them on their own ("1 script guard(s): `decide check` runs them"), not as
  "not checked" on every update. MCP `decision_record` refuses to record or add a script guard, and refuses
  `accept` when one of the chosen guards is a script guard (a proposed one written into a record by hand is
  accepted in a terminal). The refusal splits the spec as `parse_guard` does (`s""cript`, `'scr'ipt`,
  `sc"ri"pt` are the kind `script` there too), and `record`, `add_guards` and `accept` check the parsed kind
  again (`allow_scripts=False` from MCP). MCP `import` proposes only `only_in` guards; `supersede`, `link` and
  `waive` activate no guard. `decide ask` does not apply script guards (they say nothing about one dependency).
- **Trust is the boundary.** A script guard runs the project's own code with the user's privileges, exactly
  like the project's tests under `experiment run` in a trusted project. In a project not marked with
  `verinoda trust` (stored outside every repository) it is not run and is `unknown`, with the next step for
  the user and "an agent must never run it for them". A CI job that should run script guards trusts its
  checkout itself (`verinoda trust . --yes`). A record edited by hand by anyone who can write the repository
  can carry an accepted script guard: trusting a project means trusting its content, as for its tests.
- **What the child process gives.** A child process of Verinoda's own interpreter (`sys.executable`), never
  the project's `.venv`, started with `-I -B -X utf8`: no `PYTHON*` variables, no user site-packages, neither
  the script's folder nor the working folder on `sys.path`, no bytecode written, and `open()` reads UTF-8
  whatever the machine's code page. The environment is the test runs' short allowlist (`PATH`, `SYSTEMROOT`,
  `LANG`, ...: no tokens or keys) with `HOME`/`USERPROFILE`/`TMP`/`TEMP`/`TMPDIR` set to a fresh folder that is
  deleted afterwards. The working folder is the project root; the request goes on stdin (no paths on the
  command line, so spaces and non-ASCII letters need nothing). The timeout kills the child.
- **The audit hook is a tripwire, not a sandbox.** Installed before the script is read, it refuses: socket
  creation, connect, bind and name lookups (`urllib`, `http.client` too); process creation (`subprocess`,
  `os.system`, `exec*`, `spawn*`, `posix_spawn`, `startfile`, `fork`, `kill`); `ctypes` libraries and calls;
  `sqlite3` connections and extensions; adding another audit hook (CPython then drops it silently); opening a
  file for writing, appending, creating or truncating, and remove, rename, mkdir, rmdir, chmod, chown, link,
  symlink, utime, mkfifo, mknod and the `shutil` copy/move/rmtree calls; an `mmap` of a file with write access
  (`ACCESS_DEFAULT`, `ACCESS_WRITE`; `ACCESS_READ`, `ACCESS_COPY` and anonymous memory stay allowed). On
  Windows also `_winapi.CreateFile`, `CreateJunction`, `CreateNamedPipe`, `CreatePipe`, `OpenProcess` and
  `TerminateProcess`, `msvcrt.open_osfhandle`, the registry writes (`winreg.CreateKey`, `SetValue` /
  `SetValueEx`, `DeleteKey`, `DeleteValue`, `SaveKey`, `LoadKey`, `ConnectRegistry`, the reflection calls,
  `OpenKey` with write access; reads stay allowed), and `open` / `os.listdir` / `os.scandir` / `os.chdir` of a
  UNC or device path (`\\server\share`, `//server/share`, `\\.\pipe\...`; `\\?\C:\...` is local and allowed).
  A refused call raises `PermissionError` in the script ("refused in a script guard: socket.connect ..."), so
  the guard is `unknown` unless the script handles it.
- **What gets past it** (said in each result's limits, the module docstring and the README). Audit hooks are
  not a security boundary (CPython's documentation says so). Calls that raise no audit event: `os.stat` and the
  `exists()` / `is_file()` family (which reach a UNC path or a mapped network drive too), `_winapi.WriteFile`
  and `CreateFileMapping` on a handle the process already has, named anonymous `mmap` memory, a drive letter
  mapped to a network share. Native code (an extension module the script imports). Handles opened before the
  hook (the inherited standard streams). A script that digs through the interpreter - frames, `gc`,
  monkeypatching `json` or `os` - can find the nonce or change the result before it is written: the nonce
  stops a stray or naive fake result, not a determined script. Reads are not limited: the script can read
  every file the user can and print it (the output is shown back, cut). Memory and CPU are limited only by the
  timeout; on a timeout only the child is killed (it cannot start processes through the calls above, but
  native code could). An untrusted project's script does not run at all.
- **Pre-commit.** No hook ran `decide check` before (`verinoda hooks` re-indexes after commits, checkouts and
  merges). `.pre-commit-hooks.yaml` now offers `verinoda-decide-check` for the pre-commit framework (3.2.0 or
  later, `stages: [pre-commit]`): `verinoda decide check --changed`, no file names, always run; violations new
  or touched since HEAD stop the commit (exit 1), and so does a guard that could not be checked (exit 3). A
  script guard runs there like in any `decide check`, so a collaborator who has not run `verinoda trust` on
  their checkout gets exit 3 (script guards unknown) on every commit; the file's comment and the README say so.

### 112.3 Measured

Windows 11, Python 3.13, the worktree on a loaded machine:

- An empty script in a folder whose name has spaces and non-ASCII letters: 0.26-0.37 s per run (five runs),
  the child's start included.
- Loading this repository's graph in the child (`graph.json`, 36 MB, 30,971 nodes, 73,325 edges): 0.96 s, done
  only when the script asks for the graph.
- The audit hook, tried from a script: a TCP connect, `getaddrinfo`, `subprocess.run`, `os.system`, `open(...,
  "w")`, `open(..., "a")`, `os.remove`, `os.mkdir`, `ctypes` (on Windows importing `ctypes` itself fails) and a
  second audit hook are all refused; reading a file works; no file was created, changed or removed.

Review round. Two reviews found an MCP refusal that split the spec on spaces while `parse_guard` uses shlex
(`s""cript path=g.py` was recorded), MCP `accept` activating a proposed script guard, the read-only claims
connection reachable from the script (`guard._conn`: `PRAGMA query_only=OFF`, `VACUUM INTO` and `ATTACH
'file:X?mode=rwc'` wrote files outside the repository), Windows calls the hook let through (`_winapi`,
`winreg`, `msvcrt.open_osfhandle`, a writable `mmap`, UNC paths), and a result a script could forge by
printing a result line and calling `os._exit(0)`. All fixed as described above, each with a test; the audit
events were checked by name on this machine (`_winapi.WriteFile` and `CreateFileMapping` raise none and are
listed as gaps). An empty script now runs in 0.29-0.43 s (five runs). Reading the claims in the parent:
0.65 s and 4.5 MB of JSON for 20,000 claims of a synthetic 25,000-claim store, every run; this repository's
own store holds 6.

### 112.4 Not done

- Not a sandbox (above): calls with no audit event, native code, handles opened before the hook, reads and
  memory are not confined, and a script that digs through the interpreter can forge its result. Trust is the
  boundary.
- The script runs with Verinoda's interpreter and its installed packages, not the project's environment: a
  script that imports the project's dependencies fails unless they are installed there too. Helper modules
  next to the script are not importable (its folder is not on `sys.path`).
- The graph is the index's file (`graph.json`); the receiver-call edges `index.load` adds in memory are not in
  it. With no index, `guard.edges()` raises and the guard is `unknown`.
- `guard.claims()` sees the newest 20,000 stored claims; the claims are read again for every script guard run
  (0.65 s for 20,000).
- A script that starts threads which never end runs until the timeout.
- A script that reports more than 500 findings: the rest are counted under `unknown`.
- The pre-commit hook installs Verinoda in the framework's own environment; trust is still per user and path,
  so an untrusted checkout gets exit 3 on every commit while an accepted script guard is enforced.

### 112.5 Tests

`tests/test_script_guards.py` (26 tests): a violation at a cited line with the line's text and
`strong_inference`; a clean script is ok with its scope, its printed output and its limits; a raise (with the
script's line), `sys.exit(0)`, no `check`, a syntax error and `os._exit(0)` are each `unknown` and exit 3; a
script past `timeout=1` is stopped and `unknown`; the audit hook refuses network, lookups, processes,
`os.system`, writes, appends, removal, mkdir, ctypes and a second audit hook, and the files are unchanged; on
Windows it refuses `_winapi` CreateFile, CreateJunction, CreateNamedPipe, CreatePipe, OpenProcess and
TerminateProcess, `msvcrt.open_osfhandle`, `winreg` CreateKey, SetValueEx, DeleteValue, OpenKey with
`KEY_SET_VALUE` and ConnectRegistry, a writable `mmap`, UNC `open` / `listdir` / `scandir` / `chdir` and a
`\\.\pipe` path, while a registry read, a read-only `mmap` and a `\\?\C:\` path work, and no file, junction or
registry value is left behind; the child has no sqlite connection (none in `gc`, `sqlite3.connect` refused)
and gets the claims as data; a fake result line on `print`, `sys.__stdout__` and `os.write(1)` followed by
`os._exit(0)` is `unknown` ("without a result"), and the same written to every descriptor followed by a normal
end is `unknown` ("wrote to the result channel"); citations outside the repository, absolute, past the end,
without a line and of a missing file are `unknown` while `.\app\db.py:5` is accepted; a citation through a
junction out of the repository is `unknown` and an upper-case citation is given the file's spelling; a script
named `guards/kural ğ.py` (quoted in the spec) reads a UTF-8 file with Turkish letters through plain `open()`;
the spec rules (paths, `.py`, existence, timeout range, unknown keys, a hand-edited record); a script reached
through a junction or link outside the repository is not run; without `run_scripts` (and through MCP
`decision_check`) and in an untrusted project the guard is `unknown` with the reason; MCP refuses to record
one, also when its kind is written `s""cript`, `'scr'ipt`, `sc"ri"pt` or `SCRIPT`, and `record` / `add_guards`
with `allow_scripts=False` refuse the parsed kind; MCP refuses to accept a proposed script guard, which the CLI
then accepts; `update`'s summary counts a script guard on its own (not "not checked"); under `--changed` a
pre-existing script finding names the unchanged script and a changed script makes it new; `decide check
--json` runs it on a scanned project with the graph and a stored claim with its evidence (`claims(limit=1)`,
`claims(status=...)`), the text output shows the script finding's limits (the receiver-call edges among them),
and `decide baseline --record` then lets `decide check` pass; the pre-commit hook's entry parses as `decide
check`, with `stages: [pre-commit]`, `minimum_pre_commit_version: "3.2.0"` and the trust note. All in a project
folder whose name has a space and non-ASCII letters.

## 113. Installers for more agents (D140, 2026-10-01)

### 113.1 Why

`verinoda setup` and `verinoda install` connected only Claude Code and Codex. People also work in Cursor,
Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot (VS Code), Kiro, Continue and Aider. Each of these reads an MCP server list
and/or an instructions file from a documented place. This change registers Verinoda there, using the
same installer, so the same safety rules hold. `verinoda setup --agents all` now registers every
supported agent it finds.

### 113.2 Decisions

- **One installer.** The new agents go through `verinoda.agents.installer`: the same plan, the same
  manifest (`.verinoda/install-manifest.json`), the same refusals, and the same exact uninstall. The
  table of locations and the new pieces are in `verinoda/agents/more_agents.py`: the found rule, the
  rules text, the marked Markdown block, and Continue's YAML file. `installer._plan_file` is the old
  skill writer made generic (a file Verinoda owns whole). `_plan_json` / `_un_json` take the JSON
  object's name (`mcpServers`, or VS Code's `servers`) and whether the entry carries `"type": "stdio"`.
- **What each agent gets.** Every path is taken from the agent's own documentation, read on 2026-10-01:

  | agent | MCP entry | instructions | source |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Cursor | `.cursor/mcp.json`, `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, `mcpServers`, `type: stdio` | `.cursor/rules/verinoda.mdc` (`description`, `alwaysApply: true`), project only | cursor.com/docs/context/mcp; cursor.com/docs/context/rules ("User Rules aren't stored as files") |
  | Gemini CLI | `.gemini/settings.json`, `~/.gemini/settings.json`, `mcpServers` (`command`, `args`) | marked block in `GEMINI.md` (project), `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` (user) | geminicli.com/docs/reference/configuration |
  | GitHub Copilot | `.vscode/mcp.json`, `servers`, `type: stdio`, project only | marked block in `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/mcp-servers; .../custom-instructions |
  | Kiro | `.kiro/settings/mcp.json`, `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json`, `mcpServers` | `.kiro/steering/verinoda.md` (`inclusion: always`), both scopes | kiro.dev/docs/mcp/configuration; kiro.dev/docs/steering |
  | Continue | `.continue/mcpServers/verinoda.yaml` (`name`, `version`, `schema: v1`, `mcpServers` list), project only | `.continue/rules/verinoda.md` (`name`, `alwaysApply: true`), project only | docs.continue.dev/customize/deep-dives/mcp; .../rules |
  | Aider | none: Aider has no MCP client | `.aider.verinoda.md`, named by `read: [...]` in a marked block of a new `.aider.conf.yml` | aider.chat/docs/usage/conventions.html; aider.chat/docs/config/aider_conf.html |

- **Shared files vs. owned files.** Where the agent reads a folder of rule files (Cursor, Kiro, Continue)
  or a file only Verinoda writes (Continue's server file, Aider's conventions file), the installer writes
  a file of its own. That file carries the ownership marker and its sha256 is recorded in the manifest,
  so the existing rule keeps it out of the project's index. Gemini CLI and Copilot read one shared file
  (`GEMINI.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`). There the installer appends a block between
  `<!-- verinoda-managed v1 begin ... -->` and `<!-- verinoda-managed end -->`, records its hash and
  any line end or blank line it added, and removes exactly that on uninstall. The file comes back byte
  for byte. A file the installer created is deleted when nothing else is left in it.
- **The block is Verinoda's text, not the project's.** A file the manifest lists as holding the block
  (`kind: "md_block"`) is one of Verinoda's own files while it holds the block and nothing else (white
  space aside), so a fresh install's `GEMINI.md` or `.github/copilot-instructions.md` is not indexed.
  Once the user writes in it, it is indexed, block included. `agent-lint` reads every instruction file
  with the block's lines blank (line numbers kept), so the block's `-m verinoda` command is never
  reported as a missing module. Begin and end are found one after the other
  (`selffiles.find_block`), in linear time.
- **Aider.** Aider does not load `CONVENTIONS.md` unless it is told to (`--read`, or `read:` in
  `.aider.conf.yml`). When no `.aider.conf.yml` exists, install creates one holding a marked block (the
  begin and end lines are YAML comments) with the `read:` line. Users add their own keys to this file,
  so it is not a file Verinoda owns whole: keys added around the block keep re-install safe, and
  uninstall removes only the block (the file goes only when nothing else is left). The `read:` line
  names the conventions file by absolute path, because the docs do not say what a relative `read:` path
  is resolved against. An existing `.aider.conf.yml` without the block is never edited. It counts as
  set up only when a top-level `read:` entry (its line, or the indented or `-` lines under it, comments
  cut) names the file; otherwise the step is printed as a manual one (`manual` in `--json`): a
  `read: [...]` line, or, when a `read:` key exists, "add ... to the `read:` list" (never a second key).
- **Notes name only what was written.** The usage note and setup's next step are built from what this
  install wrote: the server entry only when one was written (not with `--no-mcp`), the instructions
  file only when the scope has one (not Cursor at user scope), with `~/` paths at user scope.
- **"Found".** An agent is found when its folder (`.cursor`, `.gemini`, `.vscode`, `.kiro`, `.continue`;
  Aider's `.aider.conf.yml`) exists in the project or the home folder, or when its program (`cursor`,
  `gemini`, `code`, `kiro`, `aider`) is on PATH. Claude Code and Codex count as found when their CLI is
  on PATH, as before. The setup report's `agents_found` gives the reason for each agent
  (`".kiro exists"`, ``"`gemini` is on PATH"``). For Copilot, the rule finds VS Code; whether the
  Copilot extension is enabled is not checked. Agents with no location for the chosen scope are left
  out.
- **`--agents all` changed meaning.** It used to install Claude Code and Codex whether or not they were
  present. Now it installs every supported agent that is found. `auto` (the default) is unchanged:
  Claude Code and Codex on PATH. Agents named explicitly (`--agents cursor,kiro`) are installed without
  the found check.
- **Server command.** The new agents get the same command as Codex: `mcp serve --repo <project>` at
  project scope, and `mcp serve` at user scope.
- **Scope coverage.** `install`/`setup` refuse user scope for Copilot and Continue (see Limits).
  `setup` refuses before anything is written (no `.verinoda/`, no scan), as it does for an unknown name.
  `status()` and `doctor` still report only Claude Code and Codex.
- **Graph digest.** `selffiles.config_digest` now also leaves Verinoda's own entry out of a top-level
  `servers` object (VS Code's shape). Adding the entry to `.vscode/mcp.json` therefore does not count as
  a config change for the graph.

### 113.3 Measured

- `tests/test_more_agents.py`: 26 passed, 1 skipped. The skip is the PyYAML round trip, because
  PyYAML is not installed here. The same scalars are also read back as JSON strings without it.
- `tests/test_setup.py`, `tests/test_selffiles.py`, `tests/test_docs.py`, `tests/test_line_endings.py`:
  48 passed, 1 failed. The failure is the known environment one
  (`test_setup_next_steps_name_the_command_that_runs_this_build`: the launcher check on this machine).
- `tests/test_agents.py`: 25 failed, 48 passed, the known environment failures. To check the refactored
  JSON writer anyway, I ran it with a throw-away plugin that treats this venv's redirected
  `sys.executable` as the launcher's interpreter. Result: 68 passed. The byte-for-byte `.mcp.json` and
  Codex TOML tests were among them. Five failed. Two are the skill templates being 242/243 lines
  against a limit of 240; the templates are not touched here. The other three are build-skew tests
  that the plugin itself defeats.

- **Review round.** Fixed: the marked block left in the corpus (a block-only shared file is now
  Verinoda's own file; `agent-lint` skips the block), Aider's config owned whole (now a marked block),
  the `read:` check that matched any bytes (now a `read:` entry), usage notes naming files that were not
  written (`--no-mcp`, Cursor at user scope), the quadratic block search (20,000 begin lines with no end
  now well under a second), setup refusing an agent's scope only after init and scan, and the
  ARCHITECTURE row that said `status()` compares every server. After the round:
  `tests/test_more_agents.py` 41 passed, 1 skipped; `tests/test_selffiles.py`, `tests/test_setup.py`,
  `tests/test_agentlint.py`, `tests/test_docs.py`, `tests/test_line_endings.py` 66 passed, 1 failed (the
  same known launcher failure); `tests/test_agents.py` 25 failed, 48 passed (the known ones, unchanged).

### 113.4 Not done

- **Unsure, so not written:**
  - VS Code's user-level `mcp.json`: it lives in the profile folder, and the docs only say to open it
    with a command.
  - Continue's user-level server folder: not checked against the docs.
  - Cursor's user rules: kept in its settings, not in a file.
- **The global `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` path was not confirmed.** The configuration page I read describes
  upward discovery of `GEMINI.md` and `context.fileName`, but does not spell out this path. It comes from
  Gemini CLI's memory docs as I remember them.
- **Cursor `"type": "stdio"`.** The page summary called it required. The page's own Node example omits
  it, so the field is written but its necessity is unconfirmed.
- **Continue.** The `.continue/rules/` `alwaysApply: true` frontmatter follows the rules page. The YAML
  server file follows the MCP page's example (no `type`).
- **JSONC is refused.** A `.vscode/mcp.json` with comments (VS Code allows JSONC) is not valid JSON, so
  install refuses to touch it (as for `.mcp.json`), and `--no-mcp` still writes the instructions.
- **Where user-scope servers start is not verified.** At user scope the server finds its project from
  the folder it starts in. Whether Cursor, Gemini CLI and Kiro start it in the workspace was not checked.
- **Detection is a heuristic.** A `.vscode` folder or `code` on PATH does not prove that Copilot is in
  use. A stale `~/.cursor` folder counts as found.
- **Aider's absolute path.** The `read:` path is absolute, so moving the project means re-running setup.
- **The block in a file the user also writes in stays indexed.** Search can return the block's own
  example text from `GEMINI.md` or `.github/copilot-instructions.md` once the user's text is in the same
  file; only `agent-lint` skips it.
- **Aider's `read:` check reads lines, not YAML.** Flow or block lists under a top-level `read:` key are
  read; anchors, multi-document files and other YAML forms are not.
- **No status or doctor rows.** `doctor` and `status()` do not list the new agents.

### 113.5 Tests

`tests/test_more_agents.py`, which uses a temporary home and project, stubbed PATH and a fixed launcher,
so it does not depend on this machine:

- project install, idempotence and exact uninstall for each agent;
- each agent's MCP entry shape;
- rules frontmatter;
- Continue YAML quoting;
- shared JSON and Markdown files kept byte for byte (LF, CRLF, no final newline, empty file);
- refusal to overwrite a foreign rules file;
- an edited block kept on uninstall;
- Aider with and without an existing config; keys the user adds to the config Verinoda created (re-install
  unchanged, uninstall keeps them); an existing config counted as set up only by a `read:` entry, and the
  manual step adding to an existing `read:` key;
- a block-only shared file is an own file, one with the user's text is not, and `agent-lint` skips the
  block's lines;
- the block search on 20,000 begin lines with no end;
- usage notes with `--no-mcp` and for Cursor at user scope;
- `setup` refusing Copilot and Continue at user scope before writing anything;
- user scope, and the refused user scopes;
- the found rule, plus `setup --agents all` with some agents found and with none;
- the own-file rule and the digest;
- CLI choices matching `ALL_AGENTS`, and the rules text's statuses and examples.

In `tests/test_setup.py`, the unknown-agent case now uses a name that is still unknown.

## 114. Mixin injection points (D141, 2026-10-01)

### 114.1 Why

A Mixin names places in a game class with strings the compiler never reads: the method an injector goes into
(`method = "damage(Lnet/minecraft/entity/damage/DamageSource;F)Z"`), the instruction an `@At` stops at
(`target = "Lnet/minecraft/entity/LivingEntity;isInvulnerableTo(...)Z"`) and the members a `@Shadow` stands for.
A wrong one compiles; the game stops at start with an `InvalidInjectionException`, or the injection is skipped.
`verinoda check` compared only the method name with the target's members (and the Mixin edges read the
annotations as written), so a wrong descriptor, a wrong `@At` target and a `@Shadow` of the wrong type were never
caught. MinecraftDev and minecraft-modding-mcp check these against the class files; this decision does the same
locally, from the jars the build already resolved.

### 114.2 Decisions

- A new command, `verinoda mixin-check [FILE ...] [--json]`, beside `access-check`, reading the same classpath
  (`jvmclass.discover`: `code_check.classpath`, or the one a Loom build left; one per build, the configured one for
  a build with none) through `accesscheck.ClassFiles`, which gains `code()`.
- `jvmclass.class_code()` reads a class file's members with what each method's `Code` attribute references: every
  call (`invokevirtual`, `invokespecial`, `invokestatic`, `invokeinterface`), field access (`get/putfield`,
  `get/putstatic`) and `new`, as `[kind, owner, name, descriptor]`. Instructions are walked by their lengths
  (`tableswitch` / `lookupswitch` padding and `wide` included); an opcode the specification does not define makes
  that method's code unread (`False`), never a partial list.
- The sources are read with tree-sitter (`read_mixins()`): `@Mixin` targets (class literals through the file's
  imports, package, on-demand imports and `java.lang`, nested classes as `Outer$Inner`; `targets` strings), the
  `method` selectors of every injector `verinoda check` knows, the `@At` of its `at` (one or an array) whose value
  is `INVOKE`, `INVOKE_ASSIGN`, `INVOKE_STRING`, `FIELD` or `NEW` and which has a `target`, and `@Shadow` fields and
  methods with their written types, every array dimension kept (`int[][]`), the `prefix` stripped (`shadow$`, Mixin's default, when none is written), `aliases` accepted. Strings joined with `+` and the file's
  `static final String` constants are read (`jvm_mixins.string_constants`).
- Selectors as Mixin reads them: `name` and `name*` (every overload), `name(desc)ret`, `Lowner;name(desc)` (an
  owner other than the target matches nothing, as in Mixin: `absent`); a quantifier is dropped; a regular
  expression (`/.../`) is `unknown`, not compared.
- An `@At` target is looked for in the bytecode of the methods its injector's selectors match in the class file
  (their union), with Mixin's partial matching: an owner, name or descriptor left out matches any. `NEW` takes a
  class (`pkg/Cls`, `Lpkg/Cls;`) or a constructor descriptor (`(I)Lpkg/Cls;`, then the `new` and the
  `<init>(I)V` call must both be there; a `(`-target that is no such descriptor is `unknown`, never a crash).
  When one of the injector's selectors was not compared (a regular expression, or a `method` that is not a
  constant string this reader resolves) a miss is `unknown`, and the row says which; the nearest of an absent
  `@At` are looked for among the calls of the ten closest names, so a method with thousands of calls stays
  cheap.
- `@Shadow`: a field by name and type, a method by name, parameter types and return type, compared by simple name
  and array dimensions (a type variable is erased to its bound and not compared).
- Verdicts: `exists` is `statically_verified`, the evidence `jar!class.class`. `absent` has the same evidence
  ("mc.jar!.../LivingEntity.class declares no field named helth") and is `strong_inference`, as in
  `access-check`: the classpath is what the last build resolved and may be older than the build file, so a
  name missing from it is not proven wrong for the version the build names. The nearest real ones of an
  `absent` row come by edit distance (at most half the written length, or 3, away; three at most) and are a
  suggestion: `nearest_status: strong_inference`, and the text output says "a suggestion".
- `unknown`, never `absent`, when there is nothing to compare with, each with `next`: the target class on no jar of
  an incomplete classpath (run the Loom build or set `code_check.classpath`), on no jar of a complete one (`verinoda
  check` reports an unresolved `@Mixin` target), a JDK class (`verinoda api`), a class of the project's own sources
  (`verinoda check`), an unreadable class file. Also `unknown`: a name declared only in a super class (a Mixin
  reaches only the target's own members, as `verinoda check` already says), or perhaps declared in a super
  class whose class file is not read (`java.lang.Object`, on no jar of a real classpath, only for its own method
  names), an intermediary or SRG name
  (`method_5643`, `m_1234_`) the named classpath does not carry, an `@At` whose selector matched nothing, an
  `@At` in a method with no bytecode (abstract, native) or with code this reader could not walk.
- Exit codes as `access-check`: 3 when something is absent, 4 when something is unknown, 2 when no Java file holds a
  `@Mixin`, 0 otherwise. No MCP tool: the core profile keeps its five.

### 114.3 Measured

- The verdict-audit fixture `mixmod` (four Mixins) with a planted jar holding its targets: the four selectors
  `exists`; with a planted `CheckedMixin` of 26 names: 8 planted mistakes `absent` with the right nearest (a
  misspelt `@At` INVOKE target, an `@At` FIELD with the wrong type, an `@At` NEW with the wrong constructor, a
  wrong selector descriptor, a misspelt selector, a misspelt `@Shadow` field, a `@Shadow` field of the wrong type,
  a `@Shadow` method with the wrong parameters), the inherited, intermediary, abstract and project-class cases
  `unknown`; 30 rows (16 exists, 8 absent, 6 unknown) in 0.3 s, tree-sitter parsing included.
- Without a classpath every row of the same files is `unknown` with the next step.
- Not measured on a real mod's Minecraft jar in this change.
- Review round: a review found `@Shadow shadow$name` compared with its prefix (now stripped by default),
  multi-dimensional arrays read as one dimension, an owner in a selector ignored, a malformed `@At(NEW)`
  descriptor aborting the whole command, an `@At` behind a regular-expression selector said to have matched
  nothing, names maybe inherited from a super class on no jar (`java.lang.Object`, a JDK class) reported
  `absent`, and `absent` stronger than `access-check`'s for the same evidence (now `strong_inference`). An
  absent `@At` in a method of 3,000 distinct calls took 5.0 s for its nearest; with the names ranked first the
  whole test (planted jar written, parsed and checked) takes 0.7 s. The `no_mixins` note names the files
  given instead of the project's sources when files are given.

### 114.4 Not done

- A game version bumped without a rebuild compares with the older jar; hence `absent` is `strong_inference`.
- A `@Shadow` field's `prefix` is not stripped (only a method's is).
- Not checked: `@At` `ordinal`, `opcode`, `shift`, `@Slice`, `CONSTANT` / `LOAD` / `STORE` / `JUMP` points,
  `@Desc`, MixinExtras `@Expression`, `@Overwrite`, `@Accessor` / `@Invoker` (names stay in `verinoda check`),
  `@Shadow` across a Mixin's own super classes, Kotlin Mixins, refmaps (names are compared in the classpath's
  namespace only).
- Types are compared by simple name: two classes of the same simple name in different packages are not told
  apart.
- A Mixin with several targets is checked against each; one where the name is missing is `absent` for that target.
- The JDK's class files (`ct.sym`) and the project's own compiled classes are not read for bytecode.

### 114.5 Tests

`tests/test_mixincheck.py`: the bytecode reader (references in order past `tableswitch`, `lookupswitch` and `wide`;
an abstract method has no code; a non-class file is None); selectors, `@At` INVOKE / FIELD / NEW targets and
`@Shadow` fields and methods against a planted jar, each absent row with its nearest; inherited, intermediary,
abstract-method and project-class rows unknown; `absent` is `strong_inference`; a `@Shadow` with the default
`shadow$` prefix and `int[][]` fields and returns found; a selector with another owner absent; a malformed `@At(NEW)`
descriptor unknown, not a crash; an `@At` behind a regular-expression or unresolved selector unknown with that
reason; a name maybe inherited from a super class on no jar unknown, `java.lang.Object`'s methods unknown and
its missing fields absent; the nearest of an `@At` in a method of 3,000 calls; the fixture's own Mixins found; without a classpath everything
unknown with the next step; edit-distance nearest and the selector / member parsers; the CLI's text, `--json`, exit codes and
the `no_mixins` note for named files. `tests/jvmfixtures.py` can now write a method's `Code` attribute.

## 115. Dependency structure matrix and C4 model check (D142, 2026-10-01)

### 115.1 Why

The dependencies view lists the heaviest file-to-file dependencies and the cycles view the rings between files, but
neither shows the shape of a whole project at a glance: which parts use which, in what order, and where that order
is broken. A dependency structure matrix (Lattix, NDepend, IntelliJ) does: groups on both axes, a count in each
cell, ordered so that every mark against the layering stands out. Teams that draw their architecture as a C4 model
(Structurizr) also want to know whether the drawing still matches the code: a relation in the model that no code
makes, and code dependencies the model does not show. Done when: the matrix in `ui`; model edges without code
edges listed.

### 115.2 Decisions

- **Two map views, no new command:** `verinoda map --view dsm [--group-by folder|tag] [--depth N]` and
  `verinoda map --view model [--model PATH]` (module `verinoda/dsm.py`), asked for by name like dead and hotspots.
  MCP `map_view` takes `dsm` (targets `['tag']` groups by tags) and `model` (targets `[DSL path]`); no new tool,
  the gateway's catalog line grew by the two names (one word shortened elsewhere to keep the core menu under its
  limit). `--group-by`, `--depth` and `--model` with another view are refused (exit 2).
- **The same dependencies as the cycles view:** `architecture_map._file_deps` (calls, imports, imports_from,
  uses, inherits between files; type-only and deferred imports, prose files and standard-library imports the
  graph resolved to a project module left out), summed between groups. Each cell carries its reference count,
  EXTRACTED count, relations and up to three reference lines (EXTRACTED first). A cell is `strong_inference` when
  an EXTRACTED edge is in it, else `weak_inference`: graph edges are extractions, never verification.
- **Groups:** folders at `--depth` (files at the top in `(root)`); by default the deepest depth (1-8) with at most
  30 groups. Or the committed `[architecture.tags]` (D95) with `--group-by tag`: a file two tags match counts in
  the first tag of the table (counted in the limits), untagged files in `(other)`, a tag that matches no code file
  is a problem, no tags at all is a problem with the next step - never an empty matrix that looks clean.
- **Order: row uses column, a group before what it uses.** A lexicographic topological order of the condensed
  group graph (ties in name order); inside a cycle of groups the order that leaves the fewest references pointing
  back, searched exactly up to 10 groups (dynamic programming over subsets; tested against every permutation),
  Eades-Lin-Smyth beyond. So a mark below the diagonal (`against_order`, `*` in the text) only exists inside a
  cycle, and the cycles of groups are listed.
- **Model sources:** a Structurizr DSL file (`--model`, or `dsl = "path"` in `[architecture.model]` of
