  than the facts on it, and a stale input fact is recomputed first), the facts a recomputation can change (or the
  named ones): a stale search fact is run again (the trigram index refreshed once per run, the files hashed before
  it); a derived fact whose inputs now allow another status than the recorded one, or that is stale, has its stale
  claims re-verified with `verify` (static, as `consolidate` does: one index refresh first within the budget,
  then each verify with `wait=0`) and takes the weakest of its inputs again - raised when they recovered (from
  `weak_inference` or `contradicted` too), lowered when they did not. A search is not started with less than 1 s
  left: the queue stops there and the rest is reported as not reached. The update recomputes within 20 facts and
  10 s, without `verify`: stale searches re-run and derived facts whose inputs changed are re-read (so a fact whose
  claims `update --consolidate` restored comes back in the same update); a derived fact that waits on a stale
  claim is not queued and is counted as `waiting`. `facts.refresh_on_update: false` turns that off, and an
  `update --fast` (which leaves the graph to a background build, as the MCP `index_update` does) only lowers. The
  facts' own time is reported (`facts.seconds`). A nested update started by a refresh only lowers, so a refresh
  never re-enters itself.
- **A changed result says so.** A recomputation reports `was -> now` and, when the result changed, old against
  new: for a search, the totals and the sites added and removed, compared by file and line text (a line that only
  moved is counted as `moved`, not a change); for a derived fact, the statement before and after and each input
  whose status changed. The same is the history row's payload (`fact show`). A fact whose result changed makes
  the facts resting on it stale and recomputes them in the same run when the budget allows; one whose status
  changed recomputes them too. A search that did not finish (the time ran out, a file could not be read) never
  replaces a complete result: the fact stays stale with the result it had, nothing is reported as changed or
  restored, and the facts resting on it are not touched.
- **Races.** A search fact's file hashes are read before the search reads the files (once per refresh run), so an
  edit in between leaves the fact stale at the next update rather than wrongly current. The writes that depend on
  what they read take the write lock first (`store.tx(immediate=True)`, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`), so another process
  cannot change the row in between: adding a fact (the name check, the inputs, the insert), retiring one (a second
  retire is told there is no such fact, exit 2) and every status write, which also updates only a row that is not
  retired. A name another process took anyway is caught by the unique live-name index and is the same exit 2.
- **Other queries use facts as leads, not evidence.** `query` (`--json`: `facts`), MCP `project_query` (text and
  JSON) and `analyze` (JSON and the MCP view: `facts`; text: a `facts` block before the passages) list up to five
  facts the question names (its whole name as a word, a word of the name, or two words of its statement, pattern or
  scope) with their status as re-checked on read, their statement and the lines they rest on (the claims' supporting
  evidence, or the first sites). They are not evidence for the analysis's claims: a fact's support is its claims'
  evidence, which an answer should cite directly (counting the fact as well would count the same lines twice, and
  would let an aggregate checked only at update time support a claim); a search fact's sites are matches of a
  pattern, which a claim still has to read. A store that cannot be read leaves the answer without facts and says so
  (`facts_error`).
- **Review round.** A review found that a search cut short by the time budget was saved as a changed result,
  counted as restored and made the facts on it stale; that files the search skips (over 2 MB, binary) left it
  `observed` with no match; that facts which can never recover filled the update's queue so other stale facts were
  never recomputed, and the update line named the wrong cause; that a search fact read as current after its code
  changed until the next update; that a status write could land on a fact another process had just retired, two
  retires ended in a traceback and the add was not atomic across processes; that `update --fast` ran the
  searches and did not count their time; and that a lead matched a fact's name inside another word (`db` in
  "feedback"). Each is fixed as described above and covered by a test (the cross-process cases with a second
  connection in one process, not with two processes); also: the statement says "N match(es)" (the total
  counts matches, not lines), a fact lowered to `weak_inference` or `contradicted` is recomputed once
  its inputs recover, and `fact list --status` refuses an unknown status (exit 2).
- **Storage.** Schema v10: `facts` (the definition, the result, what it rests on, the status and why, when it
  was computed) and the append-only `fact_history`. Nothing is deleted (a trigger), a fact's name, kind and
  definition never change, and a retired fact stays retired. An older `atlas.db` is migrated on first open.

### 121.3 Measured

On a copy of `examples/orders_app` (12 files), Windows, three updates after a one-line edit each: 1.69-1.76 s
without facts, 2.37-2.46 s with five search facts over the whole project (all five lowered and recomputed in each
update, about 0.14 s per fact). Adding a search fact took 0.39 s on average; the leads for a question took
0.27 ms with five facts. After the review round (one trigram index refresh per run, the read-time hash check),
measured again the same way on the same machine (the timings vary with its load; compare within one run): 0.75-0.84
s without facts, 1.06-1.12 s with five search facts (all five lowered and restored each time; the facts' own
`seconds` 0.24-0.31); adding a search fact 0.22 s on average; the leads 4.8 ms for a question naming one of the
five (the read now hashes the files a search fact matched, stat-cached).

### 121.4 Not done

- Between updates a read re-checks only the files a search fact matched: a new match elsewhere waits for the next
  update.
- A search fact over a scope with a binary or very large file is `weak_inference` for good (the search cannot
  read it); limiting it with `--path` avoids that.
- A search fact's scope is compared over the files a snapshot lists; a match in a file the snapshot leaves out
  (untracked build output) is found by a refresh but does not make the fact stale.
- Any change in a search fact's scope makes it stale, also one that cannot change the result; the update's
  recomputation restores it, at the cost of a search per fact (bounded by 20 facts and 10 s; not after
  `--fast`).
- A search fact keeps 500 sites; beyond that the change report compares the totals and the kept sites only.
- A derived fact is a conjunction of its inputs; there is no rule language (joins, negation): that is a query
  language, not stored results.
- Leads are matched by words of the question, not by meaning.
- A fact whose claim was corrected stays stale until it is added again from the correction.

### 121.5 Tests

`tests/test_derived_facts.py`: a fact on a claim keeps its status when other code changes and goes stale with the
code it rests on (the update lowers it, says why, records it, and does not run `verify`); `fact refresh` leaves it
stale while the code differs and restores it when the code is back; a search fact goes stale when a matched file
changes and refresh restores it unchanged, and a new file in its scope makes it stale; a search limited to a folder
ignores changes elsewhere; an update recomputes a search fact and the fact resting on it and reports the site added
and the statements old and new, and a line that only moved is not a change; the status is the weakest input's, a
fact on a fact is no stronger, a read caps a fact without writing and the next invalidation records it; a superseded
claim and a retired input fact leave their users stale, a retired name can be used again, deletes and definition
changes are refused; the CLI (`--json` for add, list, refresh; exit 2 on a bad name and on both kinds of input), the
`query` lead in JSON and text, its status after an update, and the `update` line; `analyze` lists the fact as a lead
(JSON, the MCP view, text); a changed result reaches the facts resting on it in the same refresh; template words of
a search fact's statement do not make it a lead; a v9 store is migrated. After review: an unfinished search keeps
the old result stale (nothing changed or restored, the fact on it untouched) and less than 1 s left stops the queue
before a search; a skipped binary file, then a file over 2 MB, make a search fact `weak_inference` with the file
named (no match found in it), and once they are gone the update raises it and the fact on it; facts that cannot
recover stay out of a limited queue and are listed, and the update line says so; a read shows a search fact and the
fact on it stale after a matched file changed, without writing; a status write onto a fact retired by another
connection is not made, a second retire is a refusal, the write lock is held from the start, a name taken meanwhile
is a refusal, an unknown `--status` is exit 2; an update with the graph deferred only lowers and the facts' time is
reported; a lead needs the fact's whole name.

## 122. Native file watcher (D149, 2026-10-01)

### 122.1 Why

`verinoda ui --watch` found edits by listing the tree every two seconds and comparing each file's size and
time. On Verinoda's own checkout one listing takes 0.92 s, so the watcher spaced its looks out to about 9 s and
needed two equal looks before updating: an edit reached the update 12-22 s after the save, and an idle watcher
still spent 1.5 s of CPU every 20 s. The MCP server had no watcher at all: an agent's edit stayed out of the
index until it called `index_update` (the reads only said which files had changed). narsil-mcp and
codebase-memory-mcp update from operating-system file events.

### 122.2 Decisions

- One module, `fswatch.py`, holds the `Watcher` (moved from `ui/server.py`, which re-exports it) and the event
  sources. No new dependency: the sources call the system through `ctypes`. On Windows `ReadDirectoryChangesW` on
  the project root, recursive (one handle for the tree, a 64 KB buffer: the limit over a network share), read
  synchronously by a daemon thread that `CancelIoEx` stops. On Linux `inotify`, one watch per folder (the ignored
  folders left out), a folder that appears later watched when its event arrives; when the per-user watch limit
  is reached the folders past it are left to the periodic look and the note says so. Elsewhere (macOS) the
  `watchdog` package when it is installed; otherwise polling.
- An event only wakes the watcher. What decides is still the tree's signature (`snapshot.list_files`, each file's
  size and modification time), so an event for an ignored file, a save that leaves the file as it was, or a lost
  event never causes a wrong update, only a look. Events under `.verinoda`, `.git`, virtual environments,
  `node_modules`, caches, editor folders and `*.egg-info` are dropped before they wake anything: an update's own
  writes do not start another update. A full system buffer (`ReadDirectoryChangesW` returning no bytes,
  `IN_Q_OVERFLOW`) or a cut record counts as "something changed".
- After an event the watcher waits until no event came for 0.3 s (at most 5 s), so a save that writes several
  files is one update. The tree is still looked at every 60 s without an event, for changes no event reports (a
  network share, a folder past the watch limit). A source that fails while running (its read returns an error)
  switches the watcher to polling, and the status says why.
- `verinoda mcp serve --watch` starts the same watcher in the server process, with the fast update
  `index_update` runs (`update --fast`: the changed files are taken in at once and the graph is rebuilt by a
  background process), so the next tool call answers from the edited code; the server's kept graph reloads when
  `graph.json` changes, as before. Off by default: a save then costs an update. Without an index the flag only
  says so (the first scan stays `index_update`'s). It does not wait for the build lock: while another build runs,
  it does nothing and looks again after the poll interval (2 s), not at the next event.
- `ui --watch`'s status (`/api/version`) gains `backend` (`ReadDirectoryChangesW`, `inotify`, `watchdog (...)`,
  `poll`) and `note` (why there are no events, the watch limit).

- Review round: a file saved while an update ran was lost (the next comparison used a look taken after the
  update, which already held it): the watcher now compares with the look taken before the update, so such a save
  updates once more. The Windows reader owns its handle and closes it when it ends (a failed reader leaked it);
  `close()` cancels with `CancelIoEx` until the reader has ended, since a read started just after one cancel
  blocked `close()` until the next file event. On Linux the reader owns the descriptor too, and the root's own
  delete or move stops the source (the watcher then polls) instead of leaving a source with no watches. A
  project folder that is deleted or moved stops the watcher with the reason; an update had created it again
  (`.verinoda/` and all). A refused index build is an error, not a counted update. `watchdog`'s observer thread
  dying counts as the source ending. The MCP server's message without an index says to restart after
  `index_update`.

### 122.3 Measured

Windows 11, Python 3.13, Verinoda's own checkout as the project (2,735 files listed), the watcher with a no-op
update, five saves of one file one second apart:

- One look at the tree (the signature): median 0.92 s (min 0.91 s) of five.
- Save to update, with `ReadDirectoryChangesW`: median 1.22 s (1.22-1.31 s): 0.3 s of quiet plus one look.
- Save to update, polling (the old watcher, unchanged): median 20.4 s (12.1-22.2 s).
- Idle for 20 s after the saves: 0.00 s of CPU and no wakeup with events; 1.52 s of CPU polling.
- End to end on the orders example (a copy, scanned, `mcp serve --watch`'s settings): a new function written to a
  file is in `graph.json` 6.6 s after the save, background graph build included (test run time).

### 122.4 Not done

- Events are filtered by folder name only, not by `.gitignore`: an ignored file written continuously (a log) wakes
  a look every few seconds (about 5 s with continuous writes; each look costs a listing, 0.92 s on Verinoda's
  own checkout), which polling did not cost more. Tracked files under `.vscode`, `.idea` or `venv` are in the
  signature but their events are dropped: they wait for the 60 s look.
- A save that lands while the update records its snapshot can be taken as indexed with the graph of the text
  before it (an `update` race, not the watcher's); a later edit of the file fixes it.

- Linux `inotify` and the `watchdog` path were not run here (Windows only): their event parsing is tested on
  synthetic records, the folder-added-later case only runs on Linux.
- A branch switch that leaves every listed file's size and time as it was is not an update (the signature is the
  same, as before); `git checkout` normally changes the times of the files it writes.
- The watcher sees the project root only: a file outside it that the index reads (a reference tree elsewhere) is
  not watched.
- Each save starts an update; with `mcp serve --watch` each one that touches the graph also starts a background
  graph build. Builds never overlap (the build lock), and a save during a build is taken in by the next look.

### 122.5 Tests

`tests/test_fswatch.py` (25): the Windows and inotify record parsers (a chain, an empty buffer, a cut record), the
folder filter, a real source reporting a write and not `.verinoda`, closing a source quickly, inotify watching a
folder created later (Linux only), no source meaning polling with the reason, one update for several events,
no update for an event without a change, the periodic look without an event, a failing source falling back to
polling, a busy build retried without a new event, polling with events off, a real edit picked up with a 60 s
poll interval (an event, not the poll), `mcp serve --watch` on the command line, and end to end: an edit
reaching `graph.json` through the watcher with no `update` call. `tests/test_ui.py` keeps its watcher test (on
the moved class).

## 123. Control and data dependence (D150, 2026-10-01)

### 123.1 Why

"Where does this argument's value come from?" is the question a reviewer asks before trusting a call, and the one
taint analysis (the next item) is built on. Joern, GitNexus, narsil-mcp and CodePrism answer it with a program
dependence graph and slices. Verinoda's graph has calls and imports between symbols, nothing inside a function:
the agent reads the function and guesses which assignments and branches matter. Done when: a slice answers
"where does this argument's value come from" with its lines.

### 123.2 Decisions

- **New command `verinoda slice PATH:LINE [--var NAME] [--arg N|NAME] [--forward] [--depth N] [--json]`**
  (module `verinoda/slicing.py`), Python only, computed from the file as it is now (no index needed inside a
  function; the index is read only to follow callers). CLI only: no MCP tool. `PATH` is relative to the project,
  else to the working directory, and must be inside the project.
- **A control-flow graph per function, statements as nodes.** A compound statement is its header (an `if`'s test,
  a `for`'s target and iterable, a `with`'s items, an `except`'s type and name, a `case`'s pattern and guard).
  Edges follow `if`/`elif`/`else`, `while` and `for` with their `else` and `break`/`continue`, `return`, `raise`,
  `with`, `match`, and `try`: an exception raised before or after any statement of the body reaches each handler
  (and `finally`), and every way out of the body, the handlers and `else` - falling through, `return`, `break`,
  `continue`, an exception - runs `finally` and then goes on to its own target (one copy of the block per target,
  shown as one line). Nested functions and classes are one statement that defines their name and reads their
  decorators, defaults and bases, and the names their body reads without binding them itself (`nonlocal` names
  included, `global` ones not).
- **Definitions and reads.** A name assigned (`=`, annotated, augmented, `for` and `with` targets, `except ... as`,
  imports, walrus, `case` captures) replaces earlier definitions, and so does `del x`; `x.a = v`, `x[i] = v`,
  `del x[i]` and a method called on a name as a statement (`items.append(v)`) update `x` - they define it without
  replacing what it held, and read it. Names a comprehension or lambda binds for itself are not reads of the
  function's names.
- **Reaching definitions** by an iterative data-flow analysis over bit sets (one bit per definition), solved in
  reverse postorder; **control dependence** from post-dominators (bitsets solved in postorder, each node's
  immediate post-dominator found by its set, then each branch edge walked up the post-dominator tree), so a
  statement after an `if` that returns or raises depends on that `if`, and a loop body on the loop's test. A node
  that never reaches the exit (inside `while True` with no way out) depends on nothing.
- **Backward slice:** from the criterion's reads (`--var`: one name read or defined there - for `a, b = x, y` the
  `x` for `a`; `--arg`: the names of one argument of the outermost call on the line, by position or keyword, not
  with `--var`; default: every name it reads), the definitions that reach them, their reads in turn, and the
  branches every node in the slice depends on. A name with no definition in the function (module, builtin,
  closure) is listed, not guessed. A line of a nested function's decorators or `def` header is that definition in
  the function around it.
- **Across callers:** when the slice reaches a parameter, the index's `calls` edges into the function (found by
  name and definition line; by name alone, with a note, when the index is older than the file) give its call
  sites; the call of that name at the cited line is read, the parameter mapped to its argument (keyword first,
  then position; `self`/`cls` is the object before the dot, except for an instance method called through its
  class, `Cls.m(obj, x)`; `*args` or `**kwargs` that may carry it make it unknown) or to its default value, and
  that argument sliced in the caller - up to `--depth` calls up (default 2, at most 3) and 8 call sites per
  parameter. A call site that cannot be read is listed with why (`unknown`), never dropped.
- **Forward slice (`--forward`):** from the definitions at the line, every node they reach and are read at,
  transitively, and the nodes a predicate among them controls, nested branches included.
- **Output:** each line with its role (`criterion`, `def`, `control`, `use`, `controlled`), the names it defines
  and reads, and the data (definition -> read, with the name) and control edges. Status `strong_inference`: the
  lines are read from the source, the dependence between them is the analysis's (the heap is approximated), never
  an observation. Exit 2 for a line outside a function or the project, a file that does not parse, a name or
  argument not on the line, or `--var` with `--arg`; a function over 4,000 graph nodes is not analysed.
- **Review round.** An exception carried the state after the statement that raised it (`result = None; try:
  result = compute()` lost the `None`): a node at the start of the body now leads to the handlers too. `return`,
  `raise`, `break` and `continue` in a handler or `else` skipped `finally`: every way out is now routed through a
  copy of the block. A nested class body was not read, and a nested function's own locals counted as reads.
  `--forward` followed control one branch deep; `--arg` took the innermost call on the line; `Acct.take(a, raw)`
  dropped `a` as if it were the object; a default was reported where `**kwargs` may pass the value; a decorator or
  `def` header line of a nested function was "no statement"; `slice ../out.py:N` read a file outside the project
  and a path relative to the working directory was not found. Reaching definitions ran against the program order
  and post-dominator sizes were recounted per pair: 9 s on the largest function of this repository, 26 s near
  the node limit. Also: `del`, `--var` on a tuple assignment, `--var` with `--arg` refused, a line listed once
  when it holds several nodes, a note that `Cls(...)` calls are not followed to `__init__`.

### 123.3 Measured

On this repository, the main checkout's index (graph loaded once, 1.7 s warm), backward slices of the last
`return` of large functions with callers followed to depth 2, before and after the review round:
`project_index/cli.py` `dispatch_command` (3,779 lines, 2,260 graph nodes) 38 slice lines in 0.5 s (9.4 s
before; at depth 0, 0.33 s against 9.04 s, and 2.0 s for `verinoda slice` end to end); `review.review` (228 lines)
126 slice lines and 67 caller slices in 2.1 s (2.4 s); `review._guard_diff` (195 lines) 83 lines, 2.1 s (2.6 s);
`analysis.analyze` (237 lines) 139 lines and 31 caller slices, 4.0 s (4.1 s). The analyses alone on
`dispatch_command`: reaching definitions 0.01 s (9.52 s), control dependence 0.02 s (0.65 s). A generated function
of 538 nodes: reaching definitions under 0.01 s (6.26 s); one of 3,964 nodes: control dependence
0.03 s (25.9 s). Every function under `verinoda/` (7,861): graph, analyses and a backward slice of each `return`
in 20.1 s in all, 0.14 s at most. On the test project the done-when holds: the second argument of
`db.execute(...)` in `save` is traced to `amount` in `checkout` (its `= 0`, the loop over the cart,
`+= price_of(...)`, the `if not cart: raise` that decides the call) and on to the `cart` that `handler` reads from
the request.

### 123.4 Not done

- Python only; one function at a time plus its callers' arguments: a value returned by a called function is a read
  of that call's names, the callee's body is not entered.
- The heap is approximated: aliasing (`b = a; b.append(x)` does not update `a`), attributes as separate locations,
  globals or attributes changed by other functions, `exec`/`eval`, `getattr` and `setattr` are not seen. A nested
  function assigning a `nonlocal` name does not define it for the function around it.
- Exceptions raised inside called functions are not followed; any statement of a try body may reach its handlers
  and `finally`, any statement of a handler or `else` its `finally`. Matching an `except` type and leaving a
  `with` block are not taken to raise.
- Callers come from the index (an INFERRED edge is a resolver's guess; its confidence is shown per hop) and are
  matched by the callee's name at the cited line; a call through a variable or `functools.partial` is not found,
  nor `Cls(...)` as a call of `__init__`. An instance method called through its class is recognised by the class
  names defined in the callee's or the caller's file.
- The edges list every definition-read pair: a name with many definitions that each reach many reads makes it
  large (the generated 3,900-node function in the tests: 1.7 million edges, 5.9 s).
- No query over the dependence graph yet (taint, the next item, builds on it); no CFG or PDG export.

### 123.5 Tests

`tests/test_slicing.py`: a return's definitions and the early-return branch it depends on, a list built in a loop,
one argument of a call sliced alone, a forward slice, control-flow forms (try/except, with, while/break, match,
walrus, comprehensions), errors, a parameter followed two callers up on a scanned project, keyword/method/default
mapping and the no-index note, and the CLI. From the review round, each scenario's slice line for line: the state
before a raising statement reaching a handler (`except`, `except*`, `finally: return`), `raise`/`return` in a
handler and `return` in `else` running `finally`, a nested class body and a nested function's own names,
nested branches in a forward slice, `--arg` on the outermost call, decorator and header lines of a nested function,
`del`, `--var` on a tuple assignment, `--var` with `--arg`, a one-line `if`, `Cls.m(obj, x)`, `**kwargs` and the
`__init__` note on a scanned project, CLI paths outside the project and relative to the working directory, and
two timings: reaching definitions on 1,800 nodes and the analyses on 3,900 (each under 3 s; before, 6.3 s for
reaching definitions on 538 nodes and 26 s for control dependence on 3,964).

## 124. Package existence and slopsquatting check (D151, 2026-10-01)

### 124.1 Why

An assistant that writes `import fastjson_schema_validator` or adds `huggingface-cli-tools` to a manifest may name
a package that does not exist - and an attacker who registers that name later gets installed (slopsquatting), as
does one who registers `reqeusts` (typosquatting). Socket MCP and Endor Labs check a new dependency against its
registry before it is installed. `check --deps` already knew which packages code imports without declaring them,
but not whether those names exist anywhere. Done when: `check` flags a dependency name the registry does not have.

### 124.2 Decisions

- **Opt-in twice.** `verinoda check --deps --registry [new|all] [--network off|cache|on] [--diff REV]` and
  `verinoda decide ask SOURCE TARGET --registry [--network ...]`. Without `--registry` (or `--network`) nothing
  changes. The network mode defaults to `off`, not to `research.network` (whose default is `cache`): the user
  turns the network on for this check explicitly. With `off` nothing is sent, the registry facts are `unknown`
  and the next step is `--network on`. CLI only: no MCP tool and no new MCP argument (the menu stays as it is).
- **Only public package names leave the machine**, only to the public registry of their ecosystem, through
  `references.transport.LiveTransport` (SSRF-guarded opener, per-host rate-limit blocks, Verinoda's
  User-Agent, no credentials) with a 10 s timeout. Names behind a private source the project configures are
  never sent (see the review round).
- **What is checked:** `new` (default) - the names a manifest declares now and did not declare at REV. The
  manifests of that commit are written to a temporary folder and read by the same reader
  (`guards.declared_dependencies`), so a version bump is not new, a name the old file only mentioned (a comment,
  a script, `name = "mylogger"`) does not hide a new `log`, and `request` next to an old `requests` is new; a
  manifest that did not exist at REV adds all of its declarations. `all` - every declaration. Both add the
  `missing` packages of `check --deps` (Python and npm imports no manifest declares). Imports of the Python
  standard library, Node built-ins, the Go standard library (no dot in the first path element) and Rust's
  built-in crates and path keywords (`std`, `core`, `alloc`, `proc_macro`, `test`, `crate`, `self`, `super`) are
  skipped.
- **Registries, one or two cheap requests each:** PyPI JSON API plus the Simple API JSON for the PEP 792
  `project-status` (a JSON 404 is called "not found" only when the Simple API also says 404; a quarantined
  project is reported as quarantined; a project the Simple API knows with no release the JSON API shows exists,
  with the caution `no_release`); npm package document plus `api.npmjs.org` last-week downloads; crates.io crate
  API; Maven Central `maven-metadata.xml` (404 = not on Central; a build may use another repository, and the
  claim says so; an answer whose root is not `<metadata>` is unreadable, not an artifact); Go module proxy
  `@latest`. Gradle plugins have no lookup (said in the limits).
- **Registry facts are `observed`**, each with the URL and the time it was read: `not_found` (HTTP 404/410, or
  npm with every version unpublished), `quarantined`, npm `security_holding` (the `0.0.1-security` placeholder
  npm publishes for a package removed for malware), `no_release`, `yanked` latest, `deprecated` (npm latest
  version; PyPI project status), `archived`, `young` (first release under 90 days before the check),
  `few_downloads` (npm under 100 last week, crates.io under 1,000 in 90 days), `known_vulnerabilities` (PyPI's
  list). The fact is observed; that it means risk is the reader's inference. Nothing is scraped and no account
  is used.
- **Name signals are local** and `strong_inference` at most: `typo_of` (optimal string alignment distance 1 for
  names of 4-8 characters, 2 from 9) and `separator_confusable` (the same letters with other `-`/`_`/`.`; an npm
  scope is part of the name, so `@types/express` is not `express`; not for PyPI names PEP 503 makes the same
  project, nor crate names that differ only in `-`/`_`) against `data/popular_packages.json` (about 500
  hand-written popular names of PyPI, npm and crates.io, plus a list of established near-names such as `boto`,
  `jinja`, `preact`, `sha1` that get no signal; `@types/<popular>` gets none either). A look-alike the registry
  shows widely used (npm 50,000 a week, crates.io 500,000 in 90 days) is a package of its own: `weak_inference`,
  no caution. `hallucination_style` (a popular name plus a generic word such as `utils`, `py`, `sdk`) is
  `weak_inference` and changes no verdict. They are computed with the network off too.
- **Verdict per package:** `flagged` (not found, quarantined, security holding), `caution` (no release, yanked,
  deprecated, archived, young, few downloads, known vulnerabilities, typo or separator look-alike), `ok`,
  `unknown`, `skipped`, with a next step ("do not install ...: check the name ...").
- **In `check --deps`** registry facts and name signals are separate findings, each with its own status:
  `not_in_registry` (observed: the registry has no such name), `registry_signal` (observed: taken down, no
  release, yanked, deprecated, young, few downloads, vulnerabilities) with the declaration or import lines and
  the registry URLs as evidence, and `lookalike_name` (strong_inference, the declaration or import lines). The
  result gains a `registry` section and the summary three counts; any such finding makes the exit 3. A
  `--diff` revision that is not a commit is an error (exit 2), and so is `--diff` with `--registry all`. In
  `decide ask` the `registry` section is added beside the verdict, which stays the guards' verdict.
- **Cache** `.verinoda/research/package-check.json` (schema `verinoda.package_check/1`), one answer per
  registry and name (as the registry compares it) with the time observed. `cache` reuses an answer younger than
  24 hours, else asks; `on` always asks and shows the cached answer (said so) only when the registry cannot be
  reached; `off` names a cached answer but does not use it. Timeouts, network errors, 5xx, 429 and unreadable
  answers are never cached and leave the package `unknown`. An entry that is not as written (no answer, a time
  that is no number, an answer that is no object or has no registry) is a miss. A save reloads the file, merges
  the new answers into the entries other runs wrote meanwhile, and replaces the file in one step (a temporary
  file and `os.replace`).
- **Review round** (a reviewer confirmed 12 defects; all fixed, each with a regression test):
  1. Dependencies no registry holds were looked up and could be flagged: npm `workspace:` / `file:` / `link:` /
     `portal:` / git / `github:` / `owner/repo` / tarball URL specs, Cargo `path` / `git` /
     `workspace = true`, PEP 508 `name @ url`, Poetry and `[tool.uv.sources]` path/git/URL sources, go.mod
     modules replaced by a local path are now skipped and never sent. An npm alias `x: npm:real@range` is
     looked up as `real`, a Cargo `json = { package = "serde_json" }` as `serde_json`, a go.mod module replaced
     by another module as that module (each says what it was declared as).
  2. Private registries were ignored, so a private name was sent to a public registry (a dependency-confusion
     leak) and could be flagged. Now read from the project: `.npmrc` (`@scope:registry=` holds that scope back,
     `registry=` all of npm), requirements `--index-url` / `--extra-index-url` / `--find-links`, `pip.conf` /
     `pip.ini`, `[[tool.uv.index]]`, `[[tool.poetry.source]]`, `[[tool.pdm.source]]`, `uv.toml`, the
     `PIP_*` / `UV_*` index variables, `.cargo/config.toml` (a replaced crates.io; a dependency's
     `registry =`), Poetry `source =`, uv `index =`, and `GOPRIVATE` / `GONOPROXY` (the environment, else
     `go env` when Go is installed). Such names are `unknown` ("not sent: ...") and never sent. With any extra
     Python index configured no Python name is sent: which names are private cannot be told.
  3. The Go standard library (`fmt`, `net/http`) and Rust built-ins (`std::io`, `crate::x`) were looked up and
     flagged in `decide ask`; they are skipped. A Go package path is read as its module (the longest go.mod
     require that prefixes it, else `host/owner/repo` on the known hosts); otherwise it is `unknown`, not sent.
     A Python import of a shared namespace (`google.cloud.storage`) names no distribution: `unknown`, not sent.
  4. Scoped npm names lost their scope in the separator comparison (`@types/express` vs `express`): the scope
     is now part of the name, and `@types/<popular>` gets no signal.
  5. Maven artifacts were looked up in lower case (`org.antlr:ST4` -> a 404 on `.../st4/`): the manifest
     readers keep the declared spelling (`declared`) beside the lower-cased compare name, and the lookup uses
     it; `decide ask` keeps the case too.
  6. npm names were looked up in lower case (`JSONStream` asked as `jsonstream`, another package): the declared
     name is looked up and cached as written.
  7. A PyPI JSON 404 with a Simple API 200 was "not found" and cached: it is now `exists` with `no_release`.
  8. Damaged cache entries crashed `cache` mode: entries are validated, a bad one is a miss.
  9. Two concurrent runs could lose each other's entries and a reader could see half a file: saves reload and
     merge, then replace atomically.
  10. One finding mixed observed facts with heuristics under the status `observed`: observed facts and name
      signals are now separate findings with their own status.
  11. An invalid `--diff` with `--registry new` was a limit line and could end in exit 0: it is exit 2; only
      "not a git work tree" stays a limit (worded without the `--stdin` advice); `--diff` with `all` is exit 2.
  12. `new` missed a Cargo or Poetry dependency whose name appeared on an earlier line (`name = "mylogger"`
      hid `log`; `serde_json` hid `serde`), because the key was located by the first line containing it. Keys
      are now located inside their own table (`^\s*NAME\s*=`, quoted keys, `[dependencies.NAME]`), and `new`
      compares declared names rather than text.
  Minors fixed too: crates.io names fold `-` and `_`; a Maven 200 that is not `<metadata>` is unreadable and
  not cached; the established near-names list.

### 124.3 Measured

Real requests by hand, 2026-10-01, from this machine (one run, `network on`, each package alone, cold cache):
PyPI `requests` 1,062 ms (two requests: JSON 192 KB and Simple API 123 KB; ok, first release 5,708 days ago);
PyPI `huggingface-cli-tools-vx` 970 ms, flagged not found; PyPI `reqeusts` 1,023 ms, flagged not found plus
`typo_of requests`; npm `left-pad` 1,046 ms (document plus downloads: 2,583,163 last week; `caution`, its latest
version is deprecated on npm); npm `react-query-hooks-pro-vx` 564 ms, flagged not found; crates.io `serde`
1,171 ms (440 KB answer); Maven Central guava 427 ms; Go proxy `github.com/pkg/errors` 521 ms. The same 8 again
in `cache` mode: 26 ms in all, 8 from the cache. pypistats.org answered HTTP 429 to its first anonymous request,
so PyPI download counts are not read. After the review round, also by hand: Maven Central `org.antlr:ST4`
581 ms, ok (asked in its declared case); npm `JSONStream` 1,564 ms, ok; npm `@types/express` 818 ms, ok with no
name signal; PyPI `reqeusts` 1,041 ms, flagged (`not_found` observed, `typo_of` strong_inference).

### 124.4 Not done

- Only public registries are asked. Names behind a private source the project configures are held back
  (`unknown`, never sent); a source configured only outside the project (a user-level `pip.conf` or `.npmrc`, a
  Gradle or Maven repository other than Central) is not read, so such a name is sent and can look missing
  (Maven's claim says "not on Maven Central").
- With an extra Python index configured, no Python name is checked at all: which names are private cannot be
  told.
- No registry here scans for malicious code; the signals are what a registry shows without an account. A
  package with no signal is not shown to be safe.
- No PyPI download counts (the JSON API has none; pypistats rate-limits). Go and Maven Central give no first
  release date in one request, so no `young` there. npm's full document can be large (megabytes for big
  packages).
- The popular-name list and the established near-names list are small and hand-written: legitimate packages
  near a popular name that are not on the second list and show no large download count (PyPI shows none) get a
  `typo_of` caution, and squats of names not on the first list get none.
- `new` reads the change from git: outside a git work tree it checks only the undeclared imports and says so
  (`all` needs no git). Cargo `workspace = true` dependencies are skipped (the workspace table is not read).
- A Go package path on a host other than the known `host/owner/repo` ones, and not required by go.mod, is
  `unknown`; a Python import of a shared namespace is `unknown`.

### 124.5 Tests

`tests/test_package_check.py` (59 tests, the network replaced by a fake transport; a transport that fails when
called proves nothing was sent; the environment and `go env` are replaced so the user's own index settings do
not leak in): PyPI and npm names the registry lacks flagged with URL and time, an old popular package ok, a young
npm package with few downloads, a yanked PyPI release with vulnerabilities, PyPI quarantine from the Simple API,
npm deprecated and security holding packages, crates.io / Go / Maven Central (found and not on Central), typo,
separator and hallucination-style names, standard-library imports skipped, network off (unknown, nothing sent,
name signals still given), cache reuse and expiry after 24 hours, `on` falling back to the cache, timeouts and
malformed or 5xx answers unknown and not cached, a JSON 404 without a readable Simple API not called missing,
the added-dependency reading of a git change, and the CLI: `check --deps --registry` findings, evidence and exit
3, `--registry all`, argument errors, `decide ask --registry` for a Python and a scoped npm package. Review round
(30 more): local, workspace, VCS and URL sources never sent and npm alias, Cargo rename and go.mod replace read;
private npm scopes, six kinds of private Python index, a replaced crates.io and GOPRIVATE; Go and Rust built-ins
and Go package paths (also through `decide ask`), a namespace import; scoped npm names; Maven and npm case kept;
PyPI project without a release; six damaged cache entries; merging with another run's entries, a truncated
file, no temporary file left; separate observed and look-alike findings; a widely used near name only weak; a
bad revision and `--diff` with `all` exit 2; outside git; Cargo keys located in their table and comments not
hiding new names; a Poetry key in its table; a Maven HTML answer; crate separators and established near-names.

## 125. Full type and name check through tsc, pyright or mypy (D152, 2026-10-01)

### 125.1 Why

`verinoda check` reads names: Python (jedi, D32), Java and Kotlin (D43, D45), and for TypeScript and JavaScript
only the imports (D46). The mistake an agent makes most often in TypeScript after an invented import is a member
that is not there (`svc.sendd()`), a call with the wrong number or type of arguments, or a value of the wrong
type - and those need the compiler, so such a file stayed under `not_checked` and the exit was 4. Every
TypeScript project already has the compiler, and many Python projects have pyright or mypy configured;
narsil-mcp and common practice run that checker. Done when: `check` on TypeScript reports members and calls, not
only imports.

### 125.2 Decisions

- **Opt-in, CLI only: `verinoda check ... --checker tsc|pyright|mypy|auto [--checker-timeout SECONDS]`**
  (module `verinoda/codecheck_external.py`, called from `codecheck.check(checker=..., checker_timeout=...)`).
  The timeout is a finite number of seconds above 0 (default 300; anything else is exit 2). The MCP server never
  calls it: `code_check` keeps its arguments and its rule that nothing the checked repository supplies is
  started. No config key either: a `.verinoda/config.json` that arrives with a repository must not turn on
  running programs. No MCP tool or argument changes (40 tools; the core menu is unchanged).
- **Trust is the boundary** (`verinoda.paths.is_trusted`, as for tests and script guards). In a project the user
  has not trusted (`verinoda trust`), nothing the repository supplies is started: a checker found inside it
  (`node_modules/.bin`, a virtual environment in it, a PATH folder in it) is not run, only one on PATH outside
  it; pyright is not run at all (it starts a Python interpreter it looks up itself, which may be the
  repository's); mypy is not run when `mypy.ini`, `.mypy.ini`, `setup.cfg` or `pyproject.toml` sets `plugins` or
  `python_executable` (both run code). Such a run is `not_run` with the step "ask the user: if they trust this
  project's code, they run `verinoda trust PATH` themselves; an agent must never run it for them", and the exit
  is 4. `auto` skips a checker the gate refuses. Every checker runs with `NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath=1`,
  so a Windows launcher (`tsc.cmd` calling `node`) never picks a program from the project folder it runs in.
- **The project's own checker, never installed or downloaded.** tsc: `node_modules/.bin/tsc` from the
  `tsconfig.json` folder up to the repository, else `tsc` on PATH. pyright: `node_modules/.bin/pyright`, the
  project's virtual environment (`--env`, `.venv`, `venv`, `env`), else PATH. mypy: the virtual environment, else
  PATH. PATH is searched in its absolute folders only, never the current directory. No `npx` (it installs on a
  miss) and no `pip`. pyright's PyPI wrapper (a launcher whose script imports `pyright.cli`, found in its first
  8 MB, its last 2 MB or the zip appended there) is refused with the reason: on first use it downloads Node.js
  and pyright's npm package, and it looks for a newer version on each start.
- **The project's configuration.** tsc runs as `tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit --pretty false --listFiles` in the
  folder of each target file's nearest `tsconfig.json` (at most 4 per check; a file with none above it in the
  repository is not compiled - tsc without the project's options would judge other code - and said so). The
  whole program is compiled; `--listFiles` says which files were in it. pyright (`--outputjson`) and mypy run from
  the repository root on the Python files being checked, each passed as `./path` (mypy also after `--`), so a file
  named like an option (`--python-executable=evil.py`) stays a file; the top folders, also as `./folder`, when the
  command line would pass 24,000 characters. `auto`: tsc for TypeScript and JavaScript; for Python the checker the
  project configures (`pyrightconfig.json` or `[tool.pyright]`; `mypy.ini`, `.mypy.ini`, `[tool.mypy]`, a
  `setup.cfg` `[mypy]` section), else the installed one, pyright first. The configuration used is named in each
  site and in the run's header.
- **Machine-readable output.** tsc's `file(line,col): error TSnnnn: message` lines with their indented
  continuation lines, its global `error TSnnnn:` lines and the `--listFiles` paths; pyright's JSON report
  (0-based lines and characters); mypy's `-O json` lines from 1.11 (decided from `mypy --version`), else the text
  form with `--show-column-numbers --show-error-codes --no-error-summary --no-pretty --no-color-output`. A mypy
  note is joined to the error before it on the same line; another note is left out, and a context line
  (`file: note: In function "f":`) is read as such. A line that is none of these is counted (`unparsed_lines`),
  never read as a diagnostic, and makes the check incomplete (exit 4 when nothing is absent): a diagnostic may be
  among them. tsc's stderr (Node's own warnings) is shown only when the run fails.
- **Sites.** Each error of the run on a file being checked, and with `--diff` on a changed line, becomes a site
  with `status` `observed`, `source` `checker` and `checker` {tool, version, config, code}; the message ends with
  the citation (`TS2339: Property 'sendd' does not exist on type 'Service'. (tsc 5.4.5, tsconfig.json)`). Kinds:
  `name`, `member`, `import`, `call`, `type`, by diagnostic code (tsc TS codes, mypy error codes, pyright rules)
  and by message when there is no code. Verdicts: a name, member or import the checker did not find is `absent`;
  a call or type that does not fit is the new verdict `mismatch`; both make the exit 3 (`status` `absent` or
  `mismatch`). An import is judged further: tsc's `TS2307` for a name a tsconfig `paths` pattern maps is `absent`
  when no file it maps to is there and `unknown` when one is; for any other bare name `unknown` when `baseUrl` is
  set (it may be the project's), else `not_installed`; mypy's `import-not-found` and pyright's
  `reportMissingImports` are `absent` when the top package is the project's and the module is not in it,
  `unknown` when the module is in the project (the checker's search path missed it), else `not_installed`; a
  module without types (`TS7016`, `import-untyped`, `reportMissingModuleSource`) is `unknown`. tsc's "Cannot find
  name 'require'. Do you need to install type definitions" (`TS2580`-`TS2593`) is `not_installed`, naming the
  `@types` package. A possibly-`None` receiver (`union-attr`, `reportOptionalMemberAccess`) and an attribute that
  is there but read-only ("Cannot assign to attribute") are `type`, so `mismatch`, never `absent`.
  `not_installed` and `unknown` sites do not make the exit 3, as for Verinoda's own. Only errors become sites;
  warnings and the errors outside the scope are counted in the run's header. At most 1,000 sites per run, the
  rest counted.
- **Syntax errors are no sites.** tsc's `TS1xxx` errors in a target file (anywhere in it) mean the file was not
  type-checked as written: it stays under `not_checked` and the check is incomplete, naming the line and code.
  mypy's exit 2 (a blocking error: a syntax error in any file it reads, a duplicate module) means it stopped
  before type-checking: the run is `failed`, its note quotes the blocking error, exit 4.
- **One site per finding.** A checker error of kind import, name or member on the line of Verinoda's own site
  of the same family (imports with imports, matched by the module spec - `./nope` - or the imported name; names
  and members by name) joins that site: the same verdict confirms it (`confirmed_by`, `tsc 5.4.5 TS2307`); a
  Verinoda `unknown` gives way to the checker's `absent` or `not_installed` (`own_verdict` keeps it); a different
  verdict leaves Verinoda's site with `checker_says` (`import yaml`: Verinoda's `not_installed`, the checker's
  `unknown`). Calls and types are never joined, nor a site Verinoda found to exist: the disagreement is listed.
- **What the compiler read is checked.** A TypeScript file in tsc's program leaves `not_checked` (it was imports
  only), unless it starts with `// @ts-nocheck`; a JavaScript file only with `// @ts-check` or `"checkJs": true`
  in its own tsconfig, read as JSON with comments (a commented-out `// "checkJs": true` is a comment; an
  `extends` chain is not followed). A file not in the program stays imports only, with a note.
- **Never a silent pass.** A checker that is not found, not run (trust, a launcher path), could not be started,
  ran past the timeout (the process tree is stopped: `taskkill /T` on Windows, the process group elsewhere),
  stopped on a blocking error, exited with a code it does not use for findings, or printed output that is not its
  report is a run with `status` `not_found`, `not_run`, `timeout` or `failed`, a note and a `next_step`, and the
  exit is 4 when nothing is absent. A tsc global error with no program (`TS18003 No inputs were found`) is a
  failure; with a program (`TS5083` a missing `extends` base) the run stands and the check is incomplete. A
  snippet (`--stdin`) is not on disk, so it is not given to a checker (exit 4, said).
- **Bounded.** Output goes to temporary files (a process the checker leaves behind cannot hold a pipe open); a
  stream that passes 16 MB stops the run and makes the check incomplete. A `.cmd`/`.bat` launcher is run by
  cmd.exe, which splits a command line at `&` and the like: when its path or an argument holds one of
  `" & | < > ^ % ! ( )` it is not started (`not_run`, with the reason).
- **Not cached.** A checker's answer depends on every file of its program and on its configuration; hashing
  those would cost about what the run does.
- **SARIF.** A checker's `absent` and `mismatch` sites carry the status `observed` (level error); its
  `not_installed` is `strong_inference` (warning) and `unknown` `unknown` (note), as for Verinoda's own.
- **Review round** (one reviewer, ten confirmed defects and five minor ones, all fixed with tests using fake
  checkers): programs of an untrusted repository were started (a `.venv` `mypy.cmd`; mypy `plugins` from the
  repository's `mypy.ini`) - now the trust gate above; repository file names were passed as options - now `./`
  and `--`; mypy's exit 2 counted as a complete run - now `failed`, and syntax errors (tsc `TS1xxx`, mypy
  `syntax`) are their own kind and never a `mismatch`; `checkJs` was found by a pattern that matched comments,
  and `@ts-nocheck` TypeScript files counted as checked - now JSON with comments and `@ts-nocheck` for every
  suffix; imports were listed twice (only `absent` was joined, by a dotted name that never matched `./nope`, kinds
  not compared) - now the joining above; `TS7016`, a `paths` alias, a project module, `union-attr`,
  `reportOptionalMemberAccess`, a read-only attribute and `TS2580` had the wrong verdicts - now as above; the help
  said a checker error makes the exit 3 while `not_installed` did not - the wording now names absent and
  mismatch; SARIF marked a checker's `not_installed` as an error; cmd.exe metacharacters in a launcher's path
  split its command line; `--checker-timeout inf` crashed and `nan` passed. Minor: `mismatch` sorts with `absent`;
  a tsc global error with a program makes the check incomplete; a runaway checker is stopped at 16 MB written,
  not only read; the PyPI wrapper test reads a bounded head and tail; mypy notes join only an error of their line.

### 125.3 Measured

No real tsc, pyright or mypy is installed on the machine this was built on, and nothing was installed for it,
so nothing was measured against a real checker. With the fake checkers of the tests (Windows, Python 3.13): a
`check --checker tsc` of two TypeScript files 0.9 s end to end (the fake answers at once; the time is the check
and starting the launcher twice, `--version` and the run); a checker told to sleep 60 s with
`--checker-timeout 1.5` stopped, and the check returned, in 2.1 s; the 39 tests of `tests/test_type_checkers.py`
27.3 s.

### 125.4 Not done

- CLI only: MCP `code_check` never runs a checker.
- In a trusted project the checker runs as configured: it, and the plugins its configuration names (mypy
  plugins; tsc loads no language-service plugins), run with the user's rights. In an untrusted one, pyright never
  runs, mypy only without `plugins`/`python_executable` in the repository's configuration files, and only checkers
  outside the repository; mypy also reads a user-level configuration, which is the user's.
- tsc compiles the whole program of each tsconfig, also for a `--diff` of one line; a solution-style tsconfig
  (`files: []` with `references`) holds no file, so its files stay imports only (`tsc -b` is not run). At most 4
  tsconfig files per check.
- tsc may write a `.tsbuildinfo` when the tsconfig asks for incremental builds; mypy writes its usual cache.
- pyright's PyPI wrapper is not started; basedpyright and other checkers are not run.
- pyright and mypy are given the files being checked: a configuration that lists other files or excludes these
  is overridden as each tool does for files on its command line. pyright is given `./path` rather than `--`
  (whether its CLI takes `--` could not be checked here).
- Classification of a diagnostic into name, member, call, import, type or syntax is a table of codes and message
  patterns; an unknown code is `type` (verdict `mismatch`). The name is read from the message's quotes and can be
  empty. A `paths` alias or `baseUrl` is read from the target's own tsconfig (no `extends`). pyright's syntax
  errors have no rule and are not told apart.
- The parsers are tested against output written in the tools' documented formats (tsc 5.x `--pretty false`,
  pyright's `--outputjson`, mypy's text form and its 1.11 `-O json`), not against output captured from real runs:
  no checker was available here. A release that changes its format is a `failed` run or unparsed lines, never a
  pass.

### 125.5 Tests

`tests/test_type_checkers.py` (39 tests, fake checkers written by the test - a Python script behind a `.cmd`
launcher on Windows - in `node_modules/.bin`, a virtual environment or on PATH): tsc member and call errors
(TS2339, TS2554, TS2345) as sites with tool, version, config and code, the compiled file leaving `not_checked`, an
error in a file out of scope and a warning not listed; the CLI text and SARIF; `--diff` keeping only the changed
line; tsc not installed and no tsconfig (exit 4, next step); a timeout stopping the checker; malformed tsc output
and a tsc configuration error as failures; pyright JSON and malformed JSON; mypy JSON (1.11) and text (1.5),
chosen by `auto` from `mypy.ini` over an installed pyright; mypy not found; a mypy error confirming Verinoda's own
absent site; a snippet not given to a checker; output lines not understood; pyright's PyPI wrapper refused; the
parsers and classification; CLI argument errors. Review round: an untrusted project's `node_modules` tsc and
`.venv` mypy never started (a marker file), mypy with `plugins` and pyright refused there and a PATH mypy without
them run; a file named `--python-executable=evil.py` passed after `--` as `./...`; mypy's blocking error a failed
run; a tsc syntax error leaving its file unchecked; `checkJs` in comments, `checkJs: false` and `@ts-nocheck`; one
site per TypeScript and Python import finding; the verdicts of `TS7016`, a `paths` alias, `baseUrl`, `TS2580`, a
project module, `union-attr`, `reportOptionalMemberAccess` and a read-only attribute; a checker `not_installed`
not making the exit 3; the SARIF levels; `&` in a launcher's path (Windows); `--checker-timeout` inf, nan, 0, -1;
the sort order, mypy context lines and notes, the bounded wrapper read; a tsc global error with a program; a
runaway checker stopped at the output cap.

## 126. Runtime diff between base and head (D153, 2026-10-01)

### 126.1 Why

`review --observe` ran the selected tests once, on the working tree, and said which changed functions they
reached. What the change did at run time was left to the reader: a query that now runs in a loop, a library call
the code did not make before, an exception type that changed, a route no longer reached. AppMap compares two
recorded runs for this; Verinoda had the recordings (the call tracer, D28; SQL and stacks, D147) but only ever
one run.

### 126.2 Decisions

- `observe(ref=...)` runs the tests on the files of a commit: the experiment runner's commit copy (`git cat-file`,
  the user's tree and index untouched), the same isolation and policy as any run. A run of a commit is filed
  under no snapshot and does not update the test map (it describes the working tree's tests); its edge flags and
  the flaws' loop search read that commit's files (`_Sources(commit=)`), and its header names `ref` and the traced
  files that differ from the working tree. Graph nodes are still the working tree's graph.
- New module `runtime/rundiff.py`. `observe_pair` runs the head (or takes a head run already made), then the same
  test ids at the base, leaving out ids whose file does not exist there (`tests_new_in_head`); `compare` reads
  the two stored runs. Keys leave lines out, so a function that moved inside its file is not a change:
  - calls: (caller file, caller qualified name, callee file, callee qualified name), calls into test code left
    out;
  - library calls: (project caller, the library callable's name), callers in test code left out;
  - SQL: the normalised statement (D147), its executions summed; a statement in both runs is "changed" when its
    larger count is at least 1.5 times the smaller and they differ by at least 3; the N+1 groups of each run are compared by statement;
  - routes: the current code's route table (`verinoda routes`, D146) mapped to the handlers each run reached;
  - exceptions: (file, qualified name, exception type) of raises in project code;
  - test outcomes: the phase outcome and the exception that ended a failed phase.
- The call tracer records raises: a `RAISE` callback (`sys.monitoring`; it cannot be disabled per code object, so
  every raise reaches it - once in each frame the exception passes through - and only the project frame where it
  starts is kept: the one whose traceback has no further entry), at most 5,000 distinct (site, type), written as
  `raise` records and kept in the run's header (2,000 project sites, test code left out, most hit first). A `pytest_runtest_makereport` wrapper records the
  type of a failed phase's exception and the innermost project frame it passed through. The setprofile tracer
  (Python < 3.12) records no raises: the comparison says so instead of reporting none.
- Statuses: an item is `observed` - present in one run, absent from the other run of the same tests - only when
  the run it is absent from is complete; otherwise `unknown` (that run may have made it). An item made only by
  tests the other run did not have is marked `new_tests_only`. Nothing says what always happens; a flaky test can
  make a difference, which the limits say.
- Review round: a selected test new in a file the base already had made the base run collect nothing (pytest exit
  4) and every head item `unknown`; a test id is now checked at the base by its class and function names (a
  parametrize suffix is not), and a comparison where no test ran in both runs is an error. The RAISE callback named
  every frame an exception passed through as raising it; only the frame where it starts is kept now. A test that
  failed the same way in both runs was a change when the exception's line moved: outcomes compare type, file and
  function. N+1 groups that appeared or went count in `changed`. `observe --compare` ran the base with the default
  tracer mode and thresholds: both runs now take the same. The base run, filed after the head, became "the latest
  run" that a later `review` reads as the working tree's: runs of another commit are left out of that query
  (`trace.latest_run`, review's observed tests). A raise list cut at its cap (or with sites dropped by the
  plugin) makes the exceptions missing from that run `unknown`. Minor: SQL items sort by executions, the raise
  line is cached per (code, offset), `observe --compare` exits 3 when the comparison failed, the test line shows
  both sides' exceptions, `review` catches any failure of the comparison.
- `review --observe` traces with the flaws recorder and, when the review has a base commit (not a planned change),
  adds `tests.observe.runtime_diff`; the text lists it under the observe line. `observe --compare REF` does the
  same from the command line. A ref that names no commit, a base run that fails, or a run that was not recorded
  is an `error` in the block, never a crash of `review`. No MCP change: the tool count stays 40.

### 126.3 Measured

Windows 11, Python 3.13.

- The end-to-end fixture (a sqlite project, 3 tests, the head with an N+1 replaced by one query, a new call and
  library call, a changed exception type): both runs and the comparison in about 6-7 s (the module fixture of
  `tests/test_runtime_diff.py`; the whole file, 14 tests with a `review --observe`, 25-29 s).
- The raise hook, the same project and plugin otherwise: a test raising and catching `ValueError` in project
  code 200,000 times took 0.80 s with the previous tracer and 1.32 s with this one (median of 5), about 2.6 us per
  raise; a test with no raise took 0.020 s with both. Raises in library code reach the callback too and are
  dropped after one dictionary lookup (not measured separately).

### 126.4 Not done

- One run of each side: a flaky test or nondeterministic code makes differences that the change did not cause.
- Calls are matched by file and qualified name: a function that moved to another file or was renamed shows as
  removed and added. Lambdas and comprehensions are matched by their `<lambda>`/`<genexpr>` names.
- Graph nodes and routes come from the current code: a route only the base served is not named.
- Raises are recorded with `sys.monitoring` only (Python 3.12+); child processes are not traced, as before.
- `review --observe` now runs the selected tests twice (base and head) and with the SQL recorder: about twice the
  time it took.
- Library calls are recorded once per call site (D28): a library call made from a new site in a function that
  already made it elsewhere is a change of site, not counted twice.

### 126.5 Tests

`tests/test_runtime_diff.py` (17): a sqlite project committed as the base and edited in the working tree, traced
at both: both runs complete and compared, a call added (`check -> audit`) and removed (`total -> price`), a
library call added (`json.dumps`), the per-id SELECT removed with its 6 executions and site and its N+1 gone, the
`SUM ... IN` statement added, `KeyError` raised instead of `ValueError` (3.12+), a test going from passed to
failed with the head's exception and site, the base run's header (ref, commit, files that differ) and no test-map
update, an incomplete base run turning the head-only items to `unknown` while the base-only ones stay observed,
routes mapped through a route table, the text, a ref that names no commit, `review --observe --json` and text,
and `observe --compare`; review round: a test new in an existing file left out at the base, an exception only
passed through (`outer`) not reported, a moved exception line not a change, the base run never the latest run, a
cut raise list making absences `unknown`, the N+1 counted in `changed`. The existing `test_runtime_trace.py` (19), `test_runtime_flaws.py` (50),
`test_trace_import.py` (12), `test_review.py` (109) and `test_testmap.py` pass.

## 127. Taint analysis (D154, 2026-10-01)

### 127.1 Why

`slice` (D150) answers where one line's values come from. The question security review asks is the reverse and
across the whole project: can a value a user sends reach a SQL string, a shell, `eval` or a file path without a
check, and along which path? CodeQL, Semgrep Pro, Pysa, Joern and Code Pathfinder answer it with sources, sinks
and sanitizers declared as data and every result shown with its path. Verinoda had the data dependence (reaching
definitions per function, callers through the index) but no notion of untrusted input.

### 127.2 Decisions

- New command `verinoda taint [PATH ...] [--local] [--depth N] [--no-builtin] [--tests] [--json] [--sarif]`, module
  `taint.py`, Python only. Exit 3 when a path is found, 0 when none, 2 on an error (bad rules, a path outside the
  project, a depth outside 0-3). No MCP tool: the core menu keeps its five.
- Library behaviour is data, `verinoda/data/taint_python.json`: 23 sources (Flask, Django, Starlette/FastAPI
  request data; `input()`, `sys.argv`, `os.environ`, `os.getenv()`), 30 sinks with the argument that matters by
  position and by keyword and a kind (sql, command, code, deserialization, path, template, xss, redirect, request),
  10 sanitizers, each for every kind of sink (`int()`, `float()`, `uuid.UUID()` ...) or for some (`shlex.quote()`
  for command, `html.escape()` for template and xss, `secure_filename()` for path). A pattern `a.b` matches a name or
  attribute chain ending in `.a.b`, `a.b()` a call of it, `*.m` any receiver's method; a sanitizer is always a call.
  A sink may hold only with a keyword (`subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`; `shell=False` or no `shell` is not a sink)
  or not with a keyword's value (`yaml.load(s, Loader=SafeLoader)`). The project adds its own in
  `[taint]` of `verinoda.toml` (or `[tool.verinoda.taint]` of `pyproject.toml`) - committed, so CI sees them - or
  replaces the library's with `builtin = false`; a malformed table is an error, never ignored.
- Threats: each library source is `remote` (request data) or `local` (argv, the environment, `input()`). Only remote
  ones are used unless `--local`, as CodeQL's default threat model: on Verinoda's own code every path found with
  `--local` starts at the user's environment (a cache folder, an artifacts folder reaching `open()`, one SQL
  statement built from a table name), which is the design of a command-line tool. The project's own sources are
  always used.
- Route handler parameters taken from the request are sources: `<name>` in a Flask path (not with an `int`, `float`
  or `uuid` converter, which the framework parses), `{name}` in a FastAPI/Starlette path, and for a FastAPI-style
  `@x.get/post/put/patch/delete` handler a parameter annotated `str`, `bytes` or `Any` (or not annotated) without a
  `Depends(...)` default.
- The search runs backward from each sink argument over data dependence only: `slicing.CFG` and its reaching
  definitions (the control dependence a slice also computes is not built). For a definition, only the part of a
  tuple assignment that defines the name is followed (`a, b = src, "c"`: `b` is clean); an update (`x.a = v`,
  `items.append(v)`) carries what the object held before too; names inside a sanitizer call are not followed. At a
  parameter: a route source, else the argument each caller passes (calls edges, at most 8 callers, `--depth`
  calls up, default 2; `*args`/`**kwargs` that may carry it is a note). At a call of a project function (by the
  calls edge at that line, else the one function of that name in the file): what its `return` statements are made
  of, two levels down, memoised per function. A library call's result is taken to depend on its arguments.
- Review round: a function called twice by one caller was followed at the index edge's line only (one edge per
  caller): every call of it in the calling function is followed now. A default was stepped and searched in the
  caller's file: it is read in the function's own file and scope. Library sinks matched only a positional
  argument: each names its keyword too (`requests.get(url=...)`, `subprocess.run(args=..., shell=True)`), and a
  sink whose argument is missing no longer hides the next one of the same name (the project's sinks are tried
  first). A sanitizer written without `()` matched nothing: a sanitizer is always a call. Unknown keys and wrong
  types in `[taint]` are errors (`sanitisers`, `agr`, `when_keyword = 1`). Sanitizers cleared a value for every
  sink: they name the kinds they clear, and the bare `escape()` (which matched `re.escape`) is gone. FastAPI
  parameters: `X | None`, `Optional`, `Annotated[..., Depends()]`, `Security()` and typed path parameters
  (`item_id: int`) are read. Module-level code is one more flow, a closure's free name is followed into the
  function around it, and a comprehension variable into its iterable. What a definition is made of is kept per
  run (a 1,200-statement function with 299 sinks: 33 s before, 2.3 s after). A path that does not exist is an
  error (exit 2) and `taint .` means the working directory. A source in the sink's own argument no longer hides
  the others reaching it.
- Each finding is `strong_inference` with `rule` `taint/<kind>`, the sink (call, match, kind, origin), the source
  (match, kind, origin: the library, `verinoda.toml [taint]` or the route) and the path source first, every step at
  `file:line` with its line and what happens there (`source request.args -> who`, `passes who as name of
  find_user (EXTRACTED call edge)`, `defines q`, `get_cmd returns it`, `sink *.execute (sql)`) and the number of
  hops between functions. One finding per source site and sink. `--sarif` writes one SARIF result per path at the
  sink with its steps as a `codeFlows` thread flow (a `warning`), through `sarif.from_taint`.
- Cost: each file is parsed once with its functions and the calls on each line, and each function's graph is
  built once per run; a search visits at most 20,000 states per sink and a function over `slicing.MAX_NODES`
  statements is a note (a source in the sink's own argument is still found).

### 127.3 Measured

Windows 11, Python 3.13, Verinoda's own checkout (indexed), the analysis without the graph load (1.6 s):

- 369 Python files (tests left out), 329 sink calls: 36.6 s with remote sources (no path found: Verinoda serves no
  Flask/FastAPI routes), 37.5 s with `--local` (21 paths: 20 `taint/path`, 1 `taint/sql`, all from `os.environ`;
  12 before the review round, which added module-level code and closures). Before the files and functions were
  indexed once per run (each lookup walked the whole tree) and the control dependence was left out, the first
  version took 249.9 s.
- One function of 1,200 statements with 299 `os.system` sinks and no source: 2.3 s (33 s before what a definition
  is made of was kept per run).
- The longest path found has 18 steps (an environment value through `experiments.run`'s result dictionary into a
  trace file's path, in a copy of Verinoda kept under `benchmarks/corpora`): the dictionary is one value to this
  analysis, so the path is real data dependence but not a real flow - the heap approximation the limits name.
- `tests/test_taint.py`: 41 tests in about 11 s.

### 127.4 Not done

- Python only; data dependence only (a branch on a tainted value is an implicit flow and is not followed).
- The heap is approximated: an attribute or item update taints its object, a dictionary or list is one value (a
  lookup in an allow-list keyed by the input is reported), and aliasing and globals changed elsewhere are not
  seen. A closure's free name is read where the inner function is defined, a global where the function is.
- Statements in a class body outside methods are not analysed one by one.
- A library call's result depends on its arguments; a project function's result is followed into its `return`s
  (two levels), not through its own parameters from that call site.
- Callers come from the index's calls edges (INFERRED ones are a resolver's guess) and are matched by name; at
  most 8 per parameter. Without an index callers are not followed and calls are resolved in their own file only.
- Sources, sinks and sanitizers are names: a sink reached through a variable, `functools.partial` or a wrapper is
  not seen, and a check written as an `if` (not a sanitizer call) does not clear a value.
- A path found is not proof of a vulnerability; no path found is not proof of safety.

### 127.5 Tests

`tests/test_taint.py` (41): a scanned Flask/FastAPI project: a source reaching an SQL sink through a caller with
every step in order, no caller hop without an index, sanitizers (`int()`, `shlex.quote()`) stopping the path, a
Flask route parameter as a source and an `<int:...>` one not, a value returned by a project function, a
`subprocess.run` without `shell=True` not a sink, a source in the sink's own argument, only the tuple part that
defines the name, an `append` carrying the taint, a FastAPI query parameter as a source and a `Depends` one not,
the counts and rules of a run, local sources only with `local`, the project's own `[taint]` rules and
`builtin = false`, ten malformed rule tables, the CLI's text, JSON, SARIF code flows and exit codes (3, 0, 2), a
function over the size limit giving a note; review round: every call in a caller, a default read in the callee's
file, keyword arguments to library sinks, sanitizers clearing their own kinds only, comprehension variables (at a
sink and at a call site), a closure and module-level code, a safe `Loader=` keyword, two sources into one sink,
project sinks before the library's and sanitizers as calls, six FastAPI parameter forms, typed path parameters,
and the CLI's missing path and `.` in a sub-folder.

## 128. Code query language (D155, 2026-10-01)

### 128.1 Why

CodeQL, Glean's Angle, jQAssistant's Cypher, NDepend's CQLinq and Joern let a user ask a question the tool's
authors did not foresee: "functions that write storage and are reachable from an HTTP handler". Verinoda had
fixed views over the graph (`trace` between two named symbols, `map`, `dsm`, `butterfly`, `routes`) and
`inventory`, whose condition language counts search hits but knows nothing about edges. A question that combines
kinds of nodes, a path of bounded length, a condition on a definition's text and an absence of an edge had to be
answered by chaining commands by hand, and nothing cited the evidence of the whole answer. Done when: a query such
as "functions that write storage and are reachable from an HTTP handler" returns its sites.

### 128.2 Decisions

- **New command `verinoda q "QUERY" [--max-rows N] [--max-expansions N] [--timeout S] [--verify] [--json]`**
  (module `verinoda/graphquery.py`). The name `query` is taken by the ranked retrieval, so the command is `q`. CLI
  only: no MCP tool is added (the count stays 40) and none goes behind `run_tool`, so the core menu is unchanged.
  Exit 0 with rows, 1 with none, 2 on a bad query, 3 when a budget cut the answer.
- **A small Cypher-like language, nothing more.** `MATCH pattern (',' pattern)* [WHERE cond] [RETURN items]
  [LIMIT n]` (the leading `MATCH` may be left out). A node is `(var:kind|kind)`; the kinds are `file`, `symbol`
  (any code symbol), `function` (functions and methods), `method`, `class`, `handler` (a handler in the HTTP route
  table, the table of `verinoda routes`), `test` (code in a test file, `testcode.is_test_file`) and `section` (a
  heading of a document). An edge is `-[rel|rel*lo..hi]->`, `<-[...]-` or `-[...]-` (either way); no relation
  means any; a length is at most 10 (`*` alone is `1..5`, `*2` exactly two, `*..4` is `1..4`, `*0..1` includes the
  start). Patterns separated by commas join on shared variables. `WHERE` compares `var.field` with a string, a whole
  number or another `var.field`: `name` (the bare name), `label`, `file`, `id` by `=`, `!=`, `~` (a Python regular
  expression, searched, at most 300 characters) and `glob`; `line` by `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`; `text` (the
  lines of the node's definition, nested definitions included; a file node's whole file) by `~` only; with `and`,
  `or`, `not`, parentheses and `exists (pattern)`. `RETURN` lists variables, `var.field` and `count(var)` (distinct
  nodes) or `count(*)` (bindings), grouped by the other items; without `RETURN` every named variable is returned.
  Keywords are read in any case. Edge variables, `OPTIONAL MATCH`, `ORDER BY`, `UNION`, sums and arithmetic are
  not in the language: each is a way to write a program, and the point is a query whose every answer can cite its
  lines.
- **Parsed by hand, checked before it runs.** A tokenizer that keeps each token's offset and a recursive-descent
  parser; no `eval`, no `ast` of Python, nothing of the query is ever executed (a regular expression is compiled by
  `re`). Before evaluation the tree is checked: every variable of `WHERE` and `RETURN` is bound by `MATCH` (a
  variable new in an `exists` pattern is existential and cannot be named outside it), the field fits its operator
  (`text` only with `~`, `line` only with numbers), each regular expression compiles, a relation is one the graph
  has or one Verinoda makes (a known relation with no edge is answered with no row and a note; an unknown one is
  refused with the relations the graph has), a node pattern has at most 12 nodes, a query at most 8 patterns and
  4,000 characters, a condition at most 30 parentheses and NOTs deep. An error is `QueryError` with the offset; its text names the
  line (for a query of several lines) and the column and draws a caret under the place (`--json`: `position`).
  Unnamed nodes get names the query cannot spell (`#1`), so `(_1)` is the user's own variable.
- **Evaluation.** Over the loaded graph (`index.load`: the receiver, Java and cross-service edges included). The
  `WHERE` conjuncts that read one variable are pushed to it and checked when it is bound (cached per node), the
  others after the patterns matched; a condition's witnesses (the edges of an `exists`, the absence of a
  `not exists`) are kept only from the branches that made it true. Each pattern is walked from its bound end, else from the end with fewer
